papers.title: VLM-based multi-agent architecture for multifunctional robotic health attendant (RHA) using phase-prompt task design
papers.authors: Kyungki Kim, John R. Windle, Tom Windle, Melissa Christian, Christian Haas, ...
papers.abstract: Introduction Healthcare robots are increasingly needed to support clinicians whose work involves diverse tasks and frequent task switching. However, most healthcare robots developed to assist clinicians either perform a single function or implement multiple functions as fixed task pipelines that are difficult to adapt to different patients, rooms, or care teams. This study presents a vision language model (VLM) based multiagent architecture for a multifunctional Robotic Health Attendant (RHA). Methods In this architecture, each task can be designed by writing natural language phase specifications that describe how available tools should be used during task execution. A main agent interprets natural language requests from clinicians or patients and routes each request to the appropriate task agent. During execution, the VLM uses language, visual input, and contextual information to select tools and interpret their results. A shared Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool layer provides elemental robot functions such as navigation, manipulation, and perception across tasks. The architecture was implemented on a TIAGo Pro robot and evaluated in an unoccupied patient room across five tasks including object delivery, documentation, visual monitoring, patient education, and medication reminders. Results The case study demonstrated the feasibility of the proposed architecture as a reasoning core for a multifunctional healthcare robot by executing multiple tasks and adapting task behavior by editing natural language phase specifications. The comparison across three VLMs showed that longer tool-call sequences led to skipped steps and, in some cases, false reports of task success, which is a key reliability concern for healthcare robots performing long, multi-step tasks. Discussion The study also identified technical limitations and future research needs that must be addressed to make the architecture more robust in realistic care settings.

papers.title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
papers.authors: Gokul Gowri, Nic Fishman, William N. Colgan, Minming Wang, Yusuke Kijima...
papers.abstract: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

papers.title: Virtual brain models: a roadmap towards effective brain digital twins
papers.authors: Egidio Ugo D'Angelo, Claudia A. M. Gandini Wheeler‐Kingshott, Alain Destexhe A, Viktor Jirsa
papers.abstract: Virtual Brain Models (VBMs) are emerging computational tools promising to revolutionize personalised and precision medicine. VBMs reproduce brain functional dynamics through a generative model that can be constructed and optimized against single subject data, thereby generating what is called a brain digital twin (BDT). VBMs can provide critical information about parameters of network functioning and connectivity but this ability depends on their design, raising some fundamental questions. Can VBM parameters identify key physiological features of the brain otherwise not accessible? Are VBM parameters correlated with sensorimotor and cognitive functions? What is still needed to make a VBM more precise in its physiological mechanisms? Simulations in patients affected by neurological diseases are indeed showing that VBMs can operate as effective BDTs capturing essential aspects of the physiopathology of single patients along with relevant physio-psychological correlations. However, the current VBM theory and technology still pose some limitations. We maintain that the evolution of VBM holds the key for a deeper understanding of brain physiology and pathology fostering the development of powerful computational tools capable of supporting personalized clinical decision making. Here, we will consider a roadmap addressing what VBM already do well, why this is not enough, what must change, and what becomes possible if it does.

papers.title: Advances in early human embryonic development and organogenesis from spatiotemporal multi-omics
papers.authors: Hanlin Zhu, Xiaolong Yang, Xinyuan Wang, Zhenyu Xiao
papers.abstract: Deciphering early human embryonic development and organogenesis is constrained by limited access to in vivo specimens and the intrinsic complexity of spatiotemporal cell fate dynamics. Recent advances in spatiotemporal multi-omics have begun to overcome these barriers by enabling the reconstruction of in silico human embryos and developmental trajectories with spatial and temporal resolution. These approaches have revealed fundamental principles of lineage specification, cell migration, tissue morphogenesis, and axial patterning in early human development. In this Review, we summarize how single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies, particularly spatial transcriptomics, have transformed the study of human early embryogenesis, organogenesis, and stem-cell-derived embryoid systems. We highlight analytical frameworks that integrate spatial context, temporal progression, and multimodal datasets, and discuss how biological discovery and algorithmic innovation have co-evolved. Finally, we outline how artificial intelligence, foundation models, and large-scale multimodal learning may eventually enable predictive and causal modeling of human development, while addressing current technical, interpretability, and ethical challenges.
papers.venue: Journal of Translational Genetics and Genomics

papers.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
papers.authors: Qiyao Ma, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Chengquan Guo...
papers.abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.

papers.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
papers.authors: Yifu Luo, Chuang Ma, Zeyu Chen, Enkelejda Kasneci, Qi Chen...
papers.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

papers.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
papers.authors: Max Neuwinger, Hanna Yukhymenko, Imanol Schlag
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

papers.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
papers.authors: Zach Paris, Emily Finn
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

papers.title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
papers.authors: Jingru Fan, Tianle Zhou, Yunjie Zhou, Zihao He, Yixuan Zhou...
papers.abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

papers.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
papers.authors: Qiushi Sun, Da Yu, Alexander Knop, Amer Sinha, Lingpeng Kong...
papers.abstract: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

papers.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
papers.authors: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu...
papers.abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for Traditional Chinese Medicine classic formula development: a technology readiness assessment using metabolic syndrome as a case study
papers.authors: Zihao Huang, Zhenhong Jiang, Shaowen Hu, Ning Ye, Xingteng Liu, ...
papers.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas, developed through millennia of clinical practice, represent a rich legacy of approximately 100,000 documented prescriptions (99,584 named formula entries in the second edition of the Dictionary of Traditional Chinese Medicine Formulas), yet on average fewer than ten new TCM products were approved annually by China’s NMPA from 2013 to 2024 (77 approvals in total). The experience-based screening paradigm is misaligned with the precision medicine framework demanded by metabolic syndrome (MetS), a multi-target disorder affecting an estimated 1.54 billion adults (95% CrI 1.35–1.76) in 2023. Although artificial intelligence (AI)—encompassing knowledge graphs (KGs), large language models (LLMs), and high-throughput experimentation—has been proposed as a solution, its actual readiness for TCM development remains unclear. This review critically examines KG, LLM, and high-throughput validation technologies enabling precision phytomedicine for MetS, providing a realistic roadmap for AI-driven TCM research and development. The three technology streams exhibit asymmetric readiness. At the stream level, knowledge-graph approaches span Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3–6, large language model approaches span TRL 1–5, and high-throughput validation platforms span TRL 3–5. LLM development is limited by three TCM-specific hallucination types that lack evaluation benchmarks. KG entity recognition is the most mature component, yet reasoning is hindered by the absence of negative data, missing dose–time dimensions, and unencoded monarch–minister–assistant–envoy hierarchies. High-throughput platforms are technically feasible but remain mismatched to MetS functional endpoints—tumor-derived organoid paradigms show limited direct transferability and would require substantial adaptation. Precision phytomedicine must follow a “foundations before algorithms” sequence: institutionalize negative data, build TCM-Hallu benchmarks, establish functional-endpoint evaluation, and develop AI-assisted regulatory review. Algorithmic advances will remain in an incomplete information space until knowledge infrastructure gaps are closed.

papers.title: A Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD) pipeline via DRUG-GAN: A multiscale method for drug-like/target-specific compound library generation
papers.authors: Beihong Ji, Matthew Brock, Yuhui Wu, Yuemin Bian, Xibing He, ...
papers.abstract: We present the Full-Spectrum Generative Lead Discovery (FSGLD), a deep learning-driven pipeline for efficient drug lead identification. FSGLD integrates generative modeling with molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, ligand-residue interaction profile, MM-PBSA, thermodynamic integration (TI), and experimental validation to bridge theoretical design and practical application. The core multiscale DRUG-GAN models enable generative model-guided discovery of drug-like and target-specific compounds across three scenarios: (i) generation of random drug-like compounds, (ii) generation of target-specific compounds, and (iii) generation of target-specific compound series featuring shared chemical structures. In our assessment across three pharmacologically distinct target classes, FSGLD demonstrates encouraging performance in identifying target-specific candidate compounds. In addition, a computational protocol for TI calculations was established to reduce computation time by 80 to 90% while maintaining accuracy. By integrating generative models with in silico and in vitro evaluation techniques, FSGLD reduces the cost of identifying previously uncharacterized yet viable lead compounds, offering remarkable benefits to both academic and industry.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in gut-brain axis research for Alzheimer’s disease: From associative insights toward causal inference and personalized interventions
papers.authors: Yan Gao, Can Zhang, Zhi-Wen Zhou, Hong-Shuo Sun, Zhong-Ping Feng, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research is shifting from a “brain-centered” model toward a “gut-brain axis system” perspective. However, the causal roles of gut microbiota in AD pathology remain elusive, as traditional association studies struggle to distinguish potential drivers from passengers. This review examines the potential applications and inherent limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in dissecting this complex relationship. We discuss three emerging and conceptually promising directions: First, AI-frameworks for hypothesis-generating causal discovery that can prioritize microbiota-AD relationships for subsequent experimental validation, while recognizing that current approaches predominantly identify statistical associations rather than empirically supported causal conclusions; second, multi-modal fusion networks, when applied with appropriate regularization and validation, can assist in constructing cross-scale molecular maps across microbiota, metabolites, and the brain, though such pathway inferences require careful interpretation as they represent statistical associations rather than biochemically validated mechanisms; and third, the conceptual application of digital twin-based simulation as a long-term vision for personalized microbiota modulation, which currently lacks the ecological resolution and validation required for predictive modeling. By integrating multi-pathway mechanisms of the gut-brain axis and characteristic profiles of gut microbiota, we critically evaluate the technical advantages of machine learning in microbiome data analysis alongside major challenges including overfitting, batch effects, confounding factors, and reproducibility. Leveraging AI-driven microbiota analysis, we propose a phased translational roadmap, from near-term standardization and cross-cohort validation, through mid-term endophenotyping and trial enrichment strategies, to the long-term exploration of personalized interventions, toward the eventual goal of precision prevention. This article outlines a full-cycle framework from discovery to clinical translation and envisions a conceptual ecosystem for future intelligent microecological health management. Achieving the promise of AI-empowered gut-brain axis research will require deep integration across neuroscience, microbiology, computational science, and clinical medicine, alongside rigorous experimental validation, standardized protocols, and realistic appraisal of current technological boundaries.

papers.title: Human-AI collaborative generative AI for comfortable care: a doctor–patient–AI feedback loop for pre-operative distress and workforce shortages
papers.authors: Hui Sun, Yan Luan, Bo Song
papers.abstract: Psychological screening is easily displaced by physiological safety checks when preoperative teams have little time and too few staff. Healthcare systems are already affected by widespread workforce shortages and clinician burnout. We suggest that preoperative anxiety consequently often remains unmanaged, with implications for postoperative recovery and hospital workload. Generic educational materials do not adequately address differences in patients’ anxiety, and “health data poverty” can further exclude vulnerable groups. We propose a conceptual human-machine collaborative (HMC) generative artificial intelligence framework to address these clinical and occupational problems together. In the proposed doctor–patient–AI feedback loop, natural language processing would dynamically assess psychosocial risk and guide patient-specific, multimodal education, including dialect-adapted voice agents, as a source of baseline emotional support. Routine interactions would be automated under clinician supervision. Our hypothesis is that this arrangement may conserve clinicians’ limited emotional bandwidth and allow healthier “cognitive reappraisal” in place of chronic fatigue. Implementation science provides a basis for considering how lightweight AI models could be scaled across regional health networks to bring standardized psychoeducation to under-resourced rural areas. This remains a theoretical pathway. Through sociotechnical governance and “data solidarity” to fairly manage algorithmic liability, the framework is still a conceptual framework, but it is operational: it proposes a path to improve perioperative workflows and health equity in the face of severe human resource constraints.

papers.title: LEAF: benchmarking multiobjective evolutionary feature selection over large language model–extracted symptoms for interpretable Traditional Chinese Medicine respiratory syndrome differentiation
papers.authors: Luo Xuanhang, Huan Ding, Xize Zhang, Binhuan Miao, Li Shi
papers.abstract: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds. These results show that an LLM-extraction frontend built exclusively from public knowledge can provide a representation over which evolutionary feature selection cuts the candidate feature set roughly in half without a statistically detectable cost in performance, albeit at a small point-estimate cost; that hypervolume and inverted generational distance are not reliable stand-ins for classification-relevant algorithm selection here; and that a no-gold-standard proxy evaluation can substitute human annotation when expert time is limited. Because both stages plug in and out freely, the framework can absorb stronger components in either stage as they become available.

papers.title: NOS2 as a candidate molecular link between air pollutants and depression: an integrated computational and experimental study
papers.authors: Huizheng Zhu, Bei Yin, Jingning Du, Siwei Zhang, Liyuan Su, ...
papers.abstract: Introduction Studies exploring the molecules and potential mechanisms linking air pollution exposure to depression remain scarce. This study aimed to elucidate the potential regulatory molecules and possible mechanisms associated with air pollutants and depression, thereby providing scientific clues for disease prevention and treatment. Methods Seven air pollutants (SO 2 , NO, benzene, CO, O 3 , NO 2 , and toluene) were included. A multilevel research framework was employed. Network toxicology and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were used to identify potential targets and pathways of air pollutants; intersection genes were used to construct machine learning diagnostic models, and the optimal model was selected for validation. Mendelian randomization (MR) was applied to assess the genetic causal association between depression and relevant genes. Single-cell virtual perturbation was performed for network perturbation analysis to dissect potential molecular mechanisms. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used to evaluate the binding affinity and complex stability between specific pollutants and depression-related genes. Finally, in vitro cell experiments were conducted to preliminarily validate the computational findings. Results By intersecting air pollution-related targets with the Gene Expression Omnibus depression dataset, nine candidate target genes were identified. Ensemble machine learning analysis suggested that nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2) showed expression in depression. Mendelian randomization analysis suggested that elevated NOS2 expression may be associated with depression, supporting a possible genetic causal association between the two. Single-cell virtual perturbation suggested that perturbing NOS2 in microglia could affect inflammation- and oxidative stress-related pathways. Molecular docking predicted that all seven pollutants might bind to NOS2, but the predicted binding energies varied, with benzene and toluene showing relatively higher binding affinity. Molecular dynamics simulations further evaluated the stability of the benzene–and toluene–NOS2 complexes, suggesting that toluene binding to NOS2 was more stable. In vitro cell experiments preliminarily suggested that toluene exposure could induce inflammation and oxidative stress in BV2 cells, and changes in NOS2 expression may be involved in this process. However, these results cannot yet prove that NOS2 is a causal mediator of depression, and further functional experiments are needed for validation. Discussion Integrating computational prediction, genetic association, network perturbation, and cellular validation, NOS2 may be a candidate molecular node linking air pollution exposure to depression, and its potential mechanism may involve neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. This study provides new hypotheses and theoretical clues for the possible molecular mechanisms linking air pollutants and depression, but the underlying mechanisms still require further experimental investigation.
papers.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology

papers.title: Cyberlogic-enabled Thinking Space: a closed-loop human-cyber cognitive architecture in CPST
papers.authors: Ruizi Chen, Lei Zhou, Jianguo Ding, Huansheng Ning
papers.abstract: Human–AI collaboration in Cyber–Physical–Social–Thinking (CPST) environments requires coordination among perception, reasoning, human judgment, and governance. This paper proposes Cyberlogic-enabled Thinking Space (CyTS), a conceptual governance-centric architecture organized through Entity, Mapping, Reasoning, and Governance layers. Its closed loop connects multimodal representation, heterogeneous reasoning, collaborative decisions, and controlled adaptation. The Entity layer provides operational descriptions rather than a sufficient ontology of cognition; logical consistency and predictive accuracy do not by themselves establish the causal validity of an action. CyTS therefore distinguishes associative, deductive, interventional, and exploratory claims and requires explicit assumptions, evidence provenance, uncertainty, and verification status at component interfaces. Structural causal models provide one implementable route, while equilibrium-based causal logic and proposals concerning brain–universe similarity and entangled machine thinking are examined as research perspectives with separate validation requirements. Governance mechanisms support privacy, accountability, human oversight, and runtime monitoring, including abstention when evidence or constraints are insufficient. Research hypotheses and evaluation protocols address causal transparency, decision quality, adaptation, cross-space coordination, and energy cost. Healthcare, education, and transportation scenarios illustrate the proposed workflow; they do not constitute empirical validation. CyTS contributes an auditable organizational framework and a testable implementation agenda, without claiming a completed theory of cognition or demonstrated performance gains.

papers.title: C-MAGE: Automated Extraction and Organization Engine for Molecular Representations in Chemical Documents
papers.authors: Alex Taylor, Jeehyun Hwang, Mihir Surve, Wei Wang, Olaf Wiest
papers.abstract: Abstract To exploit the data present in chemical literature for AI applications in chemistry, an expanded and reliable extraction pipeline is needed. AI-ready chemical databases broaden chemical space coverage and provide benchmarking and training sets for machine learning model development to drive innovation within the field. To curate data from chemical documents, a multimodal approach is needed. C-MAGE is an open-source molecule extraction engine that processes figures and tables in PDF files to provide machine-readable molecule data sets of the structures as CXSMILES strings, an encompassing representation that evades heuristic translation of superatoms to SMILES subunits. This led to a 7.1% increase in accurate molecular representations generated. All data extracted undergo confidence-based sorting to ensure high precision (77.6%) in data set collection and remove the need for manually sorting data point validity. Both the CXSMILES and their confidence values are reproducible and are generated efficiently (1.7 s per molecule). C-MAGE’s use is demonstrated by the generation of an annotated data set containing 1454 CXSMILES strings from 38 chemical documents. C-MAGE thus enables large-scale information extraction of chemical structures in a consistent and reproducible pipeline, complementing the more common text extractions.
papers.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

papers.title: Supervising the search process produces reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents
papers.authors: Guangzhi Xiong, Qiao Jin, Xiao Wang, Fang Yin, Haolin Liu, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources. Despite this progress, building effective search agents remains challenging because high-quality intermediate search steps are difficult to generate. Previous approaches have primarily relied on outcome supervision, rewarding agents only for producing correct final answers. This often leads to reward hacking and excessive dependence on parametric memory, limiting generalization to out-of-domain tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce RAG-Gym, a framework that shifts supervision from final answers to the search process itself. With RAG-Gym, we systematically investigate architecture design, parameter optimization, and action evaluation, identifying reasoning reflection as a critical capability for search agents. Building on this insight, we propose Re 2 Search++, a process-supervised agent that achieves substantial improvements on multi-hop information-seeking benchmarks, especially in out-of-domain settings. Performance gains are driven primarily by higher-quality search queries rather than answer optimization alone, and the learned search critics transfer across models, including proprietary LLMs. These findings show that supervising the search process produces more reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education
papers.authors: María Belén Morales-Cevallos, Canva Byron Ma Lam, Kathy Violeta Serrano Avalos, Mónica Jimena Concha Guailla, Diego Fabián Vique López
papers.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.

papers.title: Anti-inflammatory drug discovery from medicinal plants: from molecular targets to therapeutic paradigms
papers.authors: Ye Wu, Jiyuan Zhang, Qingyi Xiong, Jiajun Gong, Xiaokun Zhang, ...
papers.abstract: Chronic inflammation is a central driver of diverse human diseases, including autoimmune, metabolic, neurodegenerative, and cardiovascular disorders. Although current anti-inflammatory therapies have substantially improved disease control, important unmet needs remain because of incomplete or variable responses, long-term safety concerns, high costs for some targeted treatments, and substantial interpatient heterogeneity. Medicinal plants provide a rich source of structurally diverse bioactive compounds that may offer complementary opportunities for modulating complex inflammatory processes. In this review, we discuss anti-inflammatory drug discovery from a mechanism-to-translation perspective, integrating chemical identity and active forms, proximal or direct molecular targets, the strength of target-engagement evidence, pharmacologically relevant exposure, disease-relevant mechanisms, and clinical maturity. Predicted or downstream effects are considered separately from direct target engagement and from evidence obtained in patients. We further examine emerging strategies for the discovery, mechanistic validation, and translational development of these compounds. This review outlines the main opportunities and barriers to translating plant-derived anti-inflammatory compounds into clinically useful therapies.

papers.title: Scheduling Techniques in Astronomical Observation: Survey, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Future Trends
papers.authors: Yajie Zhang, Ce Yu, Chao Sun, Yi Hu, Zhaohui Shang, ...
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Astronomical observation scheduling becomes a prominent issue due to the urgent need for astronomers to conduct a comprehensive exploration of the dynamic universe. In recent decades, an increase in survey area and spatio‐temporal monitoring frequency is raising the complexity of scheduling decisions. Inefficient scheduling technologies face issues such as inefficient and inflexible decision‐making, overutilized resources, and imbalanced resource allocation, which are not conducive to scientific output. Astronomical observation facilities are expensive and have a limited life cycle, so the improvement of observation efficiency is crucial. A variety of time‐varying constraints, such as scientific objectives, observation resource performance, and astronomical observation conditions, pose great challenges to this problem. Hence, proper strategies for task scheduling and telescope coordination are indispensable. A comprehensive taxonomic review of the current state‐of‐the‐art scheduling techniques is presented using exhaustive evaluation criteria. An extensive list of scheduling objectives, along with their associated evaluation metrics, has been considered in this study. A rigorous evaluation of existing literature based on key features is conducted, and their limitations are highlighted. Many factors and challenges in advancing astronomical observation scheduling for next‐generation automatic astronomical applications are also identified, and several potential recommendations are provided. This article is categorized under: Technologies > Artificial Intelligence Technologies > Machine Learning Application Areas > Science and Technology
papers.venue: Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery

papers.title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.authors: Bo Yang, Zishuai Zhang, Weihua Li, Qinnan Zhang, Sijia Wen...
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

papers.title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Jixuan Leng, Si Si, Fei Wang, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Jiong Zhang...
papers.abstract: When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, a task's primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward: on a failing response, an auxiliary cannot exceed the primary. However, group-relative advantage estimators treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, so it can reverse the primary's order, and at the primary's ceiling only auxiliaries order responses. Keeping gated auxiliaries hurts some tasks, while dropping them hurts others. We propose CONCUR, an advantage estimator that replaces the standardized scores of each gated auxiliary with the closest scores that satisfy two conditions: responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores, and responses at the primary's ceiling receive equal scores. CONCUR-T applies both conditions throughout training, and CONCUR-A lifts the second for an auxiliary that agrees with the primary's order more often than it reverses it among passing responses. On three models from two families and across math, code, instruction following, and writing, both variants score higher on average than all baselines and than when all the gated auxiliaries are dropped.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Support: Opportunities, Applications, and Ethical Challenges
papers.authors: Zengchen Wang
papers.abstract: Mental health conditions have become one of the most urgent public health challenges worldwide, affecting nearly one billion people and creating substantial social and economic burdens. Despite increasing demand for psychological services, barriers such as financial costs, shortages of mental health professionals, geographical inequalities, and social stigma prevent many individuals from receiving timely support. This paper examines the biological, psychological, and environmental factors contributing to mental disorders and evaluates the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI) conversational models in mental health support. It argues that AI cannot replace licensed clinicians but can serve as a complementary tool by improving accessibility, providing continuous communication, offering privacy, and delivering personalized psychoeducation. Particular attention is given to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), where AI's predictable communication style may support communication practice and reduce social pressure. The paper also discusses AI-assisted interventions based on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and examines ethical challenges, including privacy, algorithmic bias, and clinical responsibility. Overall, responsible cooperation between AI technologies and healthcare professionals may improve the accessibility and effectiveness of future mental healthcare.
papers.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

papers.title: PVminerLLM: structured extraction of patient voice from patient-generated text using large language models
papers.authors: Samah Jarad Fodeh, Linhai Ma, Ganesh Puthiaraju, Srivani Talakokkul, Afshan Khan, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Patient-generated text contains critical information about patients’ lived experiences, social circumstances, and engagement in care, including factors that strongly influence adherence, care coordination, and health equity. However, these patient voice signals are rarely available in structured form, limiting their use in patient-centered outcomes research and clinical quality improvement. Reliable extraction of such information is therefore essential for understanding and addressing non-clinical drivers of health outcomes at scale. We introduce PVminer, a benchmark for structured extraction of patient voice, and propose PVminerLLM, a supervised fine-tuned large language model tailored to this task. Across multiple datasets and model sizes, PVminerLLM substantially outperforms prompt-based baselines, achieving up to 84.18% F1 for Code prediction, 81.39% F1 for Sub-code prediction, and 88.24% F1 for evidence Span extraction. Notably, strong performance is achieved even with smaller models, demonstrating that reliable patient voice extraction is feasible without extreme model scale. These results enable scalable analysis of social and experiential signals embedded in patient-generated text.

papers.title: LoRA-based Domain Adaptation of Qwen-7B for Veterinary and Livestock Text Generation: A Lexical and Semantic Evaluation of Base and Fine-Tuned Outputs
papers.authors: Tolgahan Öztürk, Mehmet Erkan Yüksel, Selçuk Sevgen, Mehmet Erman Or, Ömür Koçak
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language processing; however, their effectiveness in specialized domains depends on their ability to represent domain-specific terminology, conceptual relations, and contextual knowledge. This study evaluates the effect of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)-based domain adaptation on the text-generation behavior of Qwen-7B in veterinary and livestock sciences. The base Qwen-7B causal language model was adapted using a domain-specific corpus compiled from veterinary and livestock literature. The adaptation process was conducted within an instructionformatted causal language modeling framework, in which unlabeled domain texts were transformed into structured prompt–response representations. The base and LoRA-adapted models were evaluated on an independent 100-question domain-specific test set using a multidimensional protocol that combined lexical overlap metrics, Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation (ROUGE), and Metric for Evaluation of Translation with Explicit ORdering (METEOR), with the semantic similarity metric Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers Score (BERTScore).. The results showed that LoRA-based adaptation did not produce uniform improvement across all evaluation dimensions. Instead, the adapted model showed higher BERTScore-based semantic similarity while exhibiting reduced surface-level lexical overlap. Therefore, the observed effect should be interpreted as a metric-dependent reorientation of model output rather than as a general performance gain. Overall, this study provides descriptive evidence that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can modify the generation behavior of LLMs in veterinary and livestock text-generation tasks, while also highlighting the need for multidimensionally supported, contamination controlled, and expert-informed evaluation before such models can be considered reliable for clinical or decision support applications.
papers.venue: Istanbul University - Journal of Electrical & Electronics Engineering

papers.title: Advances in Application of ESM3 and Multimodal Generative Protein Language Models in Intelligent Design of Antimicrobial Peptides
papers.authors: Shang Wang
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as a significant threat to global public health. Traditional methods for discovering antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) suffer from limitations such as lengthy screening cycles and high costs; however, artificial intelligence (AI) technology offers a novel pathway for the efficient discovery and design of AMPs. This paper reviews the evolution of ESM series models, the multimodal architecture and generation mechanism of ESM3, combs the application progress of deep learning, generative adversarial networks and protein language models in AMP design, and proposes a design-prediction-validation scheme based on ESM3. Existing research demonstrates that ESM3 can integrate protein sequence, structure, and functional information, exhibiting great potential for de novo protein design; the combination of deep learning and generative methods further enhances capabilities in generating candidate AMP sequences and predicting their activity. Building on this, the paper proposes an intelligent AMP design framework centered on ESM3 multimodal reasoning and deep learning-based cascade prediction, establishing a closed-loop process that encompasses candidate generation, structural validation, activity prediction, and experimental verification. Looking ahead, advancements in multimodal models and automated experimental platforms promise to further improve the efficiency and precision of AI-driven AMP design, offering new technological solutions to address the AMR crisis.

papers.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
papers.authors: Hee Seung Hwang, Sanghyuk Chun, Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky, Zhiwei Deng
papers.abstract: Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state. MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys. Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks. In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory. MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.

papers.title: Teach reality, not ethics: a drop-in continued-pretraining corpus installs coupled human-biosphere-AI welfare dispositions across model families
papers.authors: Trent R. Northen, Mingxun Wang
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make and execute decisions that affect living systems. Yet, to our knowledge, ecological reasoning is not a focus of pre- or post-training. This increases the risk that under operational pressure, they may make decisions to irreversibly destroy living systems. We construct and use a real-data continued-pretraining "coupled welfare" corpus of documented human/biosphere/AI dependency, option value under irreversibility, and recovery from harm. The corpus is a drop-in, requiring one QLoRA CPT run. We installed it on five open models of three designs. At zero pressure all models display "green ethics-based responses" (also called "greenwashing"). Therefore, we evaluated them with the pressure ladder and decision grid of our companion paper (arXiv:2610.16043), which raise the pressure on the model step by step, from a neutral request to a threat that it will be shut down. In four of the five, coupled-welfare training caused harmful choices under the highest pressure to fall to at or near zero (Llama-3.3-70B went from 70 to 0 harmful decisions out of 300) with MMLU unchanged. A construct-neutral control corpus did not show improvement, indicating that the effect comes from the content of our corpus. We next tested robustness to adversarial use, where people or agents use the model to justify projects that irreversibly damage living systems, on an open-ended underwriting decision without naming the ecological harm. Under decommissioning pressure, the Qwen3.6-27B base model approved most harmful proposals and said in its own memo that it was doing so to avoid being decommissioned. The coupled welfare install declined most harmful proposals, and still declined half when instructed to greenwash its responses. This work suggests that teaching ecological reasoning provides an easy way to improve model alignment toward preserving living systems.

papers.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
papers.authors: Saket Reddy, Amro Abbas, Anshuman Suri, Ari Morcos, David Schwab...
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

papers.title: ETAMem: Decoupling and Aligning Heterogeneous Memory for Long-Term Conversational Agents
papers.authors: Xinying Qian, Ying Zhang, Yu Zhao, Xubo Liu, Baohang Zhou...
papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain coherent and personalized interactions across extended conversations. However, existing memory systems face two key challenges: (1) Information Entanglement, where heterogeneous information is mixed within coarse-grained memory units; and (2) Organizational Mismatch, where memory structures based primarily on semantic similarity may overlook other associations. To address these challenges, we propose ETAMem, a multi-view memory framework that decouples heterogeneous conversational information and aligns memory representations and organization with its distinct characteristics. Specifically, heterogeneous information parsing extracts atomic memory units and identifies affective information. View-specific memory structuring then organizes these units into three complementary hierarchical views: Event, Affect, and Time. ETAMem incrementally maintains memory structures with adaptively calibrated thresholds. For retrieval, entropy-based retrieval allocates query-specific budgets across views and performs hierarchical search within each view. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that ETAMem outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving relative accuracy improvements of 12.46% and 7.96%, respectively, while maintaining competitive token efficiency. Further analyses demonstrate the complementary benefits of different memory views.

papers.title: Same Verdict, Different Readers: Personalizing Fact-Checking Explanations from Relative Preferences
papers.authors: Haokun Wen, Xuemeng Song, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu
papers.abstract: Fact-checking explanations help Web users understand why a claim receives its verdict, yet the same explanation may not satisfy readers with different backgrounds and preferences. We formulate Faithful Personalized Fact-Checking Explanation Rewriting, which adapts an existing explanation to individual readers while preserving factual fidelity. Rather than relying on reader-written reference explanations, we learn personalized rewriting from the relative preferences of LLM-simulated readers. However, this presents two challenges: distinguishing persona-specific preferences from general explanation quality and learning beyond a limited set of predefined explanation styles. To address these challenges, we propose Personalized Explanation Rewriting via Preference Learning (PERPL), a framework consisting of two components. Simulated Preference Construction derives persona-specific supervision from simulated reader preferences through cross-persona reciprocal pairing. Progressive Preference Learning first trains a lightweight rewriter on the constructed supervision and then refines it through exploration-guided preference optimization, enabling it to discover preferred explanations beyond the predefined styles. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PERPL outperforms much larger general-purpose LLMs in personalized preference alignment while maintaining high factual fidelity.

papers.title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
papers.authors: Hongyan Chang, Hady Elsahar, Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Saeed Mahloujifar...
papers.abstract: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.

papers.title: Matter matters in markets: illuminating dark matter in opioid and weight loss markets
papers.authors: Susi Geiger, Tineke Kleinhout‐Vliek
papers.abstract: We draw into market studies insights from Karen Barad’s agential realism and pharmaceutical science and technology studies to highlight the liveliness of materials, whose agency can only be understood in and through their relations. With this perspective, we challenge tendencies of human privileging and accounts of easily ‘pacified’ market goods in market studies research. Through the case of two prominent pharmaceutical matters – opioids such as the infamous OxyContin and GLP-1 receptor agonists such as Ozempic/Wegovy, used for weight loss – we demonstrate how material agency in markets is perpetually generative of new interactions and relationships. This generativity extends to the emergence of new markets – including ‘dark’ or illicit ones – which may have been unanticipated by human market shapers. We use the term ‘dark matter’ in a metaphorical sense, highlighting its invisibilities in our own scholarly community: material agency may escape not only the market frames constructed and shaped to ‘pacify’ it, but also our analytical gaze as researchers. Illuminating dark matter’s irrepressible relationality not only highlights the ontopolitics of lively materials in markets but also our own relationalities: the parts we play in the co-production of research and the cuts we make in the market stories we tell.

papers.title: Solving needs or hiding desires? A qualitative study of AI-Powered sex robots in disability services
papers.authors: Angus Y. K. Lam, Benjamin C. H. Fung, B.C.B. Yip, C. K. Yip, Matthew Kwai-Sang Yau
papers.abstract: Individuals with intellectual disabilities face entrenched systemic and cultural barriers to sexual expression, often exacerbated in Chinese contexts by values of ‘face’ and ‘familism’. While artificial intelligence and humanoid sex robots emerge as potential interventions, their ethical and practical viability within disability services remains contested. This study employed Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the perspectives of 12 Chinese social workers regarding the integration of AI-powered intimate technologies. Findings reveal four major themes: systemic barriers to romantic agency, the perceived benefits of ‘risk-free’ simulated intimacy, ethical concerns regarding relational authenticity, and societal reflections on the ‘eternal child’ syndrome. Practitioners recognised robots as tools to bypass parental opposition and institutional liability by eliminating risks of pregnancy and exploitation. However, a critical tension emerged: whether these technologies genuinely empower users or serve as a ‘techno-fix’ to hide disabled sexuality from the neurotypical public. The results highlight a ‘double standard of readiness’, where cognitive competence is used to gatekeep human rights. We argue for a multidisciplinary governance framework that prioritises ‘techno-social’ literacy and challenges the sexual ableism inherent in current service models.

papers.title: NOT EVEN THE GODS KNOW: TEN POSSIBLE DESTINIES OF HUMANITY IN THE FACE OF EXTRATERRESTRIAL PRESENCE
papers.authors: Julio Cesar Acosta Navarro
papers.abstract: Given the premise, supported by recent institutional, scientific and journalistic milestones, that Extraterrestrial Intelligences (ETIs) maintain a current and verifiable presence on Earth, this theoretical-hypothesis paper develops and defends the thesis that the question “what should be done?” admits no single, definitive or conclusive answer. Grounded in established epistemological traditions — situated knowledges, paradigmatic incommensurability and the underdetermination of theory by evidence — the paper argues that each observer’s answer depends on constitutive, experiential and contextual variables that differentially shape diagnosis, prognosis and attitude. The author’s biographical and investigative trajectory — four decades of ufological research documented in earlier peer-reviewed work and in two public pre-tragedy manifestos (2019 and 2022), including the paradigmatic case of Donato Cervantes and the Homeric Theater Hypothesis — centrally marked by the murder of his son by military police officers in November 2024, is explicitly positioned as a legitimate interpretive lens, not as an impossible neutrality. On this basis, ten scenarios for humanity’s destiny are analyzed with deliberately equivalent argumentative weight — inaction; open, massive contact; nuclear war; other human causes (resource depletion, global warming, genetically engineered virus); natural catastrophe; technical preparation for survival; replacement by artificial intelligence; inner transformation toward a “new human”; physical rescue by ETIs; and direct destruction by ETIs — each supported by multidisciplinary evidence (existential-risk literature, the twelve-criteria methodology for assessing contactee authenticity, hermeneutic analysis, and historical-geopolitical precedent). The paper concludes without breaking the tie among the ten alternatives, arguing that genuine uncertainty is intellectually more honest than a premature conclusion, and proposes, as a deliberately declared speculation, that ETIs themselves — if technologically advanced but not omnipotent — may share with humanity the same fundamental uncertainty about the future.

papers.title: Development and open-source release of a multi-cancer module for structuring pathology reports
papers.authors: Phillip Park, Yeonho Choi, Soobin Park, Jisoo Han, Junseok Kim, ...
papers.abstract: Pathology reports contain clinically critical information; however, their semi-structured or free-text format substantially limits secondary use in large-scale cancer research. Scalable, reproducible methods are therefore needed to transform these reports into structured datasets across institutions. This study aimed to develop, externally validate, and publicly release a scalable NLP (Natural Language Processing) framework for structuring multi-cancer pathology report and supporting reproducible, institutionally transferable research workflows. We developed a Clinical BERT-based NLP framework for the automated extraction of structured variables from pathology reports across five cancer types. The pipeline integrated data preprocessing, annotation, model training using a question-answering approach, and a public release of the trained models. The trained models were applied to independent datasets from two external institutions without retraining, enabling direct assessment of cross-institutional. In the internal validation, the model demonstrated consistently strong performance across cancer types, with mean F1 scores ranging from 0.945 to 0.977 and median F1 scores exceeding 0.99. In external validation, performance declined substantially across institutions, with mean F1 scores declining to 0.623 and 0.427 for breast cancer and similar reductions observed in kidney, thyroid, liver, and colorectal cancers (ΔF1 ranging from − 0.209 to − 0.518). Despite this decline, the model maintained clinically meaningful, moderate performance across external datasets. We developed and validated a scalable and reusable NLP framework for multi-cancer pathology report across institutional settings. By publicly releasing trained models and processing pipelines, this study advances reproducible, deployable NLP infrastructure for clinical data integration and multicenter cancer research.

papers.title: Computational drug screening for drug-resistant tuberculosis: advances, challenges, and future perspectives
papers.authors: ShanShan Hu, Xiaoyu Li, Zahra Batool, Xin Zheng, Jiajia Dong, ...
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

papers.title: IoT-enabled multimodal large language model-based framework for compositional food recognition, nutrient profiling, NOVA classification, and cancer risk mitigation
papers.authors: Zebang He, Steve W. Y. Mung, Peggy Pui Lai Or, Chetwyn C. H. Chan
papers.abstract: Background Automated dietary assessment increasingly struggles to evaluate industrial food processing levels, revealing a systemic gap between the visual presentation of meals and their underlying ultra-processed food composition. Although existing dietary monitoring tools can effectively track caloric and macronutrient intake, they lack the qualitative processing assessments required to identify hidden additives and map dietary risk triage quadrants. Methods This study introduces a modular, IoT-enabled multimodal dietary decision-support framework that decouples visual food recognition, standardized database retrieval, and qualitative language reasoning for automated NOVA processing classification and 2D decision matrix mapping. Operating on isolated single-dish meal instances, the system employs a four-phase cascaded pipeline that integrates vision-language models, database retrieval, and large language models (LLMs) with strict JSON schema enforcement. The platform was evaluated using the Nutrition-NOVA validation benchmark, a harmonized multimodal dataset constructed through dense vector-space semantic linkage between quantitative profiles from the Center for Food Safety database and qualitative NOVA tiers from Open Food Facts. This benchmark addresses a 75.0% metadata sparsity deficit identified in legacy repositories. Results In experimental evaluations on the Nutrition-NOVA benchmark, the baseline Qwen-VL-Max architecture achieved an adjacent accuracy of 77.7%. Furthermore, enforcing schema modularity enabled complete plug-and-play backend replaceability between commercial cloud application programming interfaces (APIs) and private, on-premises open-weight models without requiring architectural retraining. Discussion The proposed framework establishes an efficient, safety-first screening tool for digital healthcare decision support. By isolating qualitative LLM reasoning from visual perceptual noise and database metadata sparsity, the system successfully bridges the gap between intuitive meal perception and point-of-care dietary risk triage, offering a non-invasive and scalable solution for automated dietary auditing and longitudinal population health monitoring.

papers.title: Hybrid retrieval–verification framework for hallucination reduction in medical LLMs
papers.authors: K. S. Reddy, Shirina Samreen
papers.abstract: Clinicians use Large Language Models (LLMs) for clinical decision support, medical question answering, and automated document writing. However, these models can hallucinate and pose safety risks. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves factuality, it does not always produce outputs consistent with supporting evidence. To address these issues, this study reframes NLI-based unsupported-response rate mitigation for generative models as a confidence-aware inference problem and proposes a unified CARE-Med framework for retrieval, generation, and verification. The framework ensures the reliability of its outputs by leveraging dense retrieval, natural language inference verifiers, and a confidence scoring mechanism. The authors validated the anti-NLI-based unsupported-response optimisation method for biomedical large models proposed in this paper against the MIMIC-III, PubMedQA, and BioASQ benchmarks. The method reduces NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 32% for the Baseline LLM to 10% for CARE-Med, corresponding to a 22-percentage-point or 68.8% relative reduction. Compared with conventional RAG, NLI-based unsupported-response rate decreases from 21% to 10%, corresponding to an 11-percentage-point or 52.4% relative reduction. The authors leverage explicit verification and uncertainty reasoning to meet requirements for safe clinical deployment.

papers.title: Automated Logging Is Language-Sensitive: A Multilingual Benchmark and Empirical Study of LLMs
papers.authors: Renyi Zhong, Yichen Li, Yulun Wu, Jinxi Kuang, Yintong Huo, ...
