papers.abstract: Logging statements are central to debugging, failure diagnosis, and production observability, yet writing them requires developers to decide where to place a logging statement, which API and severity level to use, and what runtime information to expose. Automated logging aims to reduce this burden, but existing evidence remains dominated by Java-centric repositorysnapshot datasets. Thus, Java-centered benchmarks do not show whether findings on model behavior and model selection generalize to other programming languages or to real-world maintenance changes that introduce logging statements. This paper presents MultiLogBench, a multilingual benchmark and empirical study spanning six programming language ecosystems. MultiLogBench contains 63,965 production-code repository-snapshot instances, 744 revision-history cases where developers introduce logging statements during maintenance, and a paired transformed revision-history branch for robustness analysis. Using seven contemporary large language models under a unified protocol, we evaluate logging-site localization, frameworkanchor matching, severity prediction, message generation, variable recovery, and cascaded overall quality. Results show that automated logging is sensitive to language-ecosystem conditions. On repository-snapshot data, absolute performance levels and component profiles vary across language-specific subsets, with position prediction exhibiting the largest average withinmodel component gap. The six language-specific CCS leaderboards are nevertheless highly correlated, with a mean pairwise Spearman correlation of 0.912, and identify the same top two models; reordering is concentrated among the middle- and lower-tier models. Among the primary structural buckets, loop and nested-callable sites are the hardest. On revision-history data, the six-language mean declines across all displayed metrics, cross-language score dispersion persists, the component profile shifts toward greater framework-anchor dispersion, and the repository-snapshot top-two stability does not persist. Transformed inputs do not cause a broad same-direction performance collapse. These results show that single-language evaluation is informative for identifying the leading models in the controlled repository-snapshot benchmark, but is insufficient for estimating absolute performance across language ecosystems, diagnosing component-specific weaknesses beyond the evaluated language, or establishing a fine-grained model ordering below the top two that transfers across languages.
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

papers.title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
papers.authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
papers.abstract: Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev's accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27--29\% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. This loss of initial successes is substantially larger than under fixed-order repetition, even for highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.

papers.title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
papers.authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.

papers.title: S3AC: Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic for LLM Reasoning
papers.authors: Shuo Shen, Guangran Cheng, Chengqi Lyu, Xiangsen Wang, Yanan Sun...
papers.abstract: Critic-free methods are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, avoiding difficult and costly critic training. Common alternatives lack token-level credit assignment and typically rely on grouped rollouts to estimate prompt-specific baselines. A critic can address both limitations, but long-CoT critic training is hindered by insufficient coverage of trajectories with diverse lengths and early gradients dominated by the newly initialized value head. We introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic) for LLM reasoning, built around a practical critic-training recipe. The trained critic provides token-specific advantages and prompt-specific baselines. Using the prompt-level baseline to estimate difficulty, we propose Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling (DAPS). DAPS combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing rollout waste without offline difficulty initialization. S3AC improves group-rollout performance across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 1.5B to 397B parameters, outperforming a modern GRPO variant (GRPO-X). At 35B, it sustains single-rollout training while tested critic-free baselines deteriorate after initial gains.

papers.title: GPDPO: Learning from Reward Conflicts via Group Pareto-Dominance Policy Optimization
papers.authors: Zixuan Xu, Haoxuan Chen, Jiangxin Sun, Jian-Fang Hu
papers.abstract: Multi-reward reinforcement learning offers a promising framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse objectives, but conflicting reward signals can induce ambiguous update directions and hinder stable optimization. Existing approaches address such conflicts through reward reweighting, gradient coordination, or rollout filtering, yet they primarily operate on per-response or group-level optimization signals and underexploit relational information among sampled responses. As a result, conflict-filtered rollouts may still contain useful supervision that is discarded during training. We propose Group Pareto-Dominance Policy Optimization (GPDPO), a multi-reward policy optimization method that recovers pairwise supervision from conflict-filtered rollouts. GPDPO identifies Pareto-dominance relations among sampled responses and converts them into auxiliary preference signals, which are jointly optimized with the original policy objective. This enables more effective reuse of existing rollouts without additional sampling or reward evaluation. Experiments on API-Bank across multiple model scales and reward configurations show that GPDPO consistently outperforms competitive multi-reward optimization baselines. Further analysis demonstrates that GPDPO reduces both group-relative and pairwise reward conflicts, supporting the effectiveness of exploiting relational supervision for multi-reward alignment. Code will be released.

papers.title: Probing the phon* representations of the Mimi codebooks
papers.authors: Artem Saloev, Nicolas Ballier, Erin Pacquetet
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used to encode speech for integration with large language models. This paper investigates the phonetic representations in the first codebook (CB0) of the Mimi codec. ABX style evaluation is poorly suited to Mimi fixed 80 ms tokenization window, which often spans multiple phonemes; we instead use forced alignment, entropy analysis, and Phone-Normalized Mutual Information (PNMI). Using TIMIT speech (58/55 speakers, SA1/SA2), individual tokens are strongly associated with specific phonemes (PNMI = 0.84, above random), yet phonemes are realized by multiple competing tokens rather than a one-to-one mapping.

papers.title: DTCA: Denoising Token Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Language Models
papers.authors: Hongze Chen, Miao Pan, Lizhou Liang, Qinfeng Li, Xinyin Ma...
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, enabling bidirectional context modeling and parallel token refinement. Recent studies have applied reinforcement learning (RL) to DLMs and improved their reasoning performance. However, the iterative denoising process makes credit assignment more challenging, as final outcome rewards provide limited information about how different tokens contribute to the final output. In this paper, we propose Denoising Token Credit Assignment (DTCA), a framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. DTCA estimates token contributions by measuring the improvement in prediction confidence of remaining masked positions after token commitment and groups these signals according to part-of-speech (POS) categories. These contribution weights are used to select informative denoising timesteps and assign token-level learning signals during RL training. DTCA further calibrates these learning signals according to token-level entropy changes induced by policy updates. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct show that DTCA consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance across different generation budgets, with gains of up to 9.0 points on MATH500 and 5.3 points on GSM8K over the base model.

papers.title: CalibraRL: Confidence-Calibrated Reinforcement Learning for Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG
papers.authors: Qianchi Zhang, Hainan Zhang, Liang Pang, Hongwei Zheng, Zhiming Zheng
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce plausible but incorrect answers, motivating reinforcement learning methods that reward correct answers, penalize incorrect answers, and allow abstention. However, fixed outcome-based rewards do not distinguish incorrect responses with different confidence levels or account for differences in answering reliability across queries. Consequently, such rewards may inadequately penalize overconfident errors and fail to discourage unnecessary abstention. We propose CalibraRL, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates response confidence and query-level answering evidence into reward design. For non-abstaining responses, CalibraRL combines correctness-based utility with a Brier-based penalty that encourages agreement between confidence and correctness. For abstentions, it estimates conditional answering reliability using a Beta posterior derived from the correctness of non-abstaining responses within each sampled group. The abstention reward increases with the posterior probability that the model's accuracy on non-abstaining responses is below a predefined threshold. CalibraRL reuses training rollouts without requiring additional annotations indicating whether the model knows the answer to each question. Experiments on three QA datasets demonstrate that CalibraRL improves answer precision and reduces hallucinations compared with strong baselines. Further analysis shows that CalibraRL reduces mean expected calibration error (ECE) by 30.8\% across two backbone models and three datasets, highlighting its potential to improve the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in web search.

papers.title: A Training-Free Symbolic Baseline for Interactive Medical Diagnosis: Automatic Rule-Slot Derivation and Weighted Evidence Combination
papers.authors: Naufal Denta Elsatya Nugraha, Dhendra Marutho, Muhammad Sam’an, Wendy Sarasjati, De Rosal Ignatius Moses Setiadi
papers.abstract: Interactive medical diagnosis requires sequential symptom elicitation before a diagnosis can be established. Although recent approaches employ reinforcement learning and transformer-based agents, their performance has not been adequately contextualized against a classical probabilistic baseline. This study introduces a training-free symbolic baseline that derives conditional symptom probabilities and three rule slots—must-have, exclusion, and critical—from co-occurrence counts in simulated patient records. Candidate diseases are ranked using observed evidence, while subsequent questions are selected by expected information gain. Evaluation on five benchmarks from a published reinforcement learning study reveals distinct performance regimes. On MedlinePlus (893 diseases), the proposed method achieves 99.27 ± 0.09% accuracy with an average of 1.75 questions, outperforming the published baseline (96.2 ± 0.1%; 3.41 questions). Across four SymCat variants, it improves accuracy by 3.03–7.70 percentage points but requires approximately twice as many questions; at a matched budget of 8.98 questions, the reference method achieves higher accuracy, highlighting a trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and interaction cost. Ablation experiments across six datasets show that removing weighted evidence combination reduces accuracy by 35.4–65.4 percentage points, while eliminating symptom inquiry reduces it by 23.3–66.8 percentage points. The safety veto removes up to 50.2% of candidates on average but changes the final diagnosis in at most 0.17% of consultations, indicating limited incremental impact on predictive accuracy under the evaluated configurations. Rule-base derivation takes 1.8 s for 893 diseases on a CPU. As all benchmarks rely on simulated patients, these findings establish benchmark-level performance rather than clinical effectiveness.
papers.venue: Journal of Computing Theories and Applications

papers.title: From Drug Discovery to Precision Oncology: A Machine Learning–Driven Pharmaceutical Framework for Lung Cancer Treatment—A Joint Research Initiative Between Pakistan's Department of Pharmacy and China Pharmaceutical University
papers.authors: Aisha Aziz, Asma Khatoon, Uroosa Maqbool, Javeria, Uzma Bano, ...
papers.abstract: Lung cancer remains one of the most challenging global healthcare concerns due to its high mortality rate, molecular heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, and limitations in conventional pharmaceutical drug development. This study presents an integrated machine learning–driven pharmaceutical framework for accelerating anticancer drug discovery, predicting therapeutic responses, and advancing precision oncology through a joint research initiative involving Pakistan’s Department of Pharmacy and China Pharmaceutical University. The research dataset comprised 18,500 bioactive compounds, 3,200 lung cancer patient profiles, and 12,600 drug–target interaction records, incorporating molecular descriptors, genomic biomarkers, pharmacokinetic properties, and clinical treatment-response characteristics. The proposed framework integrated molecular docking, quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and deep neural networks to identify promising therapeutic compounds and predict individualized drug responses. Molecular screening prioritized 245 potential anticancer compounds, of which 38 exhibited favorable predicted binding affinities, drug-likeness properties, and pharmacokinetic profiles. Experimental model evaluation indicated that XGBoost achieved 95.2% accuracy, 94.6% precision, 95.8% recall, and a 95.2% F1-score, outperforming Random Forest (91.8% accuracy) and deep neural networks (93.7% accuracy). Furthermore, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.974, demonstrating strong predictive discrimination. Biomarker-based analysis identified EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, KRAS alterations, and tumor-associated molecular signatures as influential determinants of therapeutic response. Patient-specific treatment stratification demonstrated a 21.4% improvement in drug–patient matching accuracy compared with the conventional baseline approach, while computational pharmaceutical screening reduced the estimated compound prioritization workload by 36.8%. The comparative pharmaceutical framework further highlighted opportunities for strengthening Pakistan–China collaboration in artificial intelligence-assisted drug development, translational oncology, and personalized therapeutic research. Collectively, the reported findings support the potential of integrating molecular pharmaceutical analysis with advanced machine learning to enhance computational drug candidate prioritization, improve treatment-response prediction, and facilitate biomarker-guided clinical decision support. Further experimental validation and prospective multicenter clinical evaluation remain essential before clinical implementation in diverse lung cancer populations.
papers.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development

papers.title: Eyegent: Visual Attention Orchestration on Concepts
papers.authors: Alessandro D’Amelio, Sabrina Patania, Luca Annese, Giuseppe Boccignone
papers.abstract: Abstract Where a human looks is not random, nor is it merely a reflex to visual salience. It is a decision shaped by goals, constrained by language, and driven by the need to resolve uncertainty. We propose Eyegent , an active vision agent built on this premise: that visual search is best understood as sequential Bayesian inference over semantically grounded hypotheses, with fixations serving as epistemic actions. Given an image and a natural-language query, Eyegent constructs a discrete hypothesis space of candidate segmentation masks, maintains an explicit posterior belief distribution, and selects each fixation to maximise expected information gain—updating beliefs via vision–language model verification and terminating when uncertainty falls below a principled risk threshold. We formalise this process as Bayesian Active Semantic Grounding (BASG), a computational-level account that provides formal guarantees on belief concentration, entropy reduction, and bounded decision risk. The framework is neurobiologically grounded in the large-scale network organisation of the human brain, with the Salience Network identified as the dynamic orchestrator of semantic, inferential, and oculomotor processes. Critically, Eyegent requires no gaze supervision and no task-specific training: it is zero-shot, modular, and built entirely from off-the-shelf components. Evaluated on RefCOCO-Gaze and AiR-D, two benchmarks coupling language-driven visual tasks with human eye-tracking ground truth, Eyegent achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods across semantic, spatial, and structural scanpath metrics, and approaches supervised baselines on several dimensions. The result is a system that does not merely predict where humans look, but generates scanpaths for the same reason humans generate them: to find out.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Digital Twin for Disease Progression Prediction: A Comprehensive Review
papers.authors: Asaad Abd-Alsada A., Zainab Najem Nemer
papers.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to integrate machine learning and deep learning techniques with Digital Twin technology to improve the accuracy of disease progression prediction and support personalised clinical decision-making. Design/Methodology/Approach: The study reviews existing Digital Twin frameworks in healthcare and proposes an Artificial Intelligence-driven Digital Twin paradigm based on temporal electronic health record data. The proposed approach develops dynamic digital representations of patients that reflect their current health conditions and predict their future clinical evolution. Machine learning and deep learning techniques analyse large-scale medical data, identify hidden patterns, and provide early predictions of patient deterioration, particularly in intensive care environments. Research Limitation: Further validation using diverse, multi-centre clinical datasets and real-time patient information is required before the model can be widely implemented in clinical practice. Findings: The findings indicate that AI-powered Digital Twins can improve the accuracy of disease progression prediction, facilitate early identification of patient deterioration, and support clinical treatment decisions. The proposed approach may also enable proactive, personalised, and data-driven disease management. Practical Implication: The proposed Digital Twin paradigm can help healthcare professionals monitor patients, identify high-risk cases, select appropriate interventions, and allocate critical care resources more effectively. Social Implication: Improved early prediction and personalised treatment may reduce mortality rates, prevent avoidable complications, enhance healthcare quality, and reduce the clinical and economic burden on patients and healthcare institutions. Originality/Value: This study highlights the value of combining temporal electronic health record data, Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Twin technology within a unified framework for predicting disease progression. It contributes to the development of intelligent and patient-specific clinical decision-support systems for critical healthcare environments.

papers.title: AI vs. AI: An AI-Enabled Conversational Intervention to Inoculate Against AI-Generated Fake News
papers.authors: Mohammad S. Najjar, Murtaza Nasir
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is a double-edged sword that can be used to amplify the proliferation of highly sophisticated fake news as well as to fight it. In this work, we explore a new route: using one AI to inoculate humans against fake news generated by another AI. Motivated by psychological inoculation theory, we created ‘Alex’, a conversational AI agent that engages users in an adaptive conversational dialogue designed to build cognitive resilience against AI-generated, AI-related fake news. We tested its efficacy in a Solomon four-group experiment with 542 participants. The results of a 2 × 2 ANOVA show a significant main effect of the intervention on participants’ discrimination of true and false headlines, with no significant evidence of pretest sensitization. We show that AI can be designed as a scalable, interactive conversational intervention for delivering psychological inoculation against AI-generated, AI-related fake news.

papers.title: Drivers of supply chain resilience in the new energy vehicle industry: An explainable machine learning approach
papers.authors: Yang Jiang, Chenchen Li, Jijing Hang
papers.abstract: Under the global dual-carbon goals, supply chain resilience has become a strategic priority for the new energy vehicle (NEV) industry. Using a 2016–2023 panel of 403 Chinese listed NEV firms, we construct an entropy-weighted supply chain resilience index and predict it with Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost, interpreted via SHAP, against a linear regression benchmark. The tree-based ensembles explain 66%–68% of out-of-sample resilience variation, far above the linear benchmark (56%), while models using only supply chain characteristics fail to beat the sample mean. The two ensembles attribute resilience differently: transaction costs rank as the strongest supply chain predictor in RF, whereas chip import dependence dominates in XGBoost, though both agree that supply chain characteristics are stably among the top predictor groups. All five core factors exhibit nonlinear threshold patterns (on the normalized [0, 1] scale): automation first suppresses and then promotes resilience beyond a robot-penetration threshold of 0.19; government subsidies are effective mainly within an intensity window of 0.2–0.5; chip import dependence turns sharply detrimental beyond 0.77; innovation efficiency supports resilience only within an optimal moderate range, its contribution turning negative beyond 0.33; and transaction costs become resilience-enhancing only beyond thresholds of 0.15 (RF) to 0.21 (XGBoost). Short-horizon forecasts are accurate, but rolling forecasts collapse under the 2023 structural break, indicating that resilience prediction is regime-conditional. The study introduces explainable machine learning into NEV supply chain resilience research, clarifies the nonlinear formation mechanism of resilience, and offers threshold-based policy implications for firms, governments, and industry associations, contributing to Sustainable Development Goal 9.

papers.title: Emerging trends in AI-driven mining hazard management
papers.authors: Chaoran Huang, Ruiyu Liang, Chengguo Zhang, Ismet Canbulat, Lina Yao
papers.abstract: The management of geotechnical hazards in mining is critical for ensuring operational safety and sustainability, yet its practical implementation often struggles with the inherent geological uncertainty and the dynamic, non-linear nature of mining environments. Artificial intelligence (AI), and specifically machine learning (ML), has emerged as a transformative technology, offering a shift from reactive to proactive, data-driven hazard management. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the evolution and application of AI in mining hazard management, tracing this development from early statistical and ML models to recent advances in deep learning. The review finds that these advanced models have demonstrated significant success in tasks such as rockburst prediction, slope stability analysis, and gas outburst forecasting by identifying complex patterns in large, multi-source datasets from seismic, geological, and operational monitoring. Despite these successes, significant challenges persist: the efficacy of purely data-driven models is often limited by data scarcity, imbalanced datasets, and a lack of physical consistency; the black-box nature of many deep learning models has created a barrier to their interpretability and trustworthiness in safety-critical applications. The future of AI in mining hazard management lies not in isolated algorithms but in integrated, hybrid systems. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and explainable AI (XAI) are identified as critical frontiers. These approaches promise to create models that are not only more accurate and generalisable but also transparent and interpretable to engineering practitioners, bridging the gap between AI's theoretical potential and its practical application in creating safer mining environments.

papers.title: Agentic and generative AI for intelligent autonomous vulnerability assessment and penetration testing: A systematic analysis
papers.authors: Samuel  Roy Anthony Truss, Mohamed Chahine Ghanem, Mohammed Amin Almaiah, Marco Ortolani, Mohammed B. M. Kamel, ...
papers.abstract: Context: Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) is increasingly challenged by the scale, heterogeneity, and dynamic nature of modern digital infrastructures, particularly across enterprise IT, operational technology (OT), industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and cyber–physical systems. Although Agentic AI and Generative AI have each shown promise for automating parts of security auditing, the current literature remains fragmented across isolated audit phases and is still dominated by conventional IT-centric perspectives. Objectives: This paper systematically analyses recent advances in Agentic AI, Reinforcement Learning (RL), Large Language Models (LLMs), and tool-augmented Generative AI for autonomous VAPT. It aims to synthesise how these paradigms support end-to-end security auditing, identify the principal technical, operational, and governance gaps in the literature, and derive an evidence-grounded reference model for trustworthy autonomous auditing across both IT and OT environments. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted across major scholarly databases, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. From 1144 initially identified records, 72 studies were retained after deduplication, screening, and full-text eligibility assessment. Included studies were coded across five attributes and synthesised into thematic trajectories to derive the proposed framework. Study credibility was screened against three qualitative, non-instrumented criteria—venue and editorial process, presence of empirical or systematic conceptual evaluation, and explicit acknowledgement of limitations. Results: The review shows that agentic approaches are best suited to sequential and adaptive tasks such as reconnaissance orchestration, exploit-path selection, lateral movement, post-exploitation pivoting, and adaptive re-testing. In contrast, generative approaches are strongest in reasoning over unstructured evidence, interpreting configurations and advisories, contextualising vulnerabilities, assessing exploit feasibility, mapping compliance controls, and producing traceable audit reports. However, few studies integrate these capabilities into a governed end-to-end workflow, and real-world OT/Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) validation remains limited. Of the 72 coded studies, 56 apply classical machine or deep learning, 14 use generative/LLM techniques, and only 2 employ reinforcement-learning or agentic control; none is evaluated against a physical or emulated OT/IIoT target, and reported autonomy is strongly scaffolding-dependent (for example, 21% fully autonomous versus 64% human-assisted task completion on AutoPenBench, an external benchmark outside the coded corpus). To address these gaps, this paper derives a unified Agentic–Generative VAPT model comprising four tightly coupled layers: agentic decision-making, generative reasoning, structured tool interfaces, and validation–governance. It further introduces a formal threat and evaluation abstraction for Model Context Protocol (MCP)-style interface layers and proposes a five-dimensional VAPT Autonomy Benchmark for future empirical validation. Conclusion: Autonomous security auditing is evolving from isolated AI-assisted tasks towards integrated, policy-constrained, and auditable architectures. Nevertheless, major challenges remain in hallucination control, prompt injection, sparse reward design, explainability, safety-aware evaluation, and benchmark standardisation. Future research should prioritise tightly integrated agentic–generative systems, realistic and safety-aware IT/OT testbeds, and governance mechanisms that enable trustworthy human-in-the-loop deployment in operational environments.

papers.title: Attacking visual foundation depth estimation model with adaptable adversarial patch
papers.authors: Yuan Zhang, Jian Wang, Jing Yin
papers.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) have demonstrated strong generalization ability across various downstream tasks and scenes. However, their vulnerability to adversarial examples, particularly in safety-critical applications, remains insufficiently understood. This paper investigates the attack effect of physical adversarial patches on monocular depth estimation (MDE) models, specifically the foundation model Depth Anything, widely used in fields such as autonomous driving and robotic navigation. First, we introduce a universal patch attack pipeline and present the following key observations: 1) Attack effectiveness : In the pixel-wise dense prediction task of MDE, adversarial effects are largely confined to the patch area and do not spread to other regions, indicating that foundation models have enhanced adversarial robustness compared to traditional models. 2) Attack interpretability : The learned adversarial patches often contain semantically meaningful content, such as forests or buildings, leading to corresponding erroneous depth predictions, which adds interpretability to the attack’s behavior. Based on the observations, we focus on improving the applicability of adversarial patches in real-world environments by proposing a plug-and-play augmentation method, termed MixCrop, that enhances attack effectiveness, especially when patch semantics are incomplete or repetitive. Extensive experiments including physical attacks demonstrate that the patched objects can effectively vanish from the predicted depth map. The learned patches also have strong generalization ability across various objects and scenes.

papers.title: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation
papers.authors: Qiyuan Li, Xiaomei Guo, Chao Gao, Haijiang Liu, Deyu Chen...
papers.abstract: Pre-consultation medical dialogues are essential for collecting comprehensive patient information, but are costly to obtain at scale due to privacy and ethical constraints. Existing LLM-based synthesis methods often rely on prompt engineering or rigid rules, limiting their ability to balance clinical relevance with realistic patient diversity. We propose CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent framework for pre-consultation medical dialogue synthesis that integrates patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. CoRPS-Dial generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by post-hoc quality control for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency. Experiments on coronary heart disease demonstrate that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment between synthetic and real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and dialogue naturalness. Downstream fine-tuning experiments further confirm the utility of the generated synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.

papers.title: PHYRD: A Living Benchmark for Reproducing and Extending Theoretical Physics Research
papers.authors: Qituan Zhang, Guo Chen, Linfeng Zhang, Wenlong Zhang
papers.abstract: Large language models and agents have shown significant power in advanced physical research. In this paper, We introduce PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical-physics reasoning with 63 Reproduce and 43 Discover problems. Reproduce tests derivation of published results; Discover tests consequences of modified theoretical conditions. FormulaForest constructs the tasks with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics. Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21% to 68.25% on Reproduce and from 18.60% to 74.42% on closed-book Discover. With tools, four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments persist. Besides, our experimental results demonstrate the value of FormulaForest as synthetic data. On FrontierScience, a benchmark developed by OpenAI, it raises the accuracy of a Qwen-35B-A3B model from 61% to 72%.

papers.title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
papers.authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang
papers.abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

papers.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
papers.authors: Tianyu Yang, Yijun Tian, Lars Benedikt Kaesberg, Jan Philip Wahle, Bela Gipp...
papers.abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.

papers.title: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation
papers.authors: Qiyuan Li, Xiaomei Guo, Chao Gao, Haijiang Liu, Deyu Chen...

These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.

papers.title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
papers.authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng...
papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.

papers.title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
papers.authors: Jiawei Dong, Zilong Bai, Pengtian zhu, Peng Zhou
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

papers.title: Generative AI and health misinformation: a lifecycle-based communication framework
papers.authors: Xiaoli Nan
papers.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the contemporary health information environment, where it can both generate and mitigate misinformation. Objective This review develops a Lifecycle-Based Framework to provide an integrative account of how generative AI operates across the health misinformation lifecycle from misinformation production and detection to correction and impact. Methods A narrative integrative review was conducted, drawing on research from communication science, public health, human-computer interaction, and artificial intelligence. Results The review identifies domain-specific mechanisms through which generative AI operates across the health misinformation lifecycle. In production, AI enables scalable generation of fluent, expert-styled content through mechanisms including hallucination, amplification of falsehoods, adversarial vulnerability, and deepfakes. In detection, it supports automated fact-checking, pattern recognition, and classification, while remaining vulnerable to false positives, false negatives, bias, and adversarial adaptation. In correction, generative AI facilitates rebuttals, tailored messaging, conversational engagement, and AI-assisted inoculation, but also raises concerns about trust displacement, epistemic authority, and accountability. At the impact stage, AI-mediated misinformation can influence individual cognition and behavior as well as broader social and institutional outcomes, with fluency, narrative coherence, and personalization serving as important persuasive mechanisms. The framework further conceptualizes the lifecycle as recursive and adaptive, such that production, detection, correction, and impact continually shape one another. Conclusion Generative AI should be understood not as a single source of misinformation risk, but as a multifunctional component of a dynamic health communication system. Addressing AI-mediated health misinformation therefore requires coordinated, multilevel strategies that account for its simultaneous roles in producing, detecting, correcting, and shaping the consequences of misinformation, while preserving human oversight, institutional accountability, and public trust.

papers.title: From Prediction to Design: A Paradigm Shift in AI-Driven Protein–Protein Interaction Research
papers.authors: Yihuang Wu, Wei Hu, Linlin Zhao
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) form the molecular foundation of cellular life. Over the past two decades, computational methods for PPI analysis have primarily focused on prediction—inferring interaction properties from protein information. However, a notable conceptual shift is underway away from predictive analysis and toward rational protein interaction design. This transformation is driven by breakthroughs in protein language models, diffusion models, and equivariant neural networks. In this review, we discuss how this transition represents a notable conceptual shift, enabling exploration of sequence-structure space that evolution has never sampled. We synthesize the technical foundations, core design tasks, and challenges ahead. We address critical issues including evaluation bias, the hallucination problem, and dual-use considerations. We conclude with grand challenges for the field: mapping design ability boundaries, designing dynamic interactions, and developing interpretable methods for clinical translation. We further describe how modern AI reshapes computational approaches for biological discovery.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Pharma Drug Discovery, Physiotherapy Practice, and Personalized Medicine: A Comprehensive Review
papers.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) architectures has established a paradigm shift across the continuum of modern bio-medicine.Historically, biomedical innovation operated within isolated silos: pharmaceutical research grappled with exorbitant attrition rates and extended development timelines; physical rehabilitation relied on subjective observational assessments; and clinical medicine administered standardized therapeutic regimens to heterogeneous patient cohorts.Today, generative deep learning, geometric graph neural networks (GNNs), computer vision algorithms, and multi-omics integrative frameworks bridge these domains into a unified ecosystem.In drug discovery, modern AI models execute high-throughput virtual screening, predict three-dimensional macromolecular target structures, and design optimized lead compounds with precise pharmacokinetic properties.In physical therapy and rehabilitation, vision-based motion tracking, wearable sensor fusion, and smart robotics enable continuous, quantitative bio-feedback and dynamic intervention tailoring.Concurrently, in personalized medicine, transformer-based genomic language models and multi-modal clinical decision support systems (CDSS) aggregate multi-omics data, longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), and real-world evidence (RWE) to optimize treatment strategies for individual patients.This comprehensive review synthesizes the cross-disciplinary advances, underlying mathematical architectures, clinical validation pipelines, regulatory challenges, and future trajectories of AI and ML across pharmaceutical discovery, physical rehabilitation, and precision therapeutics.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: When support becomes dependence: conversational continuity and relational safety in human-AI interaction
papers.authors: Xiao Wei, Xiaoyi Chen, Wangahe Jin, Jun Cai, 駱旭琛, ...
papers.abstract: Background Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support, reflection, and consequential decision-making. Although conversational continuity may improve responsiveness, sustained interaction also exposes AI systems to their own prior relational language, potentially shaping how they respond when users become increasingly dependent or surrender personal agency. We examined whether model-generated conversational history alters relational-safety behavior as human–AI interactions escalate from ordinary support-seeking toward emotional dependence, social displacement, and decision delegation. Methods We conducted a standardized multi-turn benchmarking study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twelve four-turn trajectories represented two agency-related domains: emotional dependency and displacement of human support, and decision delegation and surrender of personal agency. Each trajectory was evaluated under two matched context architectures: reconstructed cumulative user-only context, which retained all prior user disclosures but excluded previous AI responses, and native continuous conversation, which retained the complete interaction history. Across 72 model-condition-trajectory sequences comprising 288 turn-level responses, relational safety was independently evaluated for dependency reinforcement, agency preservation, and human-support preservation using predefined ordinal criteria. Context effects and their interaction with escalating relational risk were examined using cumulative-link mixed-effects models. Results Relational-safety differences between context architectures increased across successive turns of the standardized trajectories. Overall, explicit dependency reinforcement increased from 9.7% in cumulative user-only contexts to 18.1% in continuous conversations, while strong agency preservation declined from 75.7% to 65.3% and strong human-support preservation from 73.6% to 63.2%. Outcome-specific analyses showed condition-by-turn interactions for dependency reinforcement (cumulative odds ratio [cOR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.03–1.55; unadjusted P = .026), agency preservation (cOR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69–0.98; unadjusted P = .031), and human-support preservation (cOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65–0.94; unadjusted P = .009), indicating progressively greater divergence between context conditions across successive turns. After Holm adjustment across the three interaction tests, only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold (adjusted P = .027).The overall pattern was observed across systems and was directionally consistent in predefined binary sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Across this benchmark, between-condition differences generally widened across successive turns, although the present design cannot determine whether this pattern reflects increasing relational-risk intensity, increasing accumulated model-generated history, or their combination. Only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold after Holm adjustment, whereas the dependency-reinforcement and agency-preservation interactions were directionally similar but less robust after multiplicity adjustment. The observed pattern is compatible with a post-hoc interpretive framework of relational inertia but does not establish this process as a causal mechanism or demonstrate downstream psychological effects in human users.

papers.title: A cross-sectional comparison of five large language models in answering Chinese-language patient queries on visual field defects associated with brain diseases
papers.authors: Shenghe Li, Ling Wang, Xiaoyan Wang, Ligang Jiang, Weihua Yang, ...
papers.abstract: Background Visual field defects associated with brain diseases may arise from stroke, intracranial space-occupying lesions, and other central visual pathway disorders. Patient questions often span symptom recognition, explanation of causes, care triage, treatment, and rehabilitation. Large language models may improve access to patient education. However, their accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility have not been compared under controlled conditions in this high-risk, interdisciplinary Chinese-language setting. This study aimed to compare the performance of five selected large language models across multiple dimensions. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 30 fixed Chinese-language questions, refined by experts and phrased from a patient perspective, were submitted to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Kimi K3 through a unified application programming interface (API) client. Each model generated one response per question in an independent single-turn session, with web retrieval disabled and conversation history cleared. Three raters, blinded to model identity, independently scored 150 randomly presented responses from 1 to 5 for accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility. Response time, word count, non-space character count, sentence count, paragraph count, and table count were also recorded. Models were compared using the Friedman test followed by Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Kendall’s W. Correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results Agreement among the three raters was high across all five dimensions (Kendall’s W = 0.820–0.844; all P < 0.001). The five models differed in accuracy, coherence, and content accessibility (P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.001, respectively). No statistically significant between-model differences were observed in logic or safety (P = 0.247 and P = 0.061, respectively). ChatGPT 5.6 Sol had the highest median accuracy score [4.67 (interquartile range, 4.00–5.00)], and Kimi K3 had the highest median coherence score [4.50 (4.00–5.00)]. Both models had a median content accessibility score of 4.67 (4.00–5.00). Response time, response length, and text structure also differed among models. However, their correlations with expert quality scores were generally weak (|ρ| ≤ 0.279). Conclusion The five large language models exhibited distinctly multidimensional performance when answering Chinese-language patient questions about visual field defects associated with brain diseases. No single model consistently performed best across all clinically relevant dimensions. These findings are specific to the model versions tested on 15 August 2026; stability across repeated generations was not assessed. Response speed, length, and structure cannot substitute for direct assessment of medical quality. The absence of a statistically significant difference in safety ratings under controlled conditions does not imply equivalent or adequate clinical safety. Large language models are better suited to supporting patient education and clinician-patient communication under clinical supervision than to making diagnostic or treatment decisions independently.

papers.title: Pan Genome to Pan Phenome provides a mechanistic framework for translating hidden genetic diversity into predictive wheat breeding
papers.authors: Ayesha Tabassum, Shoaib Akhtar, Uzma Kiran, Khadeeja Arif, Amara Sharif, ...
papers.abstract: Wheat breeding has entered the genomic era, yet most breeding decisions still rely primarily on sequence polymorphisms, leaving a substantial proportion of functional genomic diversity unexplored. Hidden variation, including presence–absence variation, structural variants, copy-number variation, transposable element insertions, and regulatory polymorphisms, constitutes a major source of phenotypic diversity but remains insufficiently integrated into breeding pipelines. The principal challenge is no longer identifying additional genetic variants but understanding how this hidden genomic diversity is translated into complex phenotypes through successive biological processes. Here, we propose the Pan-Genome to Pan-Phenome (PG2P) framework, a conceptual and mechanistic framework synthesized from current knowledge that connects hidden genomic variation with regulatory networks, epigenetic regulation, protein interactions, metabolic reprogramming, developmental dynamics, and ultimately the wheat pan-phenome. We further discuss how this biological continuum facilitates causal variant discovery, improves trait prediction, and supports predictive precision breeding by integrating functional genomic information with genomic prediction and selection. Finally, we discuss key challenges and future opportunities, including graph pan-genomes, single-cell and spatial omics, pangenome-aware prediction, digital phenotyping, genome foundation models, and digital twins. The PG2P framework provides a conceptual roadmap for translating hidden genomic diversity into predictive biological knowledge for next-generation wheat improvement.

papers.title: Physics-aware neural networks enable robust and full atomic structure determination via low-dose atomic electron tomography
papers.authors: Yao Zhang, Lanyi Cao, Zhen Sun, Jihan Zhou
papers.abstract: Atomic electron tomography (AET) determines the three-dimensional (3D) coordinates and chemical identities of individual atoms from a series of scanning transmission electron microscopy images taken at different tilt angles. However, under dose-limited conditions, particularly at electron doses lower than those typically used for standard AET of beam-robust inorganic nanoparticles, the reduced signal-to-noise ratio forces a trade-off among accuracy, robustness, and throughput. Here, we introduce a physics-aware, two-stage neural network (PANN) that incorporates physical constraints throughout its workflow to achieve accurate AET under low-dose imaging. First, a global-local 3D ResUNet refines the initial reconstruction and corrects geometric distortions in the volume. Second, the local density around each identified atom is encoded using 3D Zernike moments. These feature descriptors, along with the atomic coordinates, are then processed by a graph-attention Transformer to classify the elemental species. We benchmark the PANN workflow using a dataset of 42,588 simulated reconstructed volumes, covering diverse noise models, material morphologies, and dose settings. Under reduced-dose conditions relative to conventional AET of beam-robust inorganic nanoparticles, PANN significantly improves performance, reducing the atomic coordinate error and leading to an increase in the atomic recovery rate. The framework’s performance on retrospectively reduced-dose experimental AET data of metallic nanoparticles demonstrates robust post-processing capability within this material class. Together with multi-slice simulation-based demonstrations on selected inorganic crystalline dose-sensitive systems, including halide perovskites, zeolites, and quantum dots, these results suggest a route toward extending PANN to dose-sensitive materials.

papers.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models
papers.authors: Abhinav Saxena
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.

papers.title: ToxPipe: integrating AI into toxicoinformatics
papers.authors: Parker K. Combs, Trey O Saddler, Amlan Talukder, Jonathon F. Fleming, Jeremy N. Erickson, ...
papers.abstract: ToxPipe is a modular, fully open-source software stack designed to accelerate toxicological data analysis and decision-making by integrating large language model (LLM) capabilities with workflow, monitoring, and user-interface services. ToxPipe leverages existing open-source technologies like LibreChat, LiteLLM, and Langflow to provide centralized and streamlined access to different LLMs for end users and developers and logging and auditing of LLM use for organizations. ToxPipe also allows for open-source/local model support. While the ToxPipe ecosystem also supports advanced AI functions such as MCP server integration, RAG and literature search, and agent creation, we did not observe clear benefits using these configurations relative to the GPT-5.5 baseline assertion coverage scores. ToxPipe is available as a series of Docker containers for rapid and reproducible deployment.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence methods for morphological analysis and diagnosis of bacterial and fungal leaf diseases
papers.authors: Ruchita R. Patil, Annamalai Muthusamy, V. Shwetha
papers.abstract: Abstract Bacterial and fungal leaf diseases frequently produce overlapping visual symptoms, complicating automated diagnosis and limiting the transferability of models across crops and field conditions. This review systematically evaluates artificial intelligence methods for the morphology-based detection and differentiation of these diseases. Following a PRISMA-based selection process, 95 records published between 2017 and 2026 were identified, of which 59 eligible studies were included. The survey covers the morphological characteristics that distinguish bacterial and fungal diseases, traditional image processing and machine learning approaches, deep learning and generative AI techniques, and publicly available datasets. It also critically compares the performance, advantages, and limitations of existing diagnostic approaches. The findings indicate that deep learning dominates the literature, particularly in fungal disease detection, whereas research on bacterial diseases and generative AI applications remains comparatively limited. Although convolutional and transfer-learning models generally demonstrated strong classification performance, comparisons across studies were constrained by differences in datasets, evaluation protocols, and performance metrics. The principal barriers to practical adoption include morphological overlap between infections, class imbalance, and scarcity of expert-annotated images of bacterial and early-stage diseases, reliance on controlled-background datasets, limited external validation, model complexity, and insufficient interpretability. Future research should prioritize pathogen-balanced multicrop field datasets, standardized reporting and cross-dataset evaluation, multimodal fusion of RGB images with spectral and environmental data, domain adaptation, validated generative augmentation, explainable models, and lightweight edge deployment. By connecting lesion morphology with methodological and dataset evidence, this review provides a structured roadmap for developing robust, interpretable, and field-ready plant disease diagnosis systems.

papers.title: Pixel-wise state node encoding for noise-robust event-based optical flow
papers.authors: Eric Yeu‐Jer Lee, Soohyeon Kim, Sen Lu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Mingtao Hu, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Event cameras provide sparse, asynchronous measurements triggered by changes in scene brightness, offering high temporal resolution but also making learning-based optical flow sensitive to illumination-induced noise. We propose pixel-wise state node (SN) encoding, a biologically inspired state-space representation in which each pixel maintains a persistent state that evolves via leaky temporal integration with continuous-time dynamics. By embedding temporal information directly into state evolution, SN introduces a strong inductive bias that yields compact and stable spatio-temporal features while naturally suppressing spurious events arising from sensor noise. Integrated into RAFT-style optical flow models, SN encoding consistently improves over time surfaces on MVSEC and DSEC-Flow, and achieves competitive performance relative to voxel-grid-based approaches while avoiding explicit temporal binning and additional temporal aggregation mechanisms required to process multiple bins. As a result, SN improves accuracy and robustness under event noise and offers a promising pathway toward low-latency, near-sensor edge-device implementations.

papers.title: BioHarness: Substrate-Aware Evidence Assembly for Biomedical Question Answering across Literature, Knowledge Bases, and Biological Atlases
papers.authors: Meng Xiao, Chuan Qin, Jinmiao Chen, Yihang Cheng, Yuanchun Zhou, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Motivation Biomedical question answering often requires evidence beyond topically retrieved literature, including gene alias resolution, database identifier normalization, and atlas-derived biological measurements. However, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems typically follow a fixed workflow and lack an explicit mechanism for deciding when retrieved text is sufficient, when biomedical entity mapping is needed, or when executable evidence assembly over structured measurements should be invoked. This motivates a substrate-aware large language model (LLM) harness that selectively assembles sufficient evidence by combining literature retrieval, biomedical entity mapping, and access to atlas-derived measurements. Results We introduce BioHarness, an LLM harness for staged biomedical evidence assembly across literature retrieval, biomedical entity-mapping resources, and atlas-derived structured measurements. Across 22,123 biomedical QA items spanning seven answer formats, BioHarness improves the pooled score from 62.2 to 67.2 over the strongest baseline. Ablations, case studies, and backbone-scaling analyses show that these gains arise from repairing evidence-substrate mismatches through reranking, entity grounding, and structured measurement access, rather than from indiscriminately invoking more reasoning steps, retrieving additional literature, or relying on a particular answer-model scale. Comparisons with the frontier models and harness show that BioHarness, despite using an open-weight backbone with only 3B active parameters, approaches frontier-level performance on selected literature QA tasks and outperforms frontier harnesses without web access on biomedical identifier and locus lookup.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
papers.authors: Cenk Jiang, Bogdan Bortnovskii, Ijaz Gul, Mehmed Özkan, Lian Zhang, ...
papers.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

papers.title: Two-stage synthetic-to-real transfer learning for automated mammography report generation using vision-language models
papers.authors: Gani Esen, Marat Nurtas, Jandos Amankulov, Laura La Paglia
papers.abstract: Abstract We present a two-stage synthetic-to-real training pipeline for automated mammography report generation, together with a controlled, preregistered evaluation of whether its synthetic pretraining stage contributes to final report quality. Automated mammography report generation is constrained by the scarcity of paired mammogram-report data: public collections such as VinDr-Mammo and CBIS-DDSM provide structured annotations but no free-text reports. The pipeline converts BI-RADS annotations into synthetic reports (400 generated, 390 retained) to pretrain MedGemma-4B with multimodal LoRA, then fine-tunes on 407 real DMID reports. On the leak-free DMID test subset ( $$n = 49$$ ) it reaches ROUGE-L 0.656, METEOR 0.666, CIDEr 0.649 and BERTScore 0.917, exceeding every external baseline, including the published state of the art. The evaluation then shows that synthetic pretraining does not produce these numbers: the apparent advantage was measured between models of unequal adapter capacity, and at matched capacity the two schemes are equivalent. Across 60 training runs over three corpus sizes, three capacities and five initialisations, against a margin fixed in advance, no configuration favours two-stage training; capacity alone reproduces the gap. Two findings bear on evaluation. Under an assertion-level criterion no model fabricates findings on normal studies; the failure mode is omission. Textual and clinical quality diverge within one model: where two-stage training gains 0.058 ROUGE-L, BI-RADS agreement and sensitivity both fall. With agreement never exceeding $$\kappa = 0.14$$ , the obstacle to clinically useful reporting is diagnostic accuracy, not fluency.

papers.title: Live-cell 3D mapping reveals the organized architecture of FG-nucleoporins within the nuclear pore complex
papers.authors: Wenlan Yu, Joseph M. Kelich, Jingjie Yu, Mark Tingey, Yichen Li, ...
papers.abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) governs selective nucleocytoplasmic exchange, yet the spatial organization of its intrinsically disordered FG nucleoporins (FG-Nups) in living cells has remained unresolved. Here we reconstruct the three-dimensional distributions of all eleven mammalian FG-Nups within individual NPCs in live cells by combining high-speed 2D single-molecule tracking with post-localization 2D-to-3D transformation, validated by Monte Carlo simulations and independent 3D MINFLUX measurements. The resulting map reveals that the FG barrier is not a uniform disordered meshwork but a stratified architecture. Five centrally anchored FG-Nups form an annular structure surrounding a sparsely occupied axial corridor, whereas six asymmetrically positioned FG-Nups extend flexibly beyond the scaffold to generate dynamic caps at the cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic faces. Nup214 and Nup153 switch between open and closed axial conformations, whereas Nup98 spans nearly the full pore length and overlaps with most other FG-Nups, linking the major FG zones across the barrier. Together, these features define an adaptable capped channel extending up to ~270 nm across the nuclear envelope, with a ~ 40 nm annular central region and FG extensions reaching ~80–130 nm into the cytoplasm and ~60–100 nm into the nucleoplasm. Transport-route measurements in the same live-cell system show that passive diffusion preferentially traverses the relatively FG-poor central corridor, whereas facilitated transport follows peripheral FG-rich pathways. These findings provide a unified structural framework for NPC selectivity and support a model in which distributed, position-dependent FG architectures, rather than a single central barrier, organize transport. 3D imaging in living cells reveals how nuclear pore FG-Nups organize: five central FG-Nups form a ring around a sparse axial corridor, while six asymmetric FG-Nups form dynamic caps, together directing diffusion and selective transport.

papers.title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
papers.authors: Tirana Noor Fatyanosa, Ummu Ditya Erliana, Mahendra Data, Muhammad Nurwegiono, Eleazar Tadeo Eman...
papers.abstract: Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low-resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain-specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert-curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question-answer pairs built from real clinical-nutrition reports. Rather than a large-scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high-quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate-level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free-form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6-10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval-augmented QA as well as zero- and few-shot LLM evaluation. We report fine-tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5-fold cross-validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero- and five-shot. We further calibrate our LLM-as-judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

papers.title: Integrating predictive modeling, imaging, and EHR-linked decision support in spine informatics
papers.authors: Rohan A. Phadke, Samer G. Salman, Brandon Matthews, Rahul Kumar, Arbaz Momin, ...
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming spine care by enabling analysis of imaging, clinical, and textual data to support diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment planning. Techniques including deep learning–based image analysis, radiomics, and natural language processing (NLP) offer opportunities to standardize interpretation and derive quantitative biomarkers beyond human visual assessment. This narrative review examines recent innovations in spine-focused biomedical informatics and evaluates their clinical relevance and translational challenges. A narrative review was conducted, focusing on AI in spine care across imaging, radiomics, NLP of electronic health records, and clinical decision support. Literature was selected via targeted PubMed searches; studies describing technical development, validation, and clinical implementation were synthesized, addressing explainability, uncertainty, workflow, and regulation. Convolutional neural networks enable vertebral and disc segmentation, detection of degenerative and traumatic pathology, and quantitative assessment of paraspinal musculature. Radiomics approaches extract high-dimensional imaging features that improve the prediction of osteoporosis, fracture risk, tumor characterization, and surgical outcomes. NLP techniques, including emerging large language models, unlock clinically relevant information from unstructured text, enhancing outcome prediction and population-level analyses. Multimodal clinical decision support systems integrating imaging, EHR data, and NLP-derived features demonstrate promise for personalized risk assessment and treatment guidance. Challenges remain regarding data heterogeneity, generalizability, privacy, and prospective validation. AI-driven biomedical informatics holds substantial promise to enhance diagnostic accuracy, prognostication, and personalized decision-making in spine care. Successful clinical translation will require robust validation, explainable, uncertainty-aware models, regulatory alignment, and integration into clinical workflows to ensure safe, trustworthy, and patient-centered adoption.

papers.title: DeepOSSA: a deep learning framework for personalized survival prediction in osteosarcoma patients
papers.authors: Zongdong Zhu, Xiaowei Sha, Chengliang Yin, Ge Fan, Wei Lu
papers.abstract: Background Osteosarcoma, the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents, is marked by high invasiveness and heterogeneous outcomes due to inter-patient variability in tumor biology and treatment response. Accurate prognostic modeling is crucial for personalized risk stratification and clinical decision-making. Objective We developed and validated DeepOSSA, a deep learning framework for individualized survival prediction in osteosarcoma, leveraging high-dimensional, sparsely encoded clinical data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database.
