Methods Clinical data from 895 osteosarcoma patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2018 were extracted. Continuous variables were optimally discretized using X-tile, and categorical covariates were one-hot encoded. We compared DeepOSSA against seven representative models spanning classical machine learning (support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT)), deep learning (multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and Transformer), and survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) and DeepSurv). DeepOSSA integrates a Transformer-based representation tower for high-order sparse feature crossing with a Cox-style discrete-time survival head, enabling joint optimization of feature representation and time-to-event modeling. Performance was evaluated on a held-out test set using the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score. Results DeepOSSA outperformed all baselines in discrimination and balanced classification, achieving an AUC of 0.8058 ± 0.0081 and an F1-score of 0.6506 ± 0.0060 , representing average relative improvements of 13.11% (AUC) and 8.99% (F1), respectively. Among all evaluated models, DeepOSSA achieved the highest AUC (exceeding 0.8) and demonstrated competitive performance compared with previously published, externally validated Cox nomograms for osteosarcoma. In time-dependent evaluation, its predictive advantage over CoxPH increased during long-term follow-up, where proportional hazards assumptions are most violated. Ablation studies confirmed the necessity of each architectural component, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis demonstrated that the model’s risk predictions are driven by clinically established prognostic factors. By capturing attention-based nonlinear interactions and temporal dynamics, DeepOSSA enables more precise patient stratification than traditional linear models. Conclusion DeepOSSA is a robust and interpretable framework that bridges Transformer-based representation learning with principled survival analysis. It effectively models complex, nonlinear relationships among sparse clinical features and survival outcomes, offering strong potential for translating heterogeneous clinical data into actionable insights for precision oncology.
papers.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology

papers.title: Digital Twin-Assisted Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network Framework with Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Personalized Drug Delivery Optimization
papers.abstract: The growing demand for personalized drug delivery necessitates intelligent computational approaches that can jointly analyze molecular characteristics, biological targets, physicochemical properties, and therapeutic responses.This study presents a Digital Twin-Assisted Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PI-GNN) integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to facilitate drug-target response prediction and personalized therapeutic optimization.The proposed framework was developed using 52,274 drug-target interaction records, partitioned into 36,592 training, 5,227 validation, and 10,455 testing samples.Molecular structures were transformed into graphs characterized by 23 atom-level and six bond-level features, while protein sequences were represented through 24 biological attributes.Eight physicochemical parameters-molecular weight, LogP, topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donors, hydrogen-bond acceptors, rotatable bonds, ring count, and fraction Csp3-were incorporated to provide physics-informed constraints to the learning process.Experimental evaluation on the log-transformed response yielded an R² of 0.4209, RMSE of 2.2985, and MAE of 1.5695 for the test dataset.Permutation-based XAI revealed TPSA as the dominant physicochemical contributor, with its perturbation increasing RMSE by 0.1662 and decreasing R² by 0.0868, followed by molecular weight, LogP, ring count, and hydrogen-bond donors.Molecular-level interpretability was further established using GNNExplainer to identify influential atoms associated with individual predictions.Input-ablation analysis showed that suppressing physicochemical and protein information reduced R² from 0.4209 to -5.0589 and 0.3276, respectively, indicating that the trained network relied substantially on these complementary information sources.The XAI-guided digital-twin module evaluated 10,661 valid molecular candidates, with 5,756 satisfying the specified drug-like constraints.For the selected biological target context, Drug ID 1049 was identified as the highest-ranked candidate, increasing the predicted log-response from 8.5935 to 15.5521, representing an 80.98% relative improvement on the modelled log-response scale and achieving a digital-twin score of 0.8905.Overall, the findings indicate that combining graph-based molecular learning with physicochemical knowledge, model explainability, and digital-twin-driven candidate screening offers an interpretable computational strategy for prioritizing promising drug-target configurations.The framework provides a foundation for subsequent experimental validation and the development of data-driven personalized drug-delivery systems.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: From Structured Records to Patient Narratives: Preserving Clinical Alignment in LLM-Generated Health Summaries
papers.authors: Bayram Ayadi, Florian Geissler, Johanna Schmidhuber
papers.abstract: As wearable and digital health systems increasingly generate longitudinal physiological records, communicating these observations in patient-accessible language remains a significant challenge. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising mechanism for translating structured clinical information into readable narratives, but this process may introduce semantic drift, where clinically precise meaning is distorted during simplification. We investigate evidence-grounded health summarization for menstrual health monitoring using a constrained generation framework that combines structured evidence conditioning with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using a prompt-based constrained generation framework. We evaluate semantic alignment using Natural Language Inference (NLI), atomic factuality metrics, and readability measures. Across three LLMs and 4,500 generated summaries, explicit grounding constraints consistently improve clinical alignment, particularly by improving uncertainty preservation and, once faithfulness is evaluated against retrieved evidence, generally preserving or improving faithfulness, while effects on omission remain model-dependent. We also find that improved clinical alignment comes at the cost of increased reading difficulty and medical terminology. These findings highlight the need to jointly evaluate faithfulness, uncertainty preservation, and readability when developing patient-facing medical LLM systems.

papers.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs
papers.authors: Arnon Mazza, Elad Levi
papers.abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.

papers.title: RetiJev: Fast and Source-Grounded Ophthalmic Decision Models
papers.authors: Bo Liu, Lianyu Wang, Meng Wang, Ching-Yu Cheng, Huazhu Fu
papers.abstract: Ophthalmic clinical decision support requires fast, accurate, and privacy-preserving inference, yet autoregressive large language models (LLMs) incur substantial latency and computational overhead for decisions among predefined actions. We therefore investigate a decision-oriented alternative to generative reasoning. Specifically, we first introduce RetiJev-Data, a source-grounded ophthalmology corpus comprising 78,158 clinical-decision and diagnosis questions derived from articles in PubMed Central and a MeSH vocabulary covering 531 eye diseases, and 50,074 guideline-grading questions spanning 11 grading systems, along with a 24,662-question evaluation benchmark. Based on this, we develop RetiJev, a family of 0.8B-9B decision models that directly score candidate answers without autoregressive decoding. Across all model sizes, RetiJev outperforms both a 27B LLM and the commercial Jev 1.13 decision model on guideline grading by 10.4-23.0 points. RetiJev-9B further achieves the highest accuracy on clinical decisions, improving over both baselines by 5.4-6.5 points while matching them on diagnosis. It answers a case in 158 ms on one GPU, 3.5x faster than LLM generation and 470x faster than reasoning. Models are released at https://github.com/Awenbocc/RetiJev.

papers.title: Tracing Hallucinations in LLM Reasoning for UML Class Diagram Generation: An Empirical Taxonomy and Mitigation Study
papers.authors: Mojdeh Rahmanian, Foutse Khomh, Ashkan Sami, Yanchao Yu
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate UML class diagrams from natural language requirements, but hallucinations may compromise the correctness and completeness of the resulting diagrams. Existing evaluations mostly assess the final diagram, without examining the intermediate traces of reasoning-capable LLMs, which can reveal where these hallucinations arise. We develop an empirical taxonomy of eleven hallucination sub-types organised into three dimensions: Prompt Faithfulness (deviations between requirements and reasoning), Code Faithfulness (discrepancies between reasoning and generated PlantUML code), and Reasoning Quality (problems within the reasoning). The taxonomy was derived from 60 manually annotated DeepSeek-R1 traces, applied to 120 further DeepSeek-R1 traces through a dual-LLM annotation pipeline, and examined on 20 DeepSeek-V4-Pro traces. Code Faithfulness was the most frequent dimension for DeepSeek-R1 in both datasets, whereas Prompt Faithfulness dominated for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, suggesting model-dependent failure patterns. In the manually annotated traces, reasoning-trace length showed no significant monotonic association with hallucination frequency, whereas requirement complexity was negatively associated with it, particularly for Prompt Faithfulness errors. In a mitigation experiment on 13 Golden UML ModelSet cases with three Qwen3-based models, adding Prompt Faithfulness and Reasoning Quality constraints to the generation prompt raised the pooled mean F1 score by 4.0 percentage points, whereas a post-hoc Code Faithfulness review provided no consistent further benefit. Relationship modelling remained the lowest-scoring element throughout. These results suggest that localising hallucinations within the generation process can inform targeted, prompt-based mitigation. Whether these findings generalise beyond the DeepSeek and Qwen3 model families remains to be tested.

papers.title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models
papers.authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Long Chen, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo...
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.

papers.title: Verbalizing Activation Differences with Natural Language Autoencoders
papers.authors: Andrea Blasi Núñez, Gianluca Barmina, Federico Torrielli, Thiusius Rajeeth Savarimuthu, Peter Schneider-Kamp...
papers.abstract: Activation verbalizers translate the internal representations of large language models into human-readable text. The recently proposed natural language autoencoders (NLAs) learn this by reconstructing activations through a natural language bottleneck. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond the setting they were trained for. Here, we study this question for NLAs along four closely related questions: (i) Do NLA verbalizations exhibit compositional structure with respect to their input? (ii) Do NLAs generalize to finetuned versions of the model they were trained for? (iii) Can NLAs recover finetuning objectives in model diffing? (iv) Can NLAs be specialized for model diffing? Across four models from three families, our experiments provide evidence supporting a largely positive answer to all four questions. Specifically, verbalizations of composed analogy activations mostly name the target while rarely mentioning the subtracted word, and an NLA can be reused on lightweight finetunes of its original model without retraining, with reconstruction quality degrading noticeably only for the largest model. Verbalizing activation differences between Taboo model organisms and their original models recovers the concealed secret word for most organisms, and reinforcement learning on activation differences further improves this recovery on held-out organisms. We also find that NLAs can recover the finetuning objective without the finetuned model generating any token, since the most informative token positions precede the user prompt. NLAs do not yet match state-of-the-art model diffing methods on the emergent misalignment detection task, but outperform a blackbox baseline. Our findings suggest that NLAs can meaningfully verbalize differences in activation space, rendering NLAs a promising direction for future work.

papers.title: ReflectPO: Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.authors: Rumei Li, Xunliang Cai
papers.abstract: With external tools, large language models (LLMs) can tackle complex tasks through sustained environmental interaction. LLM-based agents are therefore increasingly used to tackle complex long-horizon tasks in real-world environments. However, these tasks involve sequential, interdependent decisions and changes in environmental states. Early execution errors affect subsequent interaction histories and environmental states, and their effects accumulate along the decision chain. To address this challenge, we propose Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization (ReflectPO), a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous error recovery in long-horizon tasks. ReflectPO comprises two core components. The first is Reflection-Guided Sampling. We use branch differences and repeated visits in interaction trajectories to construct hints for error recovery. The second is Tree-Structured Credit Assignment. We organize sampled trajectories into trees and assign action-level credit using parent--child reward differences and recovery gains. Experiments over two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks show that ReflectPO outperforms multiple existing baselines in most domains. It also achieves the best overall performance on average. Further analyses show that ReflectPO effectively improves agents' ability to recognize their own deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue making progress toward task completion.

papers.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
papers.authors: Bernhard Klein, Falk Selker, Hendrik Borras, Sophie Steger, Franz Pernkopf, ...
papers.abstract: Machine learning models excel across applications like medical diagnostics, weather forecasting, natural language processing and autonomous driving, yet their inadequate handling of uncertainty remains crucial for safety-critical applications. Traditional neural networks fail to recognize out-of-domain (OOD) data, often producing incorrect predictions without indicating uncertainty. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for uncertainty estimation by providing statistically grounded probabilities alongside predictions. Despite these advantages, BNNs suffer from high computational costs in both training and prediction. Predictions require sampling over weight distributions and multiple forward passes. To address this challenge, the Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) serves as an extreme approximation of Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI). While SVI assumes Gaussian-distributed weights without restrictions on activations, PFP extends this assumption to activations. This enables a fully analytical uncertainty propagation, replacing multiple forward passes with a single, more complex forward pass operating on probability distributions. Thus, PFP requires specialized Gaussian-propagating operators absent from standard deep learning libraries. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compilation, optimization, and deployment of PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. By implementing custom operators in the deep learning compiler TVM, we develop a dedicated operator library for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. Multiple operator implementations, along with manual and automatic tuning techniques, are applied to maximize efficiency. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency. For small mini-batch sizes, critical for low-latency applications, our approach achieves speedups of up to 3900 ×. Our results show that PFP-based BNNs achieve performance comparable to SVI-BNNs for uncertainty disentanglement on the Dirty-MNIST dataset and for complex OOD detection on CIFAR-10 against SVHN, all while significantly reducing computational overhead. These findings underscore the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation and operator tuning to accelerate BNN predictions and enable their efficient deployment on resource-constrained embedded systems.
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization

papers.title: Quantum machine learning for Healthcare 5.0: Opportunities, challenges, and future directions
papers.authors: Thippa Reddy Gadekallu, Brij B. Gupta, Pronaya Bhattacharya, Rutvij H. Jhaveri, Y. Mohammed, ...
papers.abstract: Healthcare 5.0 combines artificial intelligence, the Internet of Medical Things, edge and cloud computing, and digital twins to support safer, more personal, and more efficient care. Interest in quantum machine learning is growing in this space, but the current evidence is fragmented and hard to compare across studies. Many reports focus on small tasks, use weak or inconsistent baselines, and do not separate algorithmic gains from costs caused by data encoding, repeated circuit execution, and hardware noise. This survey addresses these gaps by providing a structured synthesis of Healthcare 5.0 applications and by offering a practical comparison between classical machine learning and quantum machine learning using criteria that matter for clinical use. We review representative use cases in medical imaging, electronic health record based prediction, remote monitoring, decision support, and digital twin enabled systems. We then analyze QML integration patterns that are realistic today, with emphasis on hybrid pipelines where classical models extract features and quantum components act as narrow decision or optimization modules. Finally, we consolidate the barriers that currently limit adoption, including encoding overhead, limited qubit counts and circuit depth, training instability and reproducibility, privacy and governance constraints, and the need for careful benchmarking and reporting. We conclude with guidance on evaluation and study design to support fair comparison, clearer clinical relevance, and better alignment with Healthcare 5.0 engineering requirements.

papers.title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
papers.authors: Taewhoo Lee, Minju Song, Jungwoo Park, Chanwoong Yoon, Junha Jung...
papers.abstract: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.

papers.title: Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable
papers.authors: Marius De Kuthy Meurers, Aaron Parisi, Bernd Bohnet
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly consulted for moral judgment. We aim to improve performance on such tasks by rewarding good arguments, on the premise that arguing well increases the likelihood of judging well. We train a reinforcement learning policy initialized from a state-of-the-art language model in a self-judged tournament with masked thinking: the generated arguments are judged pairwise on argument quality by the policy itself. As an empirical basis, we extract authentic dilemmas from classic novels, using a logic solver to verify that each constitutes a conflict. We show that our judge rates argument quality like human annotators, and the policy then adopts the language register that it rewards. Testing on the external benchmarks MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES, we find that the policy becomes more decisive and invariant to the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and reframing remain a challenge to validity. Two ablation studies with synthetic dilemmas and unmasked thinking match the reordering gains, but show a weaker register shift and higher sycophancy. We conclude that consistency is not validity: consistency under reordering can be optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal.

papers.title: A new era of GPCR drug discovery: From receptor deorphanization to precision therapeutics
papers.authors: Hidetoshi Komatsu
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play central roles in the regulation of physiology and disease and constitute the largest family of therapeutic targets. Over the past several decades, GPCR-targeted medicines have transformed the treatment of numerous disorders. A major turning point in the field was the deorphanization of previously uncharacterized receptors, which not only expanded the repertoire of therapeutic targets but also revealed unexpected physiological functions and disease mechanisms. At the same time, advances in molecular and cellular pharmacology have demonstrated that GPCR signaling is far more complex than originally envisioned. Receptor responses are shaped by cellular context, signaling networks, transcriptional regulation, and temporal and spatial dynamics, resulting in diverse physiological and pathological outcomes. More recently, innovations in structural biology, computational science, artificial intelligence, and systems biology have accelerated target identification and therapeutic design. Together, these advances are transforming GPCR drug discovery from traditional screening approaches toward a systems-level understanding of disease biology and precision therapeutic intervention. This review summarizes the historical evolution of GPCR drug discovery, highlights major conceptual breakthroughs that have reshaped the field, and discusses future opportunities and challenges that may define a new era of GPCR drug discovery.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Japan Academy Series B

papers.title: Synergizing AI: A Cross-Sectoral Framework for Learning Systems in Health and Academia
papers.abstract: The rapid emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) is reshaping how educational and clinical institutions approach teaching, learning, decision support, and knowledge dissemination.This paper systematically reviews literature published between 2020 and 2025 on LLMs in higher education, then extends the analysis through a cross-sectoral framework to healthcare, where similar dynamics of personalisation, automation, and ethical risk are unfolding.In higher education, three dominant themes emerge: enhanced personalised learning, automation of academic support functions, and tensions around academic integrity and algorithmic bias.In healthcare, three parallel themes appear, LLMs as tools for medical education and simulated clinical training, their role in clinical decision support and knowledge retrieval, and their use in patient education and health literacy.Findings indicate that while LLMs show strong promise as supplementary tools across both domains, their integration remains uneven, context-dependent, and reliant on robust human oversight.The paper proposes an integrated, layered framework, presented as a flow diagram, tracing LLM capability from foundational model architecture through sector-specific application to human governance and measurable outcomes in classrooms and clinics.It argues that a policy-driven, cross-sectoral approach is essential to realise LLM benefits without compromising educational values or clinical safety, and discusses implications for administrators, faculty, clinicians, and policymakers.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: Beyond generalist AI: purpose-built foundation models for transplantation
papers.authors: Layal Jbara, Varun Kanal, Soumita Ghosh, Praveen Manickavel, Mathula Muhundan, ...
papers.abstract: Solid organ transplantation is a defining test case for clinically grounded foundation models. These models have begun to transform language, imaging, and pathology elsewhere in medicine, yet many remain built around a single patient and a static snapshot. Transplant outcomes instead arise from a dynamic donor–recipient–graft ecosystem across the care continuum, under organ scarcity and fragmented multimodal data. Published work has adapted generalist models to isolated tasks, showing component feasibility rather than transplant-native pretraining. In this Perspective, we explain why generalist medical AI may leave transplant care’s needs unmet. We define five requirements for transplant-native models: joint donor–recipient–graft representation, longitudinal continuum memory, multimodal integration, decision awareness, and continual adaptation and grounding under human oversight. We then set out a staged roadmap from data infrastructure and model development through clinical validation to governed, assistive deployment. Early use should remain bounded and assistive, judged by compatibility with transplant biology, clinical workflow, patient safety, and ethical allocation rather than scale alone.

papers.title: A Deep Autoencoder-Based EEG Framework for Binary Detection and MultiLevel Severity Assessment of Major Depressive Disorder
papers.abstract: However, today's research on identifying Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and respective severity stages according to Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals remains a challenging task due to high levels of noise, dimensionality, and small amounts of clinical data.Although feature-engineering approaches have increased the accuracy of MDD binary classification considerably, they seem insufficiently scalable and robust regarding severity stage classification.In this study, an effective MDD identification and severity staging method based on EEG signal reconstruction is proposed.It relies on the Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) method for EEG reconstruction and denoising, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for MDD identification, and Variational Autoencoders (VAE) for severity staging based on 3-stage EEG signals.The CAE approach provides reconstructed EEG signal representations for identifying MDD with a certain class balance.To increase the efficiency and accuracy of severity stage classification while addressing a lack of data, a scaled dataset of 5,000 samples was created through controlled CAE-based reconstruction and augmentation.Then, the severity stages of 3-class EEG signals were identified through a VAE method.The proposed CAE-MLP framework demonstrates a high level of accuracy of MDD identification exceeding 96%.For severity staging, the suggested VAE approach provides accuracy of 97.3% on a dataset of 299 samples and 97.84% on a scaled one of 5,000 samples.High F1-scores were observed for all classes, and misclassification occurs only between adjacent stages.The proposed framework can be used for developing robust and scalable machine learning-based solutions for MDD identification and severity staging based on EEG signals.The investigational outcomes of MLP model, which outperforms other classifiers on other EEG datasets, used in experimentation validates the efficiency of the in identification and severity staging of MDD based on EEG signals.The MLP model achieves high accuracy (up to 98.70%), high precision, and high F1-scores.These results are statistically significant based on statistical analysis results (p < 0.05) and confidence intervals.The proposed model is effective in learning complex patterns based on CAE-based features and can achieve robust and balanced classification results.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: An Explainable Data-Driven Machine Learning Framework for Automated Autism Spectrum Disorder Severity Classification
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) comprises diverse neurodevelopmental conditions with symptoms differing based on genetics, development, age, and other factors.Detecting ASD has challenges as symptoms often manifest in early life and can lead to delayed analysis.Because standard diagnostic practices rely heavily on human interpretation, making it prone to bias and inefficiency.To attain objective and effective detection, machine learning (ML) methods have become increasingly valuable.Thus, there is a need for an enhanced and accurate ML method that can successfully handle feature selection (FS) and parameter tuning for ASD severity classification.Therefore, this study presents an Advanced Evolutionary Framework for Automated Autism Detection and Severity Classification (AEF-AADSC).The major aim of this work is to design an intelligent machine learning framework to classify autism spectrum disorder severity grading.Initially, the proposed undergoes preprocessing of the raw dataset to ensure high-quality input for the learning model through missing value handling, encoding, and normalization process.Subsequently, feature selection is carried out using an Improved Genetic Algorithm, which selects the most relevant features and thereby enhances model efficiency.The selected features are then utilized for training a CatBoost classifier for accurate classification of ASD severity levels.In addition, hyperparameter optimization is carried out using Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy to further enhance predictive performance.To improve model transparency and interpretability, Explainable artificial intelligence is incorporated using SHapley Additive exPlanations, enabling analysis of feature contributions and supporting better understanding of the classification decisions.The performance validation of the proposed approach is carried out using the Autism Diagnosis Based on Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5 dataset.The AEF-AADSC method achieves improved performance with an accuracy of 96.30% compared to baseline methods in terms of different measures.Therefore, the proposed model is found to be a robust approach for the automated ASD severity grading process.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: A mechanistic theory of planning in prefrontal cortex
papers.authors: Kristopher Torp Jensen, Peter T. Doohan, Mathias Sablé-Meyer, Sandra Reinert, Alon Boaz Baram, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points. We demonstrate that combining such representations with the ubiquitous principle of neural attractor dynamics allows circuits to solve much richer problems including planning. This is achieved by embedding the environment structure directly in synaptic connections to implement an attractor network that infers desirable futures. The resulting ‘spacetime attractor’ excels at planning in challenging tasks known to depend on prefrontal cortex. Recurrent neural networks trained by gradient descent on such tasks learn a solution that precisely recapitulates the spacetime attractor – in representation, in dynamics, and in connectivity. Analyses of networks trained across different environment structures reveal a generalisation mechanism that rapidly reconfigures the world model used for planning, without the need for synaptic plasticity. The spacetime attractor is a testable mechanistic theory of planning. If true, it would provide a path towards detailed mechanistic understanding of how prefrontal cortex structures adaptive behaviour.

papers.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
papers.authors: Zhennan Wan, Jianfei Chen
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

papers.title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
papers.authors: Shibo Jin, Zhiqiu Xu, Yiling Zou, Shangyu Gong, Mayur Naik
papers.abstract: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head-to-head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement-learning study with Qwen3.8-27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held-out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM-Duels/EnvDuels.

papers.title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
papers.authors: Yikai Zhao, Saurabh Pandey, Pradeep Kumar Misra
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens - and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. We show that one layer is lost by every mainstream converter - the meaning an author encodes in how text looks - and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out, scored against the file's own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.690 to 0.150 (docling) and 0.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors - five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI's GPT-5.6. An agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling's false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours. A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues - highlight (+0.302) and colour (+0.262), both Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4 - while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within +/-0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8% of 6,460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085 beyond merely preserving it (Holm-adjusted p = 0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (kappa = 0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

papers.title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
papers.authors: Tanu Singh, Aashna Suman, Vinod Patidar
papers.abstract: Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. If undiscovered until implementation, resolving them is far more costly than addressing them early. Although ambiguity and vagueness are widely studied, less attention has been given to assumptions embedded in requirements that appear clear and reasonable. We propose HiddenLens, a novel six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline and, to our knowledge, the first framework engineered to detect, classify, question, and resolve hidden assumptions rather than merely flag ambiguity. Layer 1 uses BERT attention entropy to localise unresolved spans; Layer 2 uses CoT-prompted LLM reasoning to articulate each assumption and its failure risk; Layer 3 uses fine-tuned BERT to classify assumptions into six non-functional requirement categories: performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain; Layer 4 generates ranked clarification options using FS LLM prompting; Layer 5 enables human validation through confirmation, editing, or rephrasing; and Layer 6 rewrites the requirement using the confirmed resolution, producing an explicit, testable, and traceable requirement. We also introduce the HiddenLens Corpus (HLC), comprising 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions across six NFR categories. Inspired by PROMISE and PURE, HLC addresses the lack of annotated data for this task and is, to our knowledge, the first dataset developed specifically for it. HiddenLens outperforms keyword-based and QuARS-Adapted baselines by 71% and 61%, respectively, achieving an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79; its BERT-based NFR classifier achieves an F1-score of 0.847. These results indicate that HiddenLens can help analysts resolve hidden assumptions before they propagate through software development.

papers.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
papers.authors: My Chiffon Nguyen, Tianyi Hu, Vinod Anbalagan, Henry Gagnier, Pouya Sadeghi...
papers.abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

papers.title: BIRD-RL: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning over Stateful Data-Centric Environments
papers.authors: Ge Qu, Jinyang Li, Xiaohan Xu, Xiaolong Li, Bowen Qin...
papers.abstract: While agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training small language models (SLMs), existing frameworks are predominantly tool-centric and struggle with data-centric environments. Specifically, applying tool-centric frameworks to stateful tasks like SQL debugging introduces severe spatial inefficiencies since proper environment isolation typically requires a separate database container per rollout. Naively reusing databases without tracking evolving states across multi-turn interactions causes trajectory contamination and cross-trajectory interference, which severely destabilizes policy updates. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce BIRD-RL, a novel four-stage agentic RL curriculum that alternately enhances foundational agent reasoning and trajectory-adaptive on-policy exploration to circumvent the instability inherently associated with direct end-to-end learning. Crucially, to support this curriculum, BIRD-RL is driven by a Trajectory-scoped Persistent Execution Infrastructure, which enables safe database replica reuse while preserving trajectory isolation. This design improves spatial RL efficiency by 12.8x, successfully enabling scalable agentic RL for complex data-centric tasks without needs of Kubernettes. Empirical evaluations on the BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite benchmark demonstrate that our 7B and 14B models achieve Success Rates of 44.40% and 48.00%, respectively, showing competitive performance against strong proprietary model-based agents such as Claude-Opus-4.6 Agent (48.20%). Furthermore, BIRD-RL successfully trains unified SLMs capable of both advanced SQL debugging and generation, highlighting its broader potential for multi-objective optimization across heterogeneous, real-world data-centric tasks.

papers.title: Opinion and perspectives on artificial intelligence biology
papers.authors: Zhang Xuegong, Xiaowo Wang, Kai Ye, Dongbo Bu, Fangqing Zhao, ...
papers.abstract: As the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with life sciences is accelerating, its conceptual boundaries, methodological foundations, and future trajectories remain actively debated.Drawing on perspectives from frontline researchers active in AI research in multiple sub-fields of biology, this article examines the evolution, current states, and future directions of AI biology.We identify a paradigm shift from observation-driven inquiry toward discovery-and design-oriented research.We discuss the relationship between predictive modeling and mechanistic understanding, the relative importance of terminology, and the future relation of experiments and computation.We argue that future AI biology will require not only algorithmic adaptation or data accumulation, but more fundamental innovations in AI models, biological experiments, and construction of closed-loop systems that couple prediction with feedback.Furthermore, we appeal to the cultivation of nextgeneration scientists who are better equipped with critical thinking and can navigate both domains with equal fluency.This article is intended for a broad range of readers who may care about, work on, prepare for, evaluate, or sponsor future AI biology studies.

papers.title: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 meets artificial intelligence: a comprehensive review of AI-driven advances in drug discovery, structural modeling, and clinical translation
papers.authors: Wanli Sun, Tongtong Huo, 叶哲伟, Wu Wei, Yanqing Sun, ...
papers.abstract: Background Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily, plays pivotal roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis—including cancer, fibrosis, and fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies over the past 5 years has created unprecedented opportunities for understanding and therapeutically targeting BMP4 biology at multiple scales, from atomic-resolution structure prediction to population-level clinical prognostication. Objective This review systematically examines the intersection of BMP4 biology and AI across three core domains: (1) AI-driven drug discovery targeting BMP4 signaling pathways, (2) deep learning-based protein structure prediction and computational modeling of BMP4 and its receptor complexes, and (3) clinical AI applications for BMP4-associated diseases. Methods A narrative review with systematic search elements was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, bioRxiv, and arXiv for English-language publications from 2020 to 2026, supplemented by targeted searches via Semantic Scholar. Included studies were categorized as BMP4-specific, BMP receptor/BMP-pathway-targeted, or transferable AI methodology not yet applied to BMP4. Results We find that AI has accelerated BMP4-related research along multiple axes, though with important caveats. AlphaFold3 and related tools have generated high-confidence predicted models of BMP4-receptor complex architecture, aspects of which were previously intractable to experimental structure determination; these predictions remain to be fully validated experimentally. ML-guided virtual screening has identified first-in-class BMP pathway (receptor) modulators for FOP, although BMP4-specific small-molecule modulators have not yet been identified computationally. Single-cell transcriptomics combined with machine learning have revealed BMP4’s context-dependent roles in glioblastoma cell state transitions and cancer-associated fibroblast biology; and LASSO-Cox regression models incorporating BMP4 expression have shown promising prognostic value in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and gastric cancer, pending prospective validation. Significant gaps persist—most notably the absence of BMP4-specific de novo protein design efforts, the scarcity of large-scale training datasets for BMP4-targeted drug discovery, and the limited integration of multimodal AI approaches in BMP4 clinical research. Conclusion The convergence of BMP4 biology and AI represents a fertile research Frontier. While foundational tools are now in place, realizing the full translational potential of AI-augmented BMP4 research will require coordinated efforts in data generation, model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation. We outline priority directions for the next 5 years (approximately 2026–2031).

papers.title: Fact construction as a missing layer in legal AI: a practice-grounded framework for evaluating multi-agent legal consultation
papers.authors: Hsuan-Lei Shao, Ying-Chu Yu, Sieh-Chuen Huang
papers.abstract: Legal AI research often evaluates large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning tasks under the assumption that relevant facts are already structured and available. This assumption overlooks a prior and practically consequential stage of legal work: fact construction, namely the transformation of incomplete, fragmented, and interactionally disclosed information into coherent factual narratives. This study conceptualizes fact construction as a distinct evaluation layer in legal AI and introduces a practice-grounded framework for assessing it in AI-assisted legal consultation. Rather than proposing a legal advice system or doctrinal rule-matching architecture, we use a role-separated multi-agent workflow consisting of a fact-constrained Litigant Twin, a structured-questioning LegalAider, a NarrativeAgent for factual synthesis, and an Evaluator for factual-alignment assessment. Using 100 de-identified legal clinic consultation records, we evaluate multiple LLMs under rubric-based assessment, comparing generated factual narratives against original human-authored consultation records in terms of factual accuracy, completeness, and consistency. The results show that LLM-based agents can generate usable factual narratives under constrained conditions, particularly when cases are internally consistent, limited to a single dispute, and supported by clear actor-role relationships. However, cross-model evaluator agreement remains moderate, and outlier analysis reveals recurring structural sources of failure, including anonymization-induced referential ambiguity, third-party reporting, multi-episode case complexity, and numerically dense facts. These findings suggest that reliability in AI-assisted legal consultation depends not only on model capability, but also on interaction design, data representation, institutional record-keeping, and human oversight. By treating fact construction as a distinct analytical layer, this article contributes a practice-grounded framework for evaluating responsible LLM integration in legal settings and highlights the need for factual grounding, contestability, and human-supervised review before downstream legal analysis begins.

papers.title: Setting the basis for a natural language processing tool to improve the reporting of notifiable diseases: a descriptive study
papers.authors: Clarisa Cano-Escobar, Lourdes Estefanía Barón-Miras, Juan José Gualda-Gea, Santiago Andrés Frid, M.J. Bertran
papers.abstract: Timely reporting of notifiable diseases is crucial for public health, but it is often delayed by semimanual International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Tenth Revision (ICD-10) coding of electronic health records (EHRs). Natural language processing (NLP) could enhance timely reporting by identifying potential cases of patients in unstructured clinical documents. This study aimed to describe the clinical documents containing key terms that suggest notifiable diseases for informing the future development of an NLP pipeline in a tertiary hospital, and this study also aimed to evaluate the current semimanual hospital notification system. This retrospective observational study included all the notifiable disease episodes according to Catalonian regulations reported between May and July 2023 from a tertiary hospital in Barcelona. Information on age, sex, notification-related variables, and the healthcare area where suspicion was determined was obtained from the hospital surveillance database. The adequacy of disease suspicion on the reporting date was assessed based on the regional public health criteria. For correct and timely notifications, the frequency of the presence of clinical documents and the frequency of their inclusion of terms that raise suspicion were described. Notification delay since the first date of evidence of suspicion in the EHR was calculated. Results were presented globally and stratified by 10 disease groups, with eight being communicable disease groups. A total of 284 episodes were notified. The most frequent group was sexually transmitted diseases (25.8%), with the outpatient clinic being the healthcare area where most notifications were found (145, 51.2%). Adequate notifications accounted for 210 (74.2%) episodes, including 25 diseases. Incorrect notifications were obtained mainly due to the reporting of chronic conditions as onset diseases (34.2%). Up to 25% of notifications were delayed for 3 days or more. Terms that raise suspicion were mostly found in medical notes (93.0%–78.7%). The unreleased clinical draft, the clinical course, and the microbiology reports were available for over 50% of the episodes of six or more disease groups, with a high inclusion of such suspicion-raising terms (81.1%–94.8%). The results revealed suboptimal reliability and faster reporting in the current reporting process. As the goal was to identify notifiable diseases before the confirmation of diagnosis, suspicion-raising terms were frequently found in unstructured clinical notes. Hence, the integration of the described documents into an NLP-based workflow could improve the reporting process.

papers.title: HalluciGuard-eye: knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation for hallucination detection and mitigation in ophthalmic multimodal large language models
papers.authors: Ge Wu, Chong Ai, Weiqi Wu
papers.abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, yet scalable early detection is limited by the unreliability of AI-assisted screening. Multimodal large language models can interpret fundus photographs and support DR grading, but they frequently hallucinate - fabricating lesions or misclassifying referable DR - which directly threatens timely treatment and prevention of vision loss. We developed HalluciGuard-Eye to make AI-assisted DR assessment trustworthy. Methods HalluciGuard-Eye combines knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation with hierarchical hallucination detection. An Ophthalmic Clinical Knowledge Graph containing 47,832 medical entities and 156,294 semantic relationships was constructed from clinical guidelines and published literature. A dual-stream architecture uses a Visual-Semantic Alignment Module to verify cross-modal consistency and a Clinical Factuality Grounding Network to anchor generated content to reranked evidence. The Hierarchical Factuality Score assesses anatomical, pathological, and clinical-recommendation accuracy. The framework was evaluated on four public ophthalmic imaging benchmarks. Results HalluciGuard-Eye reduced hallucination rates by 42.2% compared with state-of-the-art medical multimodal large language models and achieved 91.6% factual accuracy for clinical entity recognition on EyePACS. For diabetic retinopathy grading, sensitivity was 89.6% and specificity was 92.1%, representing improvements of 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively, over MedRAG. In the component ablation, removing knowledge-graph retrieval lowered EyePACS HFS by 9.4 percentage points. Additional analyses yielded 87.6% critical-evidence recall@20, 89.2% lesion-location accuracy, and 88.9% sensitivity in a patient-clustered cohort. Conclusions These results indicate that knowledge-grounded retrieval and hierarchical factuality assessment can reduce hallucinations while preserving diagnostic performance in ophthalmic multimodal language models.

papers.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence for vascular aging: toward proactive detection and management
papers.authors: Ziyun Wang, Yiwen Dai, Chenxi Li, Yujian Hu, Zhengyao Ding, ...
papers.abstract: Vascular aging is a fundamental driver of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), yet identifying individuals undergoing accelerated vascular aging - and therefore at elevated cardiovascular risk - remains a significant clinical challenge. The traditional “one-size-fits-all” health risk assessments are often insensitive to early, subclinical vascular changes. The recent explosion of medical big data, coupled with the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), offer a transformative opportunity to shift vascular aging management from reactive detection toward proactive, predictive protection. This review systematically explores the integration of multimodal artificial intelligence (MMAI) and large-scale foundation models in the identification, stratification, and personalized management of vascular aging. We first delineate the multidimensional data ecosystem of vascular aging, including electronic health records (EHRs), imaging, omics, and continuous physiological signals from wearables, and analyze how deep learning architectures enable the detection of vascular aging by capturing subclinical structural and functional alterations. We then focus on the emerging role of MFMs, which transcend task-specific AI by integrating heterogeneous data types to provide holistic phenomapping. Furthermore, we discuss the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical workflows, enhancing patient adherence through natural language interaction, and accelerating research through knowledge synthesis. Despite the potential of foundation models, their clinical translation faces technical and institutional barriers. We analyze four systemic challenges: algorithmic fairness, regulatory uncertainty, explainable AI (XAI) and the lack of real-world validation. We propose a strategic roadmap aligned with international frameworks that progresses from standardized performance reporting for elderly subgroups in the near term to cost-effective, individualized interventions that intercept the health-to-disease transition in the long term. The convergence of big data and foundation models represents a shift from reactive cardiovascular care to proactive, precision-based longevity management, positioning early, AI-enabled identification of high-risk vascular aging phenotypes as a primary target for the next generation of preventive medicine.

papers.title: Integrated computational screening and biochemical validation identify natural small molecules targeting Aβ aggregation and dissociation
papers.authors: Hyewon Lee, Vijay Kumar, Soo Jung Shin, Yunkwon Nam, Sinae Jang, ...
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ), a pathological hallmark implicated in disease onset and progression. Aβ undergoes self-assembly from monomers into soluble oligomers, protofibrils, insoluble fibrils, and extracellular plaques. Our previous studies have shown that Jowiseungchungtang, which consists of 14 medicinal herbs, inhibits Aβ aggregation and ameliorates Aβ-mediated pathology in AD models. However, the active small molecules underlying these effects remain unidentified. To identify small molecules from these 14 medicinal herbs, we constructed a library of 1,751 compounds and applied an integrated in silico and in vitro workflow. First, these 1,751 compounds were filtered based on drug-likeness and predicted blood-brain barrier permeability, yielding 566 candidates. Second, molecular docking of 566 selected compounds against Aβ conformers identified five candidates predicted to interact with aggregation-prone residues critical for Aβ aggregation and fibril stabilization. Third, Thioflavin T assays demonstrated that four compounds—1-monopalmitin, isobutyl octyl oxalate, pentadecanoic acid, and dimethyl azelate—significantly inhibited Aβ 42 aggregation. Additionally, isobutyl octyl oxalate and pentadecanoic acid disaggregated preformed Aβ 42 aggregates. Fourth, molecular dynamics simulations were performed to examine the short-timescale behavior of the candidate compounds with the Aβ 17–42 dimer, showing transient ligand–Aβ interactions associated with structural rearrangements at the dimer interface. Pharmacokinetic predictions supported drug-likeness, showing blood-brain barrier permeability and systemic clearance. Collectively, these findings identify four Jowiseungchungtang (JWS)-derived candidate compounds with Aβ aggregation-inhibitory activity and provide a mechanistic and pharmacokinetic basis for further development of these compounds as potential therapeutic agents in AD.

papers.title: Are cortical microcircuits optimized for information flux?—A simulation-based reverse engineering study
papers.authors: Claus Metzner, Ali Ghebleh, Karin Prebeck, Achim Schilling, Andreas Maier, ...
papers.abstract: Introduction A sufficiently large information flux in recurrent neural networks, quantified by the mutual information between successive network states, has been proposed as a marker of rich information-processing capabilities. This raises the question of whether biological neural networks, such as cortical microcircuits, may be structurally organized to enhance information flux. Methods To investigate this possibility, we study a simplified model of the cortical layer 5 architecture, in which a densely and strongly interconnected core population is embedded within a larger supporting network. Results Surprisingly, we find that the embedding network exerts a pronounced flux-enhancing effect on the core dynamics. Systematic reverse-engineering analyses reveal that the embedding network primarily generates heterogeneous negative mean inputs that shift the core neurons into a higher-flux operating regime. Replacing the full time-dependent embedding signals by corresponding constant biases preserves this flux-enhancing effect, indicating that the detailed signal dynamics are not essential under the tested conditions. We further show that the information flux can be increased even beyond the biologically embedded case by applying optimized uniform or neuron-specific biases to the core neurons, and that similarly high values can emerge from a simple local adaptive-bias rule. Additional controls show that adaptive regulation and independently tuned inhibitory targeting further improve the embedded network, whereas removing the privileged strong-weight organization of the core abolishes the embedding advantage. Discussion These results suggest that the surrounding network acts as a distributed regulator that prevents a strongly recurrent core from becoming trapped in saturated, low-flux states, rather than as an optimizer of information flux. Our findings are relevant both for the functional interpretation of biological neural circuits and for the design of artificial recurrent systems such as reservoir computers.

papers.title: Benchmarking Arabic Dialects for Math Problems
papers.authors: Noor Abo Mokh, Teresa Lynn, Nizar Habash, Ahmed Elshabrawy, Sara Alhajeri...
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning remains underexplored for low-resource languages, including Dialectal Arabic. To bridge this gap, we introduce the DAR-MGSM (Dialectal Arabic Multilingual Grade School Math) Benchmark, the first manually curated benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in Dialectal Arabic. DAR-MGSM consists of math word problems (MWPs) requiring multi-step reasoning and covers five major Arabic dialects alongside Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The benchmark comprises two parallel versions: translated-only and translated & culturally localized. The latter version adapts entities and references to regional varieties. We evaluate eleven Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models on DAR-MGSM. The results show that the performance generally declines on the localized version, highlighting the challenges introduced by culturally grounded adaptations. However, the magnitude of this effect varies across models, with Arabic-centric models exhibiting different levels of sensitivity to localization. A mechanistic interpretability analysis shows that translated and localized variants of the same MWPs often induce distinct internal reasoning trajectories, even when aggregate accuracy remains similar. Overall, our results show that mathematical reasoning performance depends on both linguistic variety and cultural context.

papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

papers.title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents
papers.authors: Youmna Farag, Svetlana Stoyanchev, Simon Keizer, Mohan Li, Rama Doddipatla
papers.abstract: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

papers.title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Jiapu Wang
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.

papers.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
papers.authors: Mich-Seth Owusu
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

papers.title: Reward Misspecification Degrades Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.authors: Tianyi Lorena Yan, John Hewitt
papers.abstract: Monitoring the chain-of-thought (CoT) of language models (LMs) is a key strategy for detecting and preventing misbehaviors for AI safety. As such, it is critical to identify reinforcement learning (RL) practices that lead to unmonitorable chain-of-thought. One such practice may be unavoidable: reward misspecification. As RL environments become more complex, it is infeasible to have perfect verification, and models are rewarded for behaviors that are different from the true task intent. We show that reward misspecification alone already degrades monitorability. We create a testbed with pairs of true reward aligned with task intent and misspecified rewards that favor a different behavior, so that reward hacking can be induced by training and labeled verifiably. Across three models and three tasks, CoT monitorability remains low as models' hack rates increase: the CoTs keep reasoning about the task intent while the outputs violate the intent and get rewarded. To mitigate unmonitorability without prior knowledge of the true reward or the hack, we collect rollouts with diverse rewards across training steps and use a LM to infer a reward description. We then inject the description into the input, which teaches the model to verbalize the reward. This reward description training improves monitorability by an average of 24% or 42% absolute, depending on the metric, across all models and tasks, and yields CoTs that reason about the misspecified reward explicitly. Code is available at https://github.com/Lorenayannnnn/reward-misspecification-degrades-cot-monitorability.

papers.title: From RL Papers to Framework Code: Inclusion and Review in Seven Open-Source Training Frameworks
papers.authors: Taiheng Pan
papers.abstract: Practitioners use reinforcement learning methods for language models through training frameworks, so a method that a framework includes is one configuration change away for its users. We measure how often this happens. We trace seven open-source frameworks for RL post-training through their commit histories and link them to 6,939 screened arXiv papers from January 2025 to June 2026. Of 1,598 papers that propose a general RL training method, 37 reached at least one framework. Across five quarterly cohorts of papers, the number included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7 while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers. Compared with papers from the same quarters, included papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed a coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Both gaps hold without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks, while code release was equally common in both groups. The frameworks' issues and pull requests show that few methods are turned away in public. More than nine in ten of the general methods no framework included have no thread there that cites or names them, and many proposals that do appear stay open without a reply. Two further records, the frameworks' issues and the technical reports of 13 large open-weight models, show that users rarely report training failures in public and that the reports state 8 of the 13 widely included methods. We release the data as a tracker that links training failures to framework implementations and lists each framework's contribution rules and earlier proposals.

papers.title: AI-Driven Socratic Dialogues as Cognitive Scaffolds in Medical Scientific Writing
papers.authors: Auro del Giglio
papers.abstract: Medical students increasingly use large language models to generate manuscript text, bypassing the reasoning that scientific writing is meant to build. This monograph argues that the pedagogically defensible use of these tools is interrogative rather than generative. We map classical Socratic elements onto clinical writing tasks, compare the two architectures used to build Socratic writing tutors, describe how models are constrained to question rather than answer, and set out how to deploy such a coach in a medical curriculum.
