No study has yet tested this application directly; the supporting evidence is adjacent. A ready-to-use system prompt is supplied.

papers.title: Simultaneous multi-task assessment of five neurological language disorders via cross-corpus multimodal learning
papers.authors: Byounghwa Lee, Hwa Jeon Song, Byung‐Ok Kang
papers.abstract: Automated analysis of spontaneous speech may offer a scalable, objective complement to clinical assessment of neurological language disorders, yet existing approaches are largely corpus- and disease-specific. We propose a unified model that simultaneously classifies five neurological language disorders—Aphasia, Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), and Right Hemisphere Damage (RHD)—and a healthy Control class across five heterogeneous TalkBank corpora (1,638 samples). To our knowledge, this is the first model to combine multimodal input (text, speech, and tabular metadata), multi-corpus training, and multi-task output for this many disorders, fusing modalities through a Q-Former cross-attention module that feeds a shared representation to a classifier and three auxiliary clinical heads (WAB-AQ severity regression, disease-similarity retrieval, and longitudinal progression). Under five-seed evaluation the model attains test accuracy \(90.98\%\) and Macro-F1 \(86.19\%\) , outperforming all baselines, and the auxiliary heads estimate aphasia severity within the WAB-AQ’s measurement error, retrieve same-disorder patients, and track recovery. Ablation identifies Q-Former fusion and class-frequency-weighted sampling as the principal performance drivers, and an inter-disorder correlation analysis explains the dominant MCI–Control confusion, recovers an etiology-based disorder grouping, and finds paralinguistic features among the top discriminators. Leave-One-Corpus-Out evaluation shows that zero-shot generalization to unseen disease classes remains fundamentally challenging.

papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.authors: Yu Zhou, Cheng-Fu Yang, Rui Sun, Di Wu, Sibo Peng...
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

papers.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
papers.authors: Zhengyue Zhao, Liwei Jiang, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao1
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.

papers.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
papers.authors: Nardine Basta, Robin Carpentier, Benjamin Zi Hao Zhao, Dali Kaafar
papers.abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .

papers.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
papers.authors: Saurav Jha, Qianli Liao, Robert Vernon, Sarath Chandar, Quentin Fournier
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

papers.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
papers.authors: Abhinav Khattar, Aishwarya Chhabra, Ameya Velingker, Anusha Kamath, Brandon Norick...
papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.

papers.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Preference Reward Models with Evolving Penalties
papers.authors: Afonso Baldo, António Farinhas, Marcos Treviso, Ricardo Rei, Nuno M. Guerreiro
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models has moved from preference reward models to verifiable rewards, which sustain much longer optimization. Preference models are prone to reward hacking: the policy raises their score without improving response quality, or even while degrading it. Yet for open-ended tasks, where quality can neither be verified nor fully written down as rubrics, they remain valuable. We introduce Dynalize, which mitigates reward hacking online, during policy training. Periodically and asynchronously, a language model analyzes training rollouts and writes penalties for undesirable behaviors that the reward model appears to reward; a judge applies them to every rollout. In clinical counseling and creative writing, training on the reward model alone raises its score continuously but ultimately leads to a decline in external benchmarks. Dynalize sustains longer training and results in improved downstream performance. For example, we find that our method suppresses patterns incentivized by preference models that, without penalties, spread to most responses, and even to the model's reasoning, which the reward model does not explicitly score. Furthermore, we show that its gains hold in multi-turn training, and even after we retrain the reward model on the discovered behaviors.

papers.title: Where RL Breaks: Localizing and Repairing Failures via Targeted Continued Pretraining
papers.authors: Xinyi Wang, Danqi Chen
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve reasoning in language models, yet growing evidence suggests that it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do. This raises a practical question: when RL fails, what is the base model missing? We look inside the RL policy's own rollouts and find that failures are localized: whether a rollout fails is strongly predicted by a small set of characteristic n-grams, ranging from reflection phrases such as "let's recheck" to specific operations such as "the inverse of A". These failures persist throughout RL training, although they are not beyond the model's reach: other sampled answers to the same question are often correct. Building on this observation, we use the failure $n$-grams to retrieve text from the pretraining corpus and continue pretraining the base model on it before RL. The resulting corpus has only 35M tokens, 3--4 orders of magnitude smaller than typical mid-training. We evaluate this approach on OLMo2 and Qwen3 models trained with RL on (1) GSM8K; (2) a mixture of math, commonsense, and knowledge questions; and (3) general math and science reasoning. Despite its size, the corpus yields consistent gains: our approach outperforms continued pretraining on the same amount of text sampled from the pretraining corpus across 10 out of 11 settings, including by $2.0$ points on GSM8K when inserted before mid-training. The retrieved text also transfers across model families: text retrieved for OLMo2-1B's failures improves Qwen3-4B on the mixture by $1.9$ points over the same baseline. Together, our results suggest that where RL fails is a cheap and effective signal for selecting pretraining data.

papers.title: Synthetic corroboration: when AI interpretation looks like independent evidence
papers.authors: Yiran Du
papers.abstract: People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. AI–human equivalence, failure to predict information seeking, or reduction to established constructs would narrow or defeat the AI-specific account.n psychological fluency or agreement.

papers.title: Borrowing Wisdom, Not Men: A Contemporary Interpretation of the Setswana Proverb “Monna Ke Selepe, Wa Adingwa”
papers.authors: Goitseone Emelda Leburu, Kgashane Johannes Malesa
papers.abstract: Proverbs form a vital component of African indigenous knowledge systems, embedding moral guidance, social norms, and intergenerational wisdom. This article offers a contemporary reinterpretation of the Setswana proverb “Monna ke selepe, wa adingwa” (“a man is an axe; he is borrowed”) within the context of gender-based violence (GBV), intimate partner violence, and father absenteeism in South Africa. Traditionally linked to male mobility within extended family networks, the proverb is reframed as a metaphor for the transmission of positive masculine values, ethical guidance, and communal mentorship rather than the physical presence or ownership of men. Drawing on an integrative literature review that synthesises scholarship on Indigenous Knowledge Systems, critical and positive masculinity theories, and strengths-based social work approaches, the article demonstrates how culturally resonant symbols can bridge tradition and contemporary practice. Findings highlight the underutilisation of indigenous narratives in GBV prevention, the enduring influence of hegemonic masculinities, and the interconnectedness of father absence with cycles of violence and relational instability. The discussion advances practical implications for social work, proposing the integration of proverb-based dialogues into community interventions, fatherhood programmes, and mentorship initiatives. By positioning the “axe” as a transferable resource of wisdom and responsibility, the article contributes to the decolonisation of social work practice and offers a culturally grounded pathway toward non-violent, accountable, and relational masculinities that support GBV prevention and strengthen communal care.
papers.venue: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)

papers.title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.authors: Jingrui Wu, Wangyun Dan
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is important for understanding regulatory mechanisms and prioritizing therapeutic interventions. Existing methods have made progress by modeling perturbation-conditioned expression shifts with neural networks, graph priors, foundation-model representations, or distributional generative models. However, combinatorial perturbation prediction remains challenging because much of the response can be explained by additive single-perturbation effects, while the biologically informative signal often lies in a smaller non-additive residual induced by perturbation interactions. Directly generating the full post-perturbation expression profile may therefore allocate substantial capacity to the dominant additive component and underemphasize synergy-specific structure. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SynGeneFlow}, a synergy-aware flow matching framework that anchors the source distribution at an additive prior and learns a residual flow toward the true perturbed state. SynGeneFlow further incorporates perturbation-conditioned gene interaction modeling, where a static gene-gene mask provides biological structure and a perturbation-dependent deformation bias dynamically modulates gene-gene coupling. To preserve population-level response structure, we align both endpoint distributions and biological residual distributions with MMD-based regularization. We evaluate SynGeneFlow on genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks under observed-single, held-out, and cross-modality settings. The results demonstrate that residualizing flow matching around additive perturbation effects provides a biologically grounded and robust framework for single-cell perturbation response prediction.

papers.title: Global Research Trends in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Drug Delivery Technology: A Bibliometric and Science Mapping Analysis (2015–2026)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have emerged as transformative technologies in pharmaceutical research, significantly influencing the design, optimization, and personalization of drug delivery systems.AI-assisted approaches are increasingly applied to predict drug release kinetics, optimize formulation parameters, identify novel drug carriers, enhance therapeutic efficacy, and accelerate pharmaceutical product development.Despite the rapid growth of this interdisciplinary research area, a comprehensive understanding of its global scientific evolution, collaborative networks, and emerging research themes remains limited.The present study aims to systematically map the global research landscape of AI and ML applications in drug delivery technology through a bibliometric analysis of publications published between 2015 and 2026.Bibliographic records will be retrieved from the Scopus database using a predefined search strategy, screened according to established inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed using Bibliometrix (R-package) and VOSviewer.The study will evaluate annual publication trends, citation performance, influential authors, institutions, countries, journals, collaborative networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, and emerging research hotspots.The findings are expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and development of AI-driven drug delivery research, identify influential contributors and collaborative patterns, and highlight promising directions for future investigations.The study also seeks to offer practical insights for researchers, pharmaceutical scientists, healthcare professionals, policymakers, and industry stakeholders by identifying technological innovations that can enhance drug development processes and improve patient-centric therapeutic outcomes.By integrating bibliometric techniques with science mapping, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI-enabled pharmaceutical technologies and provides a strategic research agenda for advancing intelligent drug delivery systems.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: MODELING AND PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF A PVBASED EV CHARGING STATION USING INC MPPT AND ANN CONTROLLER
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified the need for efficient, reliable, and sustainable charging infrastructure.Photovoltaic (PV)-based EV charging stations present a promising solution by utilizing renewable energy to reduce dependency on fossil fuels.However, the nonlinear characteristics of PV systems and varying environmental conditions pose significant challenges in achieving optimal performance.This paper presents a detailed study and analysis of a PV-powered EV charging station employing the Incremental Conductance (INC) Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) technique integrated with an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) controller.The INC algorithm ensures accurate and fast tracking of the maximum power point (MPP), while the ANN controller enhances system performance by providing adaptive and intelligent control.The proposed system includes a PV array, DC-DC boost converter, ANN controller, and EV battery charging unit.The system is evaluated based on efficiency, stability, and dynamic response.Results demonstrate improved performance in terms of reduced oscillations, faster convergence, and higher energy utilization compared to conventional methods.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Engineering Technology: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Outlook
papers.authors: Sabit Ekin, Farid El Breidi, Milad Saadat, Mohammed Metwaly
papers.abstract: This systematic study examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI and large language models, is reshaping Engineering Technology across education, research, laboratory environments, and professional practice.

papers.title: Experimental Design Signatures Emerge from Topic Modeling of Graphene Oxide Literature
papers.authors: Henry Julio Kobs, Henrique Ferreira, Yang Liu, Amauri Jardim de Paula, Carlos E. Andrade, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract The literature on graphene oxide (GO) comprises hundreds of thousands of publications spanning synthesis, characterization, and applications in diverse domains. Advancing GO materials requires a structured knowledge map derived from systematic mining of this extensive corpus. However, extracting meaningful insights from this vast, heterogeneous, sparse, and unstructured data remains a challenge. To address this challenge, Natural Language Processing techniques, including topic modeling, community discovery, and parameter extraction, are here employed to establish a framework. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) was applied to the full text of more than 120,000 articles, enabling the identification of eight macro-domains within the GO literature, and neural topic modeling was subsequently employed to characterize the granularity and heterogeneity of these domains. Parameter extraction was performed using Large Language Models (LLMs) on a subset of 8000 full-text articles, with a proto-ontology incorporated into the extraction prompt. Even with a broad prompt, an F1 score of 94% was achieved against manual validation. The extracted parameters were then clustered through community modeling and compared with the LDA-derived topics. At this intermediate resolution of the literature, we demonstrate the application of a recommendation system for relevant parameters according to the material family and application domain. The applicability of the framework at higher resolutions was further demonstrated through the construction of a data set of CO2 adsorption for graphene- and GO-based materials. This data set was subsequently employed in a downstream predictive case study using an Extremely Randomized Trees Regressor, with different training-test splitting strategies evaluated to assess in-domain and out-of-domain generalization at article-level resolution.

papers.title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
papers.authors: Yucheng Ruan, Xiang Lan, Jingying Ma, Yizhi Dong, Kai He, ...
papers.abstract: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectures, and training objectives; (4) the evolution from adapting traditional Pre-training/Pre-trained language models to the utilization of large language models; (5) an identification of persistent challenges and potential future research directions in language modeling for tabular data analysis. GitHub page associated with this survey is available at: https://github.com/lanxiang1017/Language-Modeling-on-Tabular-Data-Survey.git .

papers.title: An Explainable Federated Vision–Language Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Automated Medical Report Generation Across Distributed Healthcare Institutions
papers.abstract: Automated generation of medical reports using AI can help speed up diagnosis and reduce doctor workload, but currently, the most efficient forms of automation use centralized training, which requires hospitals to share sensitive patient data. This raises concerns about the privacy and regulatory issues of sharing patient information to generate reports. In addition, clinicians have difficulty trusting AI-assisted diagnosis because the visionlanguage models used for automated report generation are not easily interpretable. To tackle these issues, an Explainable Federated Vision-Language Learning Framework (EFVLL) has been created to generate automated medical reports that preserve patient privacy through distributed healthcare institutions. Hospitals can use federated learning to build a collaborative global vision-language model without having to share raw patient information. The EFVLL framework also includes an explainable attention mechanism that will help clinicians understand how specific areas of the image and text are related to the report being generated, increasing the transparency and interpretability of automated reports. Further, the EFVLL will improve generalization across non-homogenous datasets and comply with data privacy and regulatory requirements. The EFVLL framework has been validated with multiple large standard datasets (e.g., RSNA), and therefore it is suitable for implementation and use in a distributed healthcare environment.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
papers.authors: Yinuo Xu, Jadie Adams, Brian Hu, Shivani Kumar, David Jurgens...
papers.abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. We introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Steering and Targeted Acquisition), which infers a latent profile from users' (full or partial) survey answers, and maps the profile through a hypernetwork to a user-specific steering intervention in a frozen LLM to select answer choices or generate free-text responses. Given the same evidence, VISTA matches or beats in-context profiles on synthetic preferences (Food2D), the World Values Survey (WVS), and PrimeX, without adding prompt tokens. To reduce the cognitive burden of completing full surveys, VISTA also chooses which questions to ask and when to stop: on WVS it stops after 6% of the questionnaire while retaining 94% of the full-history gain, where standard adaptive testing retains at most 42%. The dominant steering direction is an interpretable value axis on which VISTA places unseen users accurately. Our results point toward pluralistic alignment that adapts to individuals at deployable cost.

papers.title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
papers.authors: Ponhvoan Srey, Jason Lucas, Pittawat Taveekitworachai, Junyoung Lee, Anh Tuan Luu
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. Specifically, we instantiate contrastive generative likelihoods as Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE), which compares the likelihood of the same claim under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and derive its probabilistic counterpart, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP). We show analytically that CFP calibration depends on the differential error between the two surrogate conditionals, allowing errors shared across them to cancel and yield tighter calibration bounds. Empirically, CFP substantially improves calibration while maintaining factual discrimination comparable to its strongest competitor. Nonetheless, discrimination is uniformly weak across methods in lower-resource languages, which simultaneously undermines the utility of the measured calibration. To this end, we interpret a likelihood geometry, within which an evidence-bearing direction is induced, along with an orthogonal evidence-invariant direction. In our investigation, we selectively align target-language claims with stronger English evidence only along the factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.

papers.title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
papers.authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.

papers.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
papers.authors: Rajdeep Pandhare, Delzaan Bharucha
papers.abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models

papers.title: Sycophantic AI, critical-feedback tolerance, and the case for productive friction in medical training
papers.authors: Zhi Chen, 贾波, 吉康祥, Huilin Sheng, Mengyun Sui, ...
papers.abstract: Concerns about generative AI in medical training often focus on eroded reasoning and deskilling. Such competence-based accounts are incomplete. We identify a neglected casualty: critical-feedback tolerance (CFT), the capacity to receive disconfirming evaluative feedback and remain productively engaged. Affirmation-optimized systems may lower CFT undetectably, surfacing only under authentic critique. This conceptual Perspective defines CFT, differentiates it from six established constructs, specifies measurable facets, and states explicit refutation conditions.

papers.title: Preparing the next generation of health researchers by embedding public and patient engagement into Canadian graduate education: reflections from graduate students
papers.authors: Ingrid Nielssen, Halle Deakin, Rachel Kidd, Minnella Antonio, Ibadat Warring, ...
papers.abstract: Public and Patient Engagement (PPE) in health research has become an established practice and is increasingly now an imperative for publicly funded health research grants. Graduate students represent the next generation of health researchers; therefore, it is essential they gain PPE knowledge and skills within academic landscapes that promote collaborative research with those whom research is intended to benefit. By securing theoretical knowledge and practical experience early in their research careers, effective PPE can become well-established in all academic, health research and healthcare domains. However, many academic institutions struggle with implementing the necessary systemic and cultural change to moving the science and practice of PPE forward within their institutions. Nine students enrolled in a graduate level PPE course at the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada engaged in an end-of-term reflexive class exercise that centred on the question “What would make patient engagement more possible for graduate students during their graduate degrees?” As a result of iterative review and discussion of the responses, four key themes were identified: (i) embed PPE elements into health research graduate program structure, (ii) offer opportunities to support hands-on learning and practice of PPE, (iii) integrate public, patient, and community members into graduate program design and delivery, and (iv) emphasize ethical community-based research considerations and researcher reflexivity. For health science graduate students to inclusively integrate PPE theory and principles into their research work, it is important that the academic institutions they are enrolled in keep pace with current research imperatives, and ethical and funding practices. This means regularly assessing and evaluating ways their institutional systems, processes, and programs are responding and evolving. In this reflective commentary we offer our considerations, and suggested guidance on best practices to continue to ‘move the needle’ on embedding PPE culture and practice in academic institutions in Canada and globally. We hope to initiate response and further discourse from other graduate students and from patient partners who have shared their lived experience insights to graduate student research studies, and mentorship and governance roles in health science graduate level curriculum and program planning. It is important to include people whom health research is supposed to benefit in deciding what should be researched and how research should be carried out and put into practice. Organizations that fund public health research, such as the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), now make it essential that research teams include patient and community research partners in the research studies they fund. Graduate students are students who have completed an undergraduate degree and are working to obtain Master or Doctorate degrees. Completing these degrees often includes a comprehensive research project. This project provides an opportunity for them to get real-world experience working with patient and community members to ensure their projects are relevant to what matters to people and to learn how respectfully and inclusively work with patient and community members. Academic institutions, like universities, are often slow to keep up with this evolving idea and practice. Nine students from a University of Calgary graduate course about Public and Patient Engagement (PPE) in health research, collectively with their three course instructors, wrote this commentary to help universities, researchers, and patient and community members to start and keep discussions going about how to best do this. We hope to inspire all universities to embed PPE in their graduate studies programs and courses. We also hope to initiate further discussion, including from patient partners who have shared their lived experience insights to graduate student research studies, mentorship and governance roles in health science graduate programs and curriculums and other students.

papers.title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning
papers.authors: Oladimeji Macaulay, Ala Jararweh, David Arredondo, Luis Tafoya, Shrey Poshiya, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene’s utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

papers.title: Towards Unified Approaches in Self-Supervised Event Stream Modeling: Progress and Prospects
papers.authors: Levente Z´olyomi, Tianze Wang, Sofiane Ennadir, Oleg Smirnov, Lele Cao
papers.abstract: The proliferation of digital interactions across diverse domains, such as healthcare, e-commerce, gaming, and finance, has resulted in the generation of vast volumes of event stream (ES) data. ES data comprises continuous sequences of timestamped events that encapsulate detailed contextual information relevant to each domain. While ES data holds significant potential for extracting actionable insights and enhancing decision-making, its effective utilization is hindered by challenges such as the scarcity of labeled data and the fragmented nature of existing research efforts. Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to address these challenges by enabling the extraction of meaningful representations from unlabeled ES data. In this survey, we systematically review and synthesize SSL methodologies tailored for ES modeling across multiple domains, bridging the gaps between domain-specific approaches that have traditionally operated in isolation. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of SSL techniques, encompassing both predictive and contrastive paradigms, and analyze their applicability and effectiveness within different application contexts. Furthermore, we identify critical gaps in current research and propose a future research agenda aimed at developing scalable, domain-agnostic SSL frameworks for ES modeling. By unifying disparate research efforts and highlighting cross-domain synergies, this survey aims to accelerate innovation, improve reproducibility, and expand the applicability of SSL to diverse real-world ES challenges.

papers.title: THE SCIENTIFIC DISCOURSE ON PHARMACOLOGY AND BIOINFORMATIC ANALYSIS IN MODERN DRUG DESIGN: FROM TARGET DISCOVERY TO TRANSLATIONAL OPTIMIZATION THROUGH INTEGRATED MOLECULAR, COMPUTATIONAL, STRUCTURAL, SYSTEMS AND PRECISION MEDICINE APPROACHES
papers.authors: Nodar Sulashvili, Margarita Beglaryan, Nana Gorgaslidze, Naira Chichoyan, Vira Kravchenko, ...
papers.abstract: Drug discovery has evolved from a largely empirical discipline into a knowledge-intensive enterprise that depends on the integration of pharmacology, structural biology, computational chemistry, and bioinformatics. Modern pharmacotherapeutic design is no longer satisfied by the demonstration that a molecule binds a macromolecular target. Instead, a candidate must be considered within a broader context that includes disease mechanism, network position of the target, tissue expression, structural tractability, off-target liabilities, pharmacokinetic behavior, and the probability of translation from preclinical systems to humans. Bioinformatic analysis has become central to this process because it enables the organization and interpretation of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, phenotypic, and chemical data at a scale that cannot be managed by traditional reductionist workflows alone. Pharmacology remains equally indispensable because the relevance of computational outputs depends on mechanistic interpretation, exposure-response understanding, and a realistic view of efficacy and safety in complex biological systems. This review examines how pharmacology and bioinformatic analysis jointly inform contemporary drug design across the discovery pipeline. It discusses target identification and validation, structural bioinformatics, structure-based and ligand-based design, network pharmacology, multi-omics analysis, ADMET prediction, and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modeling. It also addresses the increasing role of machine learning, not as a replacement for experimental science, but as a tool for prioritization, pattern recognition, and iterative decision support. Particular emphasis is placed on the limitations of current approaches, including database incompleteness, bias in training sets, uncertain biological annotation, and the common error of overinterpreting docking scores or predictive probabilities as proof of therapeutic success. The central argument is that the most reliable drug design strategies emerge when computational breadth is combined with pharmacological depth. In that integrative framework, bioinformatics helps define what should be tested, while pharmacology determines what the resulting signals actually mean for drug action, safety, and translation.

papers.title: A machine learning-based platform for predicting the potential energy of small molecules
papers.authors: Alexandra Farcaș, Paul Pernes, Aurel Baloi, Bogdan Belean
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of molecular potential energy after energy minimization is vital for the rational design of targeted therapeutics. In this study, we present a machine learning platform that leverages sophisticated neural network architectures to predict the potential energy of small molecules. Accurate prediction of molecular potential energy can facilitate the computational characterization of drug- and gene-delivery-related molecules and support molecular modeling workflows. Our methodology involves designing and evaluating deep learning models, including convolutional neural network–bidirectional long short-term memory architectures, with and without multihead attention mechanisms. These models are trained on a comprehensive dataset comprising small molecules structures. By utilizing atom-wise sequential representations that preserve key geometric and chemical information, our approach effectively estimates potential energies and surpasses traditional descriptor-based machine learning methods. The integration of attention mechanisms enhances model generalization by capturing complex structural relationships, thereby streamlining virtual screening processes. Comparative analyses against existing benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of sequence-based neural networks in molecular energy prediction, paving the way for more efficient drug discovery and polymer informatics. This platform offers a robust, computationally efficient tool for virtual screening and energy estimation of candidate molecules, supporting the advancement of targeted therapeutics through rapid molecule prioritization based on predicted potential energies.

papers.title: TD-interpreter: enhancing the understanding of timing diagrams with visual-language learning
papers.authors: Jie He, Vincent Theo Willem Kenbeek, Zhantao Yang, Meixun Qu, Ezio Bartocci, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce TD-Interpreter, a specialised machine learning (ML) workflow that assists engineers in understanding complex timing diagrams (TDs), originating from a third party, during their design and verification process. The outcome of this workflow is a visual question-answer environment which allows engineers to input a set of TDs and ask design and verification queries regarding these TDs. To address limited training data availability, we developed a synthetic data generation pipeline that aligns visual information with its textual interpretation. We then implemented TD-Interpreter using a lightweight 7B Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), guided by both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). We also developed extensive TD-reasoning benchmarks from simple retrieval tasks to complex reasoning problems in the real world. Our experimental results show that TD-Interpreter substantially outperformed both the untuned base model, and commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.2), on the evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed workflow.

papers.title: Role of Chatbots and Virtual Assistants in the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
papers.authors: Manish Kumar, Pranav Bhati, Ritu Mishra, Rajiv Yadav, Sushma Chaturvedi
papers.abstract: The rising prevalence of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) calls for new digital tools and chatbots and virtual assistants are emerging as important enablers of patient care. In this article, we review their core technologies, including rule-based designs and advanced AI models using natural language processing, machine learning, and dialogue systems, and their roles in T2DM support, such as education, medication compliance, blood glucose tracking with tailored insights, dietary and physical activity changes, and connections with wearable devices and electronic health records. Clinical data from meta-analyses, randomised trials and implementation studies show significant impacts, including HbA1c reductions of 0.5–1.2%, increased patient engagement, and economic benefits. But there are still challenges, including technological limitations (such as accuracy issues), privacy concerns, moral questions (such as bias and access inequality), and issues with broad adoption by diverse groups. Future directions include next-generation AI with multi-sensory capabilities, harmonised regulations, and embedding into pharmacy-led clinical workflows to enable inclusive and effective T2DM management.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: TDD-Net: A Metadata-augmented Transformer Framework for Depression Detection from Primary Social Media Data
papers.authors: V. Lavanya, Ashok Kumar T. A.
papers.abstract: Mental illnesses are on the rise all over the world and there is a need to detect depression through digital footprints in an automated and early manner.The traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) paradigms do not usually have context-based and user behavioral information.To overcome these shortcomings, this research paper suggested the Transformer-Based Depression Detection Network (TDD-Net) that combined textual information with user-centric behavioral metadata built on a fully primary and consented social media dataset.The data included self-written posts, captions, comments, patterns of interactions and anonymized profile data.Text cleaning, sentiment normalization and tokenization were done by using a systematic preprocessing pipeline.A RoBERTa encoder was used to learn the semantic representation of text, and a metadata embedding network was used to learn longitudinal behavioral signals, including posting frequency, intensity of engagement, and diurnal activity patterns.The linguistic and metadata vectors were fused with a fusion layer and a multi-head attention classification head was applied to predict the risk of depression.This transformer fusion, which is metadata-enhanced, boosted personalization in depression detection.An experimental assessment revealed an accuracy of 97.18, and better precision, recall, and F1-scores.These findings show that the model has high predictive accuracy, and it is used in practice in mental health monitoring.TDD-Net is a big improvement over the conventional text-only approach by making good use of extensive behavioral cues.
papers.venue: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems

papers.title: OmniTFT: an EHR-driven multi-target forecasting model for ICU clinical decision support systems
papers.authors: Wanzhe Xu, Yutong Dai, Yitao Yang, Zhenhua Zhang, Martin Loza, ...
papers.abstract: Background Accurate multivariate time-series forecasting of vital signs and laboratory results is crucial for electronic health record (EHR)–driven clinical decision support systems in intensive care units (ICUs). However, vital signs are susceptible to noise and exhibit rapid fluctuations, while laboratory results are characterized by missing values and measurement lags, making it challenging to forecast heterogeneous ICU variables within a common framework. Methods We introduce OmniTFT, a Temporal Fusion Transformer-based multi-target forecasting model for ICU EHR time series. OmniTFT combines state-balanced sliding-window sampling with three training regularizers: frequency-aware embedding shrinkage, historical group-entropy regularization, and shock-alignment regularization. A shared backbone with target-specific heads enables multiple forecasting tasks within a common training and inference framework while preserving target-specific temporal resolutions and forecast horizons. OmniTFT was trained on MIMIC-IV ( n = 13,277) and independently validated on two cohorts: the MIMIC-III CareVue cohort ( n = 4,188) and the eICU cohort ( n = 23,238). Component ablation and sampling sensitivity analyses were conducted using a fixed patient partition and ten different training seeds. Results On the MIMIC-IV test set, OmniTFT achieved the lowest MAE for five of eight targets, ranked second for creatinine and respiratory rate, and ranked third for temperature. In a retrospective analysis in eICU, adding the OmniTFT forecast of the subsequent unobserved 24 h to the complete observed record improved discrimination for incident moderate-to-severe acute kidney injury compared with the observed record alone (AUROC 0.763, 95% CI: 0.674–0.852 vs. 0.693, 0.598–0.787, ΔAUROC + 0.070, DeLong p = 0.009), and identified 73.3% vs. 57.8% of subsequent events when 30% of patients were flagged for review. Conclusions OmniTFT provides a shared-backbone framework for forecasting heterogeneous ICU variables while preserving target-specific temporal configurations. Retrospective results in disease-enriched cohorts support broader external validation and suggest its potential as an EHR-integrated forecasting component for clinical decision support.

papers.title: Tracing the Cosmic Origins: Machine Learning Reconstruction of the Primordial Density Field from EoR Observations
papers.authors: Anchal Saxena, P. Daniel Meerburg, Guochao Sun, Tzu‐Ching Chang, Lluís Mas-Ribas
papers.abstract: Abstract Reconstructing the initial conditions of the Universe from late-time tracers would unlock cosmological information buried by non-linear structure formation and astrophysics. We reconstruct the initial density field corresponding to z = 300, with its linear amplitude extrapolated to z = 0, from simulated 21-cm and CO(1–0) line-intensity maps at z = 8 generated with the semi-numerical code, LIMFAST. Using a three-dimensional U-Net, we reconstruct the initial conditions and evaluate their impact on cosmological parameter constraints. The two tracers probe complementary environments: 21-cm emission traces neutral, low-density regions of the intergalactic medium, while CO traces overdense, star-forming regions. We additionally train and evaluate the reconstruction on maps incorporating SKA1-Low– and COMAP-ERA–like instrumental response and thermal noise. In the noiseless case, combining both tracers delivers the most accurate reconstruction across ionisation states, with the cross-correlation coefficient between the reconstructed and true initial density fields, |C(k)| ≳ 0.90 for k ≲ 0.75 Mpc−1. With observational effects, small-scale information is degraded, but the joint reconstruction retains substantial large-scale coherence, with |C(k)| ≳ 0.70 for k ≲ 0.3 Mpc−1. To quantify the cosmological information gain, we perform simulation-based inference using power-spectrum summaries pre- and post-reconstruction. Across an ensemble of realisations, reconstruction yields the largest improvements for σ8 and ns, with a median aggregate marginal compression of 1.17 bits in the noiseless case, corresponding to a 56% reduction in the factorised product of prior-normalised 68% marginal widths. With observational effects, the corresponding median compression is 1.29 bits. These results demonstrate that joint 21-cm–CO reconstruction can recover cosmological information beyond that captured by the pre-reconstruction summaries.
papers.venue: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

papers.title: ADMP-GCN: Interpretable Adaptive Message Passing Graph Learning for Patient-specific EEG Seizure Prediction with Human-in-the-Loop Validation
papers.authors: Ashwini B. Patil, Megharani Patil
papers.abstract: Automated seizure prediction based on multichannel Electroencephalography (EEG) using Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a challenging task that mandates accurate and interpretable results for improved clinical decisionmaking.However, brain connectivity modelling on the evolving patient-specific and seizure-dynamic EEG signals makes the problem highly complex.Recently, Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approaches have shown promising results for improved seizure prediction by modelling brain functional connectivity and inter-channel interactions.However, they employ redundant channel representations and a fixed propagation mechanism, which potentially limit their practicality.To address these potential limitations, this paper introduces a unified framework that employs an explanation-constrained topology-aware graph learning model.In this context, a novel Adaptive Depth Message Passing Graph Convolutional Network (ADMP-GCN) is introduced that models topology-conditioned message propagation to enable heterogeneous receptive fields within EEG connectivity graphs while considering channel reduction for improved efficiency and robustness.Following model training, multilevel post hoc explainability is performed using SHAP, Integrated Gradients (IG), and GNNExplainer to interpret feature, layer, and graph-level contributions to seizure prediction.Finally, a human-aligned composite supervision is introduced that balances prediction accuracy and explanation quality.The proposed model is validated using the CHB-MIT dataset, and it is found that the proposed model results in improved accuracy of 95.10% and sensitivity of 96.33% compared to existing graph-based seizure prediction models.In conclusion, the results reveal a viable and clinically relevant seizure prediction that balances performance and applicability.
papers.venue: International journal of intelligent engineering and systems

papers.title: Data Optimization for LLMs: A Survey
papers.authors: Ou Wu
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data

papers.title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
papers.authors: Minxian Xu, Jingfeng Wu, Shengye Song, Satish Narayana Srirama, Bahman Javad, ...
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. Results Our analysis reveals that supporting LLMs at scale requires a transition from general‐purpose cloud infrastructure toward LLM‐aware, cross‐layer, and adaptive systems. Existing approaches have improved distributed execution, elastic resource management, multi‐tenant serving, and hardware utilization, but important gaps remain in cross‐layer coordination, workload‐aware orchestration, data and context management, interoperability, security, and system‐level optimization. Based on these gaps, we develop a research agenda covering future directions in sparse and heterogeneous computation, LLM‐enhanced system software, prompt and context management, autonomous cloud management, decentralized intelligence, edge‐cloud collaboration, personalized LLM services, and emerging computing paradigms. Conclusion Cloud‐native and distributed systems will play a central role in enabling the next generation of LLM services. Future infrastructures should evolve toward more intelligent, elastic, interoperable, secure, and heterogeneous platforms that jointly optimize computation, memory, communication, data, and service objectives. Continued advances in system design, standardization, and cross‐disciplinary collaboration will be essential for realizing scalable and sustainable LLM infrastructures.

papers.title: AI-driven whole-life costing for decision-ready UK public building retrofits
papers.authors: Ziru Tao, Paul Baguley, Rashid; id_orcid 0000-0001-9983-5929 Maqbool, Obuks Ejohwomu
papers.abstract: Abstract Public-sector building retrofits in the United Kingdom require decisions that balance whole-life cost, carbon reduction, service continuity and auditability under limited data and constrained capital budgets. This paper develops a decision-ready whole-life costing (WLC) workflow that integrates environmental, social and governance (ESG) priorities with uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence (AI) for public-building retrofit appraisal. The workflow combines national non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and Display Energy Certificate (DEC) data, Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) delivery evidence and stakeholder inputs to construct a scenario library of public-building archetypes, retrofit actions and appraisal constraints. Stakeholder priorities from interviews, a questionnaire and a co-design workshop are translated into transparent weights using fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (F-AHP). These weights parameterise a reinforcement learning (RL) planner, while a Bayesian convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (BCNN–LSTM) surrogate provides uncertainty-bounded energy, carbon and cost trajectories for repeated policy evaluation. Results show that the workflow supports auditable retrofit sequencing across archetype and budget conditions and improves composite ESG performance relative to conventional WLC-only, £/tCO 2 e and static multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) baselines. For 1000 matched archetype–budget cases, the trained deep Q-network (DQN) decision-search stage achieves a 30.03-fold speedup over traditional scalar feasible-sequence enumeration. The contribution is an integrated and explainable WLC–ESG–AI workflow for early-stage public retrofit decision support. The current validation remains based on public datasets and scenario-level evidence so future work should extend the framework using project-specific metered data, digital twins and live portfolio deployment.

papers.title: A multi-stage validation framework for trustworthy large-scale clinical information extraction using large language models
papers.authors: Maria Mahbub, Gregory M. Dams, Josh Arnold, Caitlin Rizy, Sudarshan Srinivasan, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting clinically meaningful information from unstructured health records, yet real-world deployment is constrained by limited scalable, trustworthy validation approaches. Conventional evaluation relies on annotation-intensive reference standards and incomplete structured data, limiting population-scale use. We propose a multi-stage validation framework for LLM-based clinical information extraction that enables rigorous assessment under weak supervision by integrating complementary validation strategies. The framework combines prompt calibration, rule-based filtering, semantic grounding, judge-LLM evaluation, expert review, and predictive validity analysis to quantify uncertainty without exhaustive manual annotation. We applied this framework to extract substance use disorder (SUD) diagnoses across 11 substance categories from 919,783 clinical notes. Rule-based filtering and semantic grounding removed 14.59% of LLM-positive extractions that were unsupported or structurally implausible. For high-uncertainty cases, the judge LLM showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert. Using judge evaluations as references, the primary LLM achieved an F1 score of 0.80. LLM-extracted SUD diagnoses predicted subsequent engagement in SUD specialty care more accurately than structured-data baselines. By unifying complementary validation strategies, this work presents a generalizable human-in-the-loop framework for establishing the trustworthiness of LLM-based clinical information extraction at scale while minimizing the need for exhaustive manual annotation.

papers.title: An artificial intelligence framework for end-to-end rare disease phenotyping from clinical notes using large language models
papers.authors: Cathy Shyr, Yan Hu, Rory J Tinker, Thomas A. Cassini, Kevin Byram, ...
papers.abstract: Phenotyping is fundamental to rare disease diagnosis, but manually curating structured phenotypes from clinical notes is labor intensive and difficult to scale. Existing artificial intelligence (AI) approaches optimize individual components of phenotyping but generally do not operationalize the full workflow of extracting features from clinical text, standardizing them to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, and prioritizing rare disease-relevant HPO terms. We developed RARE-PHENIX, an end-to-end AI framework for rare disease phenotyping that integrates large language model-based phenotype extraction, ontology-grounded standardization to HPO terms, and supervised ranking of HPO terms. We trained RARE-PHENIX using data from 2671 patients across 11 Undiagnosed Diseases Network clinical sites, and externally validated it on 16,357 real-world clinical notes from 143 patients at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Our findings suggest RARE-PHENIX generates structured, prioritized HPO terms highly concordant with clinician curation, demonstrates potential downstream disease-prioritization signal, and may support human-in-the-loop rare disease phenotyping in real-world settings.

papers.title: Joint molecular optimization for efficient virtual screening via machine learning
papers.authors: Naman Jain
papers.abstract: Joint molecular optimization serves as the central focus of this research, which explores the synergistic integration of machine learning (ML) and virtual screening (VS) for drug discovery. This study addresses these limitations by integrating molecular docking and ML to predict and balance multiple molecular properties concurrently. Traditional VS methods often fall short by primarily targeting single molecular properties, such as binding affinity, overlooking the necessity of simultaneously optimizing multiple crucial parameters like ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) profiles. Key objectives include developing and evaluating multi-objective optimization strategies and employing ML models (e.g., logistic regression, SVM, neural networks) to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. This research balances efficacy and safety metrics to refine VS and demonstrates the effect of combining these strategies on benchmark data. This work contributes a controlled, reproducible framework and an explicitly defined multi-objective prioritization procedure intended to support more efficient and transparent virtual screening, offering valuable insights for researchers in drug discovery, computational chemistry, and ML. Claims of reduced clinical attrition or improved clinical success would require prospective experimental validation and lie beyond the scope of this computational study.

papers.title: Ranking and Partitioning of Attention Heads for Sparse and Continual Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning
papers.authors: Ruizhe Shi, Zaiwen Yang, Qiubo Wang, Banghua Zhu, Maryam Fazel
papers.abstract: We study sparse and continual reinforcement learning fine-tuning of language models through attention-head ranking and partitioning. For sparse learning, we rank attention heads by gradient norm to identify a small subset of heads that can be trained effectively. For continual learning, we partition heads across tasks to reduce cross-task interference and preserve previously learned capabilities. Theoretically, we relate gradient norm to training effectiveness, and further characterize why sparse, separated head updates can remain stable. Empirically, across math, instruction-following, and coding tasks, tuning higher-ranked heads consistently outperforms tuning lower-ranked ones while often matching denser baselines, and head partitioning improves retention while preserving adaptation to new tasks.

papers.title: TrajOnco: a multi-agent framework for temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHR for multi-cancer early detection
papers.authors: Sihang Zeng, Young Won Kim, Wilson Lau, Ehsan Alipour, Ruth Etzioni, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate estimation of cancer risk from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) could support earlier detection and improved care, but modeling such complex patient trajectories remains challenging. We present TrajOnco, a training-free, multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed for scalable multi-cancer early detection. Using a chain-of-agents architecture with long-term memory, TrajOnco performs temporal reasoning over sequential clinical events to generate patient-level summaries, evidence-linked rationales, and predicted risk scores. We evaluated TrajOnco on de-identified Truveta EHR data across 15 cancer types using matched case-control cohorts, predicting risk of cancer diagnosis at 1 year. In zero-shot evaluation, TrajOnco achieved AUROCs of 0.64–0.80, performing comparably to supervised machine learning in a lung cancer benchmark while demonstrating better temporal reasoning than single-agent LLMs. The multi-agent design also enabled effective temporal reasoning with smaller-capacity models such as GPT-4.1-mini. The groundedness of TrajOnco’s output was supported by human evaluation. Furthermore, TrajOnco’s interpretable reasoning outputs can be aggregated to reveal population-level risk patterns that align with established clinical knowledge. These findings highlight the potential of multi-agent LLMs to execute interpretable temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHRs, advancing both scalable multi-cancer early detection and clinical insight generation.

papers.title: PharmAI: domain-specific QA generation by adaptive learning and fine-tuning of small language models
papers.authors: Shenbagarajan Anantharajan, Saranraj Loganathan, Rajkumaran Soundarraj, E Emerson Nithiyaraj
papers.abstract: Background Domain-specific medical question-answering (QA) models face bottlenecks due to scarce labeled data, specialized terminology, and constrained computational hardware. Objectives The study aims to develop an efficient pharmaceutical question-answering (QA) system that can be trained and deployed on consumer-grade hardware using Small Language Models (SLMs). Materials and methods The pipeline processes four pharmaceutical textbooks containing 3,977 total pages, producing 7,370 semantically similar text chunks and 2,144 synthetic QA pairs under four questioning categories: definition, mechanism, comparison, and clinical application. Three Small Language Models (SLMs), namely SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5–1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2–1B-Instruct, are fine-tuned under the same QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation) configurations and then evaluated with retrieval metrics (Recall@K, Mean Reciprocal Rank) and generation metrics (ROUGE-1/2/L, Semantic Similarity, BERTScore). Architectural decisions including NF4 4-bit quantization, CPU-based FAISS indexing, and completion-only loss masking are implemented due to hardware constraints and validated via ablation analysis. Results SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5–1.5B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2–1B-Instruct demonstrated identical retrieval performance, achieving a Recall@1 of 0.517, Recall@3 of 0.732, Recall@5 of 0.797, and an MRR of 0.628. Similarly, the generation performance evaluation revealed that Qwen2.5–1.5B FT outperformed the other fine-tuned SLMs, achieving the highest scores across all metrics (ROUGE-1 = 0.47, ROUGE-2 = 0.25, ROUGE-L = 0.38, and BERTScore = 0.72). In comparison, SmolLM2-1.7B FT and Llama-3.2–1B FT exhibited comparable performance, with ROUGE-1 scores of approximately 0.35, ROUGE-2 scores of 0.16–0.17, ROUGE-L scores of 0.25–0.26, and BERTScores of 0.66, indicating lower lexical and semantic alignment with the reference outputs than Qwen2.5–1.5B FT. Conclusion We evaluate retrieval and generation performance using comprehensive metric suites, incorporating a category-wise breakdown that reveals comparison questions to be the most challenging for single-passage retrieval architectures.

papers.title: Application of LLM combined with knowledge base in improving C-TIRADS grading of thyroid nodules
papers.authors: Qian Qu, Hanwen Bi, Xiaofei Yu, Rui Zhou, Zhen Liu, ...
papers.abstract: Objective This study used the unified text-based grading results of senior sonographers as the primary reference (this text benchmark is not pathological diagnostic gold standard) to evaluate the concordance of text-derived C-TIRADS grades assigned by six large language models (LLMs), with and without FastGPT Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge base assistance. Our primary endpoint was the concordance between grading and physician consensus—a measure fundamentally distinct from pathological diagnostic accuracy. Only a small subgroup with pathological confirmation was used for a supplementary exploratory analysis of the correlation between model risk stratification and pathological benign or malignant findings. Methods Six LLMs were configured using the C-TIRADS criteria. A FastGPT knowledge base was built from 11,489 thyroid ultrasound records collected at Yantai Yuhuangding Hospital between 2022 and 2023. Cases were assigned to manual, LLM, and knowledge-base-augmented LLM groups. C-TIRADS grading concordance with expert ultrasound consensus, and grading speed were assessed. A subgroup of 62 pathologically confirmed nodules was used for supplementary exploratory analysis. AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and Mantel-Haenszel linear trend χ2 were computed to examine the alignment of model C-TIRADS risk tiers with pathological benign and malignant findings. Results Among the standalone LLMs, DeepSeek-V3 achieved the highest numerical grading concordance (81.14%). Following the integration of the RAG knowledge base, overall grading consistency improved significantly ( P < 0.001), with Doubao-pro-128k demonstrating the highest overall concordance at 89.04%. Concordance increased significantly for C-TIRADS Categories 1 and 3 ( P = 0.027 and P < 0.001, respectively), increased numerically for Category 2 ( P = 0.596), and decreased numerically for borderline Category 4A ( P = 0.106). The average concordance across all categories rose significantly from 70.39% to 79.75% ( P < 0.001). The knowledge-augmented Doubao-pro-128k model exhibited excellent inter-rater agreement ( linear-weighted Kappa>0.8, Bonferroni-corrected P<0.006 ).
