The average single-case grading duration of all 12 AI risk tiering pipelines (6 LLMs with/without knowledge base) was 1.30 s, which was 15 times faster than manual grading (19.25 s). Stratified trend and ROC analyses were performed on 62 thyroid nodules with pathological outcomes. Within this small-sample exploratory pathological subgroup, the Doubao-pro-128k integrated with knowledge base established a significantly ascending malignant risk gradient, achieving an AUC of 0.783 (95% CI : 0.635, 0.932) for distinguishing benign from malignant lesions. In comparison, knowledge-enhanced Doubao-pro-128k exhibited a trend toward better matching trend with pathological malignancy distribution and numerically the highest positive Youden index of 0.277 (95% CI : 0.071, 0.482). Conclusion Doubao-pro-128k integrated with knowledge base accelerated text grading and improved overall sonographer concordance; category-specific concordance increased significantly for C-TIRADS 1 and 3, increased numerically for Category 2, and declined numerically without statistical significance for borderline C-TIRADS 4A, indicating that these ambiguous nodules require further optimization. Exploratory pathological analysis revealed variable model-pathology alignment at the C-TIRADS ≥ 4A cutoff: DeepSeek-V3 integrated with knowledge base produced a negative Youden index, while Doubao-pro-128k integrated with knowledge base showed a tentative trend toward better reflected pathological malignancy gradients.

papers.title: AI-Powered Scoring System for Detecting Drug-Drug Interaction Insights from Scientific Literature
papers.authors: Charbel Alhelou, Nour Allam
papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) present major challenges in clinical care, impacting patient safety and therapeutic outcomes. Traditional detection methods, often based on curated databases, may miss newly emerging interactions or require frequent manual updates. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer novel tools for real-time, automated DDI detection directly from biomedical literature. This study introduces an AI-powered approach to identify DDIs, assign relevance scores to publications, and benchmark performance against conventional databases. Methods: We developed an NLP pipeline incorporating sentence classification to detect safety and interaction-related content, and named entity recognition (NER) to extract drug-drug interaction types, their clinical impact, and patient features. The sentence classification module is based on a BERT architecture fine-tuned from microsoft/BiomedNLP-BiomedBERT-baseuncased-abstract-fulltext, and the NER module uses the open-source model d4data/biomedical-ner-all. A DDI relevance score was designed to quantify each article’s significance based on weighted parameters derived from model outputs, with weights informed by domain experts (title relevance: 50 points, DDI impact: 40 points, publication type: 10 points). The system was validated on a manually curated dataset. We applied ANOVA and sensitivity analyses, and evaluated performance using recall, precision, and F1-score, comparing our method to established DDI resources. Key Content and Findings: The pipeline was validated on 7,751 articles across 15 query types. ROC analysis identified a relevance score threshold of 75%. Drug-family queries achieved the highest F1-score (0.872), followed by single-drug (0.731) and drug-drug queries (0.684). ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc analysis confirmed statistically significant differences in relevance scores between annotation groups (p < 0.05), with full stratification across all three groups for drug-drug family queries. Compared with manually compiled expert reference lists, our system retrieved substantially more relevant articles without requiring manual updates. Conclusion: AI-driven NLP approaches can enhance clinical decision support systems by providing comprehensive, evidence-based DDI detection and prioritization, offering scalable support for safer pharmacological decision-making. Keywords: Drug-drug Interactions; Natural Language Processing; Artificial Intelligence; Pharmacovigilance; Clinical Decision Support.

papers.title: Enhanced Short-Text Clustering Based on a Multirepresentation Fusion Model
papers.authors: Ali Sabah, Dhurgham Ali Mohammed, Zaid Alaa
papers.abstract: Short-text clustering has become increasingly important because of the exponential growth of textual data. However, traditional methods struggle with sparsity, limited context, and poor cluster cohesion. Recently, innovations have made word embedding algorithms, including Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText, available for effectively learn semantic relationships. Although these methods have advantages, they tend to concentrate on semantics area. These limitations are addressed in this study by adopting an enhanced short-text clustering method based on multirepresentation. Specifically, this study integrates heterogeneous embeddings into a unified framework using weighted L2-normalized concatenation, followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-based dimensionality reduction that retains 95% of the variance, thereby create a unified semantic representation. Unlike simple concatenation approaches of embeddings, pre-space normalization operations are added before the fusion operation to avoid the presence of dominant embedding bias. The proposed model was evaluated on four benchmark datasets, namely, StackOverflow, AgNews, BioASQ, and SearchSnippet, via the k-means and k-medoids clustering algorithms. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in the clustering quality metrics. Compared with the results of the baseline models Bag of Words (BoW)/Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), the average gains were statistically significant: 29% in silhouette score, 8% in adjusted Rand index, and 8% in normalized mutual information over the best (single) embedding baseline (GloVe with k-medoids) and 63%, 35%, and 40%, respectively, over traditional BoW/TF-IDF methods. Most improvements are found to be statistically significant at p < 0.05. Additionally, PCA was applied to reduce noise and dimensionality, potentially improving clustering outcomes. Received: 5 February 2026 | Revised: 12 June 2026 | Accepted: 14 August 2026 Conflicts of Interest The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement Data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Author Contribution Statement Ali Sabah: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization. Dhurgham Ali Mohammed: Software, Validation, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – review & editing, Visualization. Zaid Alaa: Methodology, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – review & editing, Visualization.
papers.venue: Journal of Computational and Cognitive Engineering

papers.title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
papers.authors: Joran Michiels, Anis Ismail, Maarten De Vos, Alejandro Sifrim
papers.abstract: Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl's do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-$β$ stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning using pretreatment complete blood count parameters and demographic characteristics for gastric cancer risk stratification: a temporal validation study
papers.authors: Yongfeng Qiao, Qian Long, Jin Tang, Xin Wang, 王守力
papers.abstract: Background Gastric cancer (GC) is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, while endoscopy is invasive and conventional serum tumour markers have limited sensitivity. A low-cost, widely available tool that can identify patients at higher risk and prioritise them for endoscopic evaluation could therefore strengthen early-detection pathways. The complete blood count (CBC) is routinely available and well suited to such first-contact risk stratification; however, existing CBC-based machine-learning models are often developed in cohorts that mix prevalent, postoperative, on-treatment and surveillance records, potentially confounding the haematological signal. We therefore developed and temporally validated an explainable CBC-based model to stratify the risk of newly diagnosed GC versus benign gastric disease in a rigorously verified, treatment-naïve cohort. Methods In this retrospective single-centre study, 2,044 patients (477 pathologically confirmed, newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve GC and 1,567 benign gastric-disease controls) were assembled through case-by-case chart review, patient-level identity de-duplication and application of the same prespecified comorbidity-screening criteria. The baseline CBC was obtained at admission before treatment. A parsimonious model incorporated six routinely available variables: age, sex, and neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte and platelet counts. Eight algorithms were trained using five-fold cross-validation in the training cohort (n = 1,309) and evaluated in a temporally separated validation cohort (n = 735). Random forest was designated as the reference explainable model and interpreted using SHAP. Model behaviour in tumour-marker-negative GC and robustness in sensitivity analyses were also assessed. Results Discrimination was similar across algorithms. In temporal validation, random forest achieved an AUC of 0.831 (95% CI 0.798–0.864), which was numerically similar to that of the highest-AUC model, XGBoost (AUC 0.832), with substantially overlapping 95% confidence intervals. Random forest had a low Brier score (0.133) and showed positive net benefit across the evaluated threshold-probability range. SHAP identified lymphocyte count, male sex and age as the leading predictors, with an identical feature ranking under XGBoost (Spearman ρ = 1.00). Adding derived inflammatory ratios did not improve discrimination (ΔAUC −0.010, p = 0.139). Among temporal-validation patients with triple-negative GC, defined as CEA-, CA19-9- and CA72-4-negative disease, the model classified 62.7% (95% CI 50.0–73.9) as high risk. Conclusions A six-variable model combining pretreatment CBC parameters with age and sex discriminated newly diagnosed GC from benign gastric disease in a temporally separated validation cohort and showed broadly acceptable graphical calibration and a low Brier score. The model classified a substantial proportion of tumour-marker-negative GC cases as high risk, supporting further evaluation as a low-cost pre-endoscopic triage aid. External multicentre validation is required.

papers.title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions
papers.authors: Alexey A. Bokov, Ivan I. Panin, Nikolay B. Nechaev, Mikhail Yu. Valkov, Valeria Yu. Chernina...
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM--MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Eight single-model pipelines generated independent role-specific opinions and interactive-consilium reports under free-form and structured clinical-reasoning conditions. A physician-calibrated LLM Judge evaluated 3,040 final reports and the corresponding structured primary-role outputs. Model identity separated report quality more strongly than response format. Structured final reports had higher overall mean scores in seven of eight model pipelines, with their clearest advantage in management (2.740 vs. 2.436). Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation.

papers.title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty
papers.authors: Yuan-Chen Chang, Niklas Herbster, Gauthier Gidel, Tommaso Tosato
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishonesty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model's hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data.

papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.authors: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar...
papers.abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing
papers.authors: Tianxiang Fei, Jiazheng Kang, Mao Zheng, Xingyan He, Xiang Yu
papers.abstract: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory-30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.

papers.title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
papers.authors: Daniel Palacios, Guantong Qi, Mikael Guzman Karlsson, Shawntel K. David, Mohammed Sameeruddin...
papers.abstract: Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.

papers.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
papers.authors: Manya Wadhwa, Pranav Narayanan Venkit, Hiroaki Hayashi, Yu Li, Tuhin Chakrabarty...
papers.abstract: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.

papers.title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
papers.authors: Yufeng Peng, Yixin Zhang, Ziyi Liu, Zhikun Xu, Jiarong Yang...
papers.abstract: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.

papers.title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
papers.authors: Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

papers.title: Stress-testing consentAI: a pipeline for evaluating a conversational educational adjunct to surgical informed consent
papers.authors: Anthony Abou Mrad, Jayanth S. Pratap, Aviona Conti, William Azar, Paola Vargas, ...
papers.abstract: Informed consent is delivered inconsistently, and the comprehension it should produce is often poor. We built ConsentAI, a conversational educational adjunct that guides patients through a surgeon-authored consent form and gates progression on demonstrated understanding. Before any patient-facing trial, we asked how such an agent can be evaluated at scale, and which methods can be trusted. Eight clinicians scored 50 simulated laparoscopic cholecystectomy sessions on a 10-item rubric. We tested four LLM judge architectures against this clinician reference under a pre-specified, imbalance-robust plan. No single judge reproduced clinicians’ failure calls. Only jury aggregation improved sensitivity (0.421; 95% CI, 0.26–0.61), and no architecture reached a usable triage point. A constant pass-everything labeler topped raw agreement and AC1 yet scored zero on Matthews correlation and Cohen’s kappa. Evaluating clinical conversational agents therefore requires multiple clinician ratings and imbalance-robust metrics, treating clinician adjudication as a measurement layer, not ground truth.

papers.title: Research progress on the application of multi-scale computational methods in the research and development of anti-tuberculosis infection drugs
papers.authors: yajing ZHAO, Chao Wang, Wenjing Shang, Xun Peng, Mingyu Zhang, ...
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), driven by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a leading cause of mortality from infectious disease worldwide.​ The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains—coupled with protracted treatment regimens and the persistence of latent infection—has not only compromised first-line chemotherapies but also underscored the stagnation of conventional drug development pipelines. In this review, we systematically synthesize how multi-scale computational strategies are reshaping anti-TB drug discovery and explicitly delineate their hierarchical integration—a cohesive framework that, to our knowledge, has yet to be comprehensively mapped in the existing literature.​ We survey four interconnected computational layers: (i) systems and network pharmacology for macroscopic target and pathway prioritization; (ii) machine learning (ML) for mesoscopic virtual screening, resistance classification, and ADMET prediction; (iii) molecular docking for microscopic elucidation of ligand–target binding modes; and (iv) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for atomic-level validation of binding poses and assessment of complex stability. Representative studies demonstrate that this workflow has pinpointed pivotal TB vulnerabilities (e.g., MmpL3, InhA, DprE1, ATP synthase, and FtsZ), enabled ML models to predict drug resistance from genomic data with high fidelity, and identified promising candidates such as vazabitide A (predicted binding affinity of −85.8 kcal/mol against Pks13) alongside repurposed agents (e.g., aldoxorubicin, quarfloxin). Critically, these computational predictions are reinforced by orthogonal experimental validation spanning in vitro enzymatic and phenotypic assays, in vivo infection models, clinical pharmacokinetic profiling, and multi-omics corroboration. We conclude that the top-down pipeline-spanning network pharmacology to ML, docking, and MD-integrated with bottom-up feedback constitutes a closed-loop paradigm that accelerates lead identification while addressing emergent drug resistance.​ Nevertheless, inherent limitations in predictive reliability and cross-layer error propagation necessitate rigorous downstream experimental validation. Looking forward, generative artificial intelligence, self-driving laboratories, and standardized cross-method benchmarking are poised to consolidate this multi-scale pipeline into a robust engine for next-generation anti-TB therapeutics.

papers.title: Nonuniformity in Multi‑Physical Field Drying of Fruits and Vegetables: Mechanisms, Cascade Amplification, and Artificial Intelligence–Driven Control
papers.authors: Yabin Feng, Yao Wang, Kui Suo, Jixian Zhang, Zhenfeng Yang, ...
papers.abstract: Nonuniformity is the most critical yet unresolved bottleneck limiting the industrial adoption of multi-physical field drying (microwave, radio frequency, infrared, and ultrasound) for fruits and vegetables. While individual physical field technologies and AI applications have been reviewed separately, a conceptual framework that explains how nonuniformity originates, amplifies, and can be intelligently controlled is currently lacking. This review provides a problem-driven analysis of nonuniformity in physical field drying, proposing a three-stage cascade framework (Initiation → Amplification → Termination) to elucidate the multi-scale coupling between microscopic energy defects and macroscopic quality failure. We further critically evaluate the transition from black-box artificial intelligence (AI) modeling to advanced closed-loop intelligent control strategies involving physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and digital twins, structured along a perception-prediction-control paradigm. The cascade framework reveals that initial minor heterogeneities are self-reinforced through positive feedback loops, necessitating early-warning prediction. AI-driven adaptive control, coupled with synergistic cross-field designs, may provide opportunities to interrupt this amplification process at early stages. We provide a strategic roadmap emphasizing multimodal sensing and physics-based hybrid modeling to achieve precision, uniformity, and sustainability in next-generation industrial drying systems. This review offers a distinctive problem‑oriented perspective that complements prior technology‑centric surveys by placing nonuniformity as the central narrative and offering a conceptual framework for its prediction and control.
papers.venue: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety

papers.title: Landscape and training opportunities in artificial intelligence for biosciences in Latin America: the BiotrAIn project
papers.authors: José Arturo Molina-Mora, Flavio E. Spetale, Túlio de Lima Campos, Pedro Eduardo Romero, Lucas Inchausti, ...
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining biosciences by enabling the analysis of complex, large-scale biological and medical data. Latin America has demonstrated remarkable potential through studies applying AI to biomedical sciences often using locally generated data and addressing regional needs. However, the integration of AI into research and healthcare in this region faces several structural challenges, including insufficient infrastructure, lack of specialized training, fragmented research systems, and continuously constrained funding. To overcome existing limitations, capacity building at the regional level is crucial. This includes developing localized AI training programs and the reinforcement of a collaborative research framework. Collaboration across institutions and countries, along with engagement from industry and government, is key to fostering an enabling environment for the responsible and effective use of AI. One promising response to these challenges is the BiotrAIn project, a partnership involving EMBL-EBI, the University of Costa Rica, and CABANAnet, with support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. The project is structured around three pillars: knowledge exchange, curriculum development, and regional training. BiotrAIn exemplifies how strategically designed, regionally adapted programs can build AI capacity in biosciences and foster more equitable scientific development across Latin America. Strategic efforts like BiotrAIn serve as essential building blocks toward a more robust, ethical, and sustainable AI ecosystem in the region, while offering a model that could be adapted by other regions globally. Ultimately, with coordinated investment, inclusive policies, and collaborative networks, Latin America can position itself as a significant contributor to global AI-driven bioscience.

papers.title: Deep learning for biodegradable metallic biomaterials: from degradation modeling to performance prediction with a practical case study
papers.authors: Tongfei Shen, Xiaohui Wang, Huaicheng Li, 潘中泽, Zhaoliang Gao
papers.abstract: Biodegradable metallic implants are transitioning from laboratory concept to clinical deployment, yet predicting their corrosion rate and residual strength in the physiological environment remains a substantial scientific challenge. The interplay of electrochemical, mechanical, and biological factors creates a high-dimensional problem that conventional modelling cannot easily capture, while experimental datasets are often too sparse and fragmented for traditional statistical approaches. Deep learning architectures, including graph, recurrent, and transformer networks, combined with physics-informed loss functions, now offer accurate forecasts of degradation rates, yield strength, and biological responses. Interpretation tools such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and attention mapping further reveal which alloying elements and processing parameters dominate performance, tightening the prediction-experiment loop. This work also demonstrates MAGIC (Multi-task Alloy Gated-network with Integrated Constraints), a multi-task learner that fuses composition and processing modalities through learned uncertainty weighting. On a magnesium alloy dataset of 600 records it delivers cross-validated R 2 values of 0.864 for ultimate tensile strength and 0.907 for yield strength, with root-mean-square errors of 28.0 and 26.8 MPa for ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS), outperforming seven standard baselines and providing a reproducible template. The boundary of this contribution is explicitly emphasised: MAGIC predicts the pristine (as-processed) ultimate tensilestrength and yield strength of undegraded material; it does not predict corrosion rates or post-implantation residual strength, and the coupling between corrosion damage and mechanical degradation is identified as a key open direction rather than a solved capability. Substantial barriers persist, notably the gap between in vitro and in vivo environments, scarce openly shared data, and the rigorous demands of clinical validation. Nevertheless, deep learning is progressively integrating into biodegradable metal research, and the central question is evolving from feasibility to whether the community can establish the required data infrastructure and interdisciplinary trust.

papers.title: Manacá-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge
papers.authors: Bruno Leonardo Santos Menezes, Carlos Leonardo Souza Cardoso, Fabio André Machado Porto
papers.abstract: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. We document three DPO attempts, all negative, including a case where the training reward margin reaches 1.0 while free generation does not change at all, and show that safety came from a dedicated safety-SFT (LLM-jp AnswerCarefully style), refined over three iterations until closing the safety-helpfulness frontier. A controlled scan of the fraction of general data in the safety-SFT mix (10% to 60%) reveals a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40-50%. The final model is compared against four external PT-BR models on the same items, with Wilson confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction: the lower bound of its safety interval (94.1%) lies above the upper bound of all four baselines. We also report a methodological finding for LLM-judge evaluation: on two of six safety items in MT-Bench-PT, the judge categorically refuses to assign a score regardless of the evaluated response, silently reducing the effective N of that category in every prior report of the project. We complement this with an n-gram decontamination check and a Chinchilla-anchored compute-budget table that attributes the gap in general capability to pre-training scale rather than alignment methodology. All code, raw data, logs, and scripts that produce every reported number are publicly released.

papers.title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Rusali Saha, Nitya Khurana, Ruihong Huang, Kuan-Hao Huang
papers.abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. Across six LLMs, we find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at one point in time but do not reliably capture how those attitudes change. Their predictions for different years tend to stay close together, failing to capture much of the observed change. Specifying the intended year in the prompt also offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses. These findings suggest that models often present a largely static picture of cultural attitudes, highlighting the need to evaluate cultural awareness across time.

papers.title: Equal CER, Unequal Damage: Severity-Weighted Character Error Rate for OCR
papers.authors: Nguyen Nguyen, Yongyi Zang
papers.abstract: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a typo as much as a wrong name. We introduce semCER, which keeps CER's alignment and denominator and charges each grapheme edit a severity from an LLM judge, with no word segmentation. Normalized CER keeps the score of a whole transcription, where it tracks readers as well as semCER or better, and semCER breaks that score down into named edits. The charges track readers' ratings edit by edit in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese and put the edits readers rate most severe near the top of a sorted list. On pairs drawn where CER and semCER disagreed, readers side with semCER more often than with normalized CER in English and Chinese, and equally often in Vietnamese. Across 16 languages, the judge charges a wrong diacritic or tone mark almost nothing in Spanish but nearly a wrong letter's severity in Telugu. Where we can count real words, a general VLM's wrong letter forms one far above chance while a classical pipeline's stays near it. We release the 61 million judged edits, the aggregated reader ratings, and the distilled scorer at https://github.com/nguyenx2t/semcer.

papers.title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech
papers.authors: Ghazal Kalhor, Sima Kamandloo, Mehrsa Shamsian, Behnam Bahrak
papers.abstract: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. In this study, we introduce a fine-grained, multi-hop benchmark for explainable Persian hate speech analysis, covering content triage, target identification, hate tactic and moral foundation analysis, textual evidence extraction, harmful narrative inference, and severity assessment. By evaluating state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), we find that performance generally declines as tasks require more fine-grained semantic and inferential reasoning. Proprietary models generally outperform open-weight models, while reasoning-oriented models show no consistent advantage. Incorporating intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves severity prediction compared with one-shot assessment. Our analysis further reveals that Incitement to Violence or Harm is most strongly associated with higher severity, while political-affiliation targets are particularly associated with subversion-based moral framing. Overall, this work provides insights into LLM-based hate speech analysis and supports more accountable moderation of Persian-language social media. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/From-Triage-to-Impact.

papers.title: Taking the PULSE of Medical Reasoning: Step-Level Retrieval Timing for Knowledge-Grounded Inference
papers.authors: Danyang Zhao, Sendong Zhao, Yanrui Du, Haochun Wang, Ming Ma...
papers.abstract: Reliable medical reasoning requires LLMs to dynamically access external biomedical evidence to improve factual trustworthiness and reasoning accuracy. However, indiscriminate retrieval can introduce noise and latency, raising a critical retrieval-timing problem: at each reasoning step, the system must decide whether the model's internal knowledge is reliable or external evidence is needed. We propose PUlSE, a lightweight probing method that uses the model's internal representations as intrinsic signals for step-level retrieval control. Our posterior trajectory analysis reveals that erroneous steps exhibit substantially higher inter-layer volatility than correct ones, suggesting unstable internal knowledge. Based on this finding, PUlSE trains a compact probe on inter-layer geometric features to detect factual errors upon step completion, and uses it as an adaptive trigger for retrieval and step regeneration. Across four medical benchmarks, PUlSE-timed retrieval matches exhaustive per-step retrieval in accuracy while reducing retrieval calls by 72%, and can transfer to an unseen legal domain, indicating potential domain-agnostic generality. Overall, our study provides an initial step toward shifting retrieval-trigger design from surface-level confidence estimates to internal activation dynamics for adaptive access.

papers.title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
papers.authors: Haocheng Yang, Licheng Pan, Yiming Dong, Xiaoxi Li, Yuan Lu...
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. Although some methods prompt an LLM to directly assign weights, direct weighting requires a holistic judgment over all criteria that LLMs struggle to make reliably. To address these limitations, we propose Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting (ICW), which derives the weights of criteria from pairwise importance comparisons made by an LLM. Specifically, ICW transforms the holistic judgment over all criteria into a series of pairwise importance comparisons, checks and revises inconsistent comparisons, and derives the weights from the principal eigenvector of the comparison matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ICW consistently outperforms uniform weighting and competitive weighting methods, and translates into better policy models in downstream reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
papers.authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and anti-cancer drugs: advancing discovery, personalization, and precision oncology
papers.authors: Faizan ul Haque Nagrami, Pahchan Shukla, Ruchi Yadav, Jyoti Prakash
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics. By summarizing current evidence and targeting research gaps, this review offers a clear view of how AI is enhancing the discovery, personalization, and validation of anticancer treatments.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation
papers.authors: Zijian Cao, Pei Zheng, Zhihui Qi, Yang Yao, Donglin Xie, ...
papers.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being evaluated to integrate clinical, imaging, immunological, and molecular data for decision-making in neuroimmunology. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.

papers.title: NiCLIP: neuroimaging contrastive language-image pretraining model for predicting text from brain activation images
papers.authors: Julio A. Peraza, James Doliver Kent, Thomas E. Nichols, Jean-Baptiste Poline, Alejandro I de la Vega, ...
papers.abstract: Predicting cognitive processes from brain activation maps remains a key challenge in neuroscience. Meta-analytic functional decoding provides an estimation of behavioral profiles associated with specific brain regions; however, existing methods fail to capture the full semantic content of the neuroimaging literature. To address this, we present NiCLIP, a contrastive language-image model trained on over 23,000 articles to predict cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. NiCLIP achieves optimal performance when using full-text articles and a curated cognitive ontology with precise task-concept-domain mappings. Our results show that NiCLIP accurately predicts cognitive tasks from Human Connectome Project group-level maps across multiple domains (e.g., emotion, language, motor) and precisely characterizes the functional roles of specific brain regions, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and temporoparietal junction. However, NiCLIP showed limitations with noisy subject-level activation maps. NiCLIP represents a significant advancement in functional decoding, offering a powerful tool for hypothesis generation and scientific discovery. Researchers developed NiCLIP, an AI model that decodes cognitive tasks, concepts, and domains from brain activation patterns. Trained on over 23,000 papers, NiCLIP excels at group-level decoding, outperforming traditional decoders.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Pharmacovigilance for Neuropsychiatric Therapies: Advancing U.S. Drug Safety Surveillance and Regulatory Decision-Making
papers.authors: Rebecca A Omachonu, Sandra A. Uzuh, Kehinde Akinola, Kelvin Ovabor, Augustine Odibo
papers.abstract: Neuropsychiatric medications, including antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, anxiolytics, and newer agents such as esketamine, are widely prescribed, but their adverse effects are often subjective, delayed in onset, and difficult to separate from the illness being treated.Post-marketing surveillance in the United States relies on the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), MedWatch, the Sentinel System, and Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS).This narrative review, reported according to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), examines how well these systems detect neuropsychiatric adverse events and what artificial intelligence (AI) can add.PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for literature published since January 2000, supplemented by regulatory and institutional sources.Spontaneous reporting misses most adverse drug reactions, while stigma, diagnostic overshadowing, and uncertainty about whether a symptom reflects the drug or the disorder further reduce reporting of psychiatric effects.Disproportionality signals, such as those reported for dissociation and suicidal ideation with esketamine, need cautious interpretation because notoriety bias, solicited reporting under REMS, and confounding by indication can inflate them.Long-latency effects such as tardive dyskinesia and antipsychotic-induced metabolic change fall outside the observation windows of premarket trials and most spontaneous reports.Natural language processing (NLP) can retrieve adverse events documented in free-text psychiatric records with good accuracy, and large language models (LLMs) show early promise for structuring adverse event narratives, but most AI studies are retrospective proofs of concept, and models trained on biased data can reproduce existing inequities.AI is therefore best used to widen and prioritize signal detection, with causality assessment and regulatory decisions remaining with clinicians and regulators.Priorities include prospective evaluation of AI tools in live pharmacovigilance workflows, linkage of FAERS with electronic health record and claims data, point-ofcare reporting tools, and efforts to reduce the stigma that discourages reporting of psychiatric adverse effects.

papers.title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
papers.authors: Boya Zhang, Yuanchao Ma, Jiageng Wu, Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn, Rodrigo Gameiro...
papers.abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator $κ$ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

papers.title: Towards clinical communication training with LLM-based conversational virtual patients and automatic evaluation systems
papers.authors: Andrea Bayona, Rubén Manrique, Christian Grévisse
papers.abstract: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.

papers.title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
papers.authors: Xiaoqing Lian, Pei Liu, Jiahui Tan, Quan Zou, Chen Lin...
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.

papers.title: Deciphering isonicotinylation and mast cell-associated pathogenic patterns in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: evidence from ensemble learning-driven multi-omics and in vitro validation
papers.authors: Sunrui Yu, Duojia Xu, Yuting Hua, Hangfeng Mo, Yujin Liu
papers.abstract: Background Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is dystrophin-deficiency skeletal and cardiac muscle disease. Protein post-translational modification (PTM) and aberrant immune cell activation play a key role in its pathogenesis. Objective Our study aims to investigate isonicotinylation (Kinic)-associated signature modulatory patterns in mast cells and DMD pathogenesis. Methods We first performed integrated bioinformatic methods, such as WGCNA, GSVA, and CIBERSORT to identify Kinic and mast cell (KM)-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in DMD patient muscle bulk profiles (GSE38417 and GSE109178). Next, consensus clustering and assembling machine learning pipeline identified KM-associated diagnostic model and molecular subgroups in training the DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE6011), and then, diagnostic model performance was examined in the independent DMD patient muscle bulk set (GSE32720). In addition, SHAP analysis decoded the main contributor in KM-associated diagnostic model construction, and contributor molecular and immune characters in DMD were estimated in GSE6011 and the DMD mouse muscle single-cell transcriptomic dataset (GSE213925) assisted by computational virtual cells. In addition, the deep learning framework and network pharmacology identified the drug synergy strategy for the treatment of DMD. Finally, the in vitro assay identified expression patterns of the main contributor. Results KM-associated molecular patterns can potentially guide the diagnostic and molecular stratification for DMD patients. USP18 can be considered an upregulated and mast cell-distributed hub gene involved in pathogenesis of DMD. In addition, finafloxacin with BRD-K10482608 can be considered two potential therapeutic candidates for DMD patient clinical applications. Conclusion Our investigation described a novel forecasting and therapeutic model for DMD patients, which potentially enhances DMD patient clinical translation.

papers.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
papers.authors: Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Jiawei Zhou, Yuzhang Shang...
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.

papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.authors: Jiaru Zou, Yunzhe Qi, Sirui Chen, Federico Bianchi, Shang Zhu...
papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

papers.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding
papers.authors: Xuyang Liu, Shihao Wang, Xinyu Wei, Minghan Li, Zeqing Wang...
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

papers.title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
papers.authors: Kawai Chung, Chunkit Chan, Yuxuan Liu, Yauwai Yim, Xi Yang...
papers.abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
papers.authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Yusuke Iwasawa...
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.

papers.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
papers.authors: Wenlin Zhong, Hao Wang, Kun Yuan, Fan Yang, Jinluan Yang...
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

papers.title: Teacher-Guided Tool Learning for Small Language Models via Bidirectional KL Constraints
papers.authors: Haoxuan Gao, Qin-Wen Luo, Xiang Chen, Yu Tian, Zequn Sun...
papers.abstract: External tools can extend the capabilities of small language models (SLMs), enabling their deployment in resource constrained environments. However, their limited capabilities make it difficult for SLMs to discover effective tool use behaviors through reinforcement learning alone, while direct teacher supervision suffers from teacher student behavioral distribution mismatch and may propagate erroneous preferences. To address these challenges, we propose Selective Teacher guided Policy Optimization (SeTPO), which coordinates student exploration with selective teacher guidance and persistent demonstration supervision. Specifically, SeTPO incorporates reverse KL derived token level teacher feedback into policy advantages on low reward trajectories, while auxiliary forward KL supervision preserves teacher demonstrated behaviors throughout training. Under an idealized bidirectional KL objective, we theoretically establish that the optimal policy achieves expected reward no lower than the teacher's while retaining a guaranteed fraction of the teacher's probability mass. Extensive experiments on BFCL v4 and API Bank demonstrate that SeTPO achieves superior overall performance over supervised fine tuning, reinforcement learning, and distillation baselines across all three student scales.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice
papers.authors: Bénédicte Nobile, Philippe Courtet
papers.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI's potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians' confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

papers.title: DinoDental : Benchmarking DINOv3 as a Unified Vision Encoder for Dental Image Analysis
papers.authors: Kun Tang, Xinquan Yang, Mianjie Zheng, Xuefen Liu, Xuguang Li, ...
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The scarcity and high cost of expert annotation remain major barriers to developing reliable AI systems for dental imaging. DINOv3, a state‐of‐the‐art self‐supervised vision foundation model pretrained on 1.7 billion images, offers a promising way to reduce this dependence on labelled data. However, its transferability to dental imaging has not been systematically evaluated, because dental radiographs and intraoral photographs exhibit distinctive acquisition characteristics, domain shifts and clinically subtle findings. To address this gap, we introduce DinoDental, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating whether DINOv3 can serve as an off‐the‐shelf encoder for comprehensive dental image analysis without domain‐specific pretraining. Built from multiple public datasets, DinoDental covers classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation across panoramic radiographs and intraoral photographs. We further analyse transfer performance by varying model size and input resolution, comparing frozen features, full fine‐tuning, and parameter‐efficient Low‐Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and examining LoRA rank sensitivity, computational efficiency and run‐to‐run stability. Our experiments show that DINOv3 is competitive across panoramic and intraoral dental imaging tasks, with particularly strong results in intraoral image understanding and boundary‐sensitive dense prediction, while also exhibiting clear task‐ and modality‐dependent behaviour. Collectively, DinoDental provides a systematic framework for evaluating DINOv3 in dental image analysis and establishes a practical benchmark to guide model selection and adaptation for dental AI research. The code and benchmark configurations are publicly available at https://github.com/tangkunszu/DinoDental .

papers.title: Generating MeSH terms using large language models: From individual models to ensemble strategies
papers.authors: Danielle Hyunsook Lee
papers.abstract: This study evaluates how effectively large language models (LLMs) can assign Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) to biomedical articles, examining individual models and ensemble strategies. Five LLMs were tested: two biomedical (MMed-Llama-3-8B and Med42-v2-70B), two general-purpose (Mistral-7B and Llama-3-70B), and one commercial (Claude). Open-source models were adapted through Low-Rank Adaptation fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); Claude through five-shot prompting and RAG. Four ensemble strategies were applied: majority voting, Bayesian fusion, reliability-weighted voting, and cascade. On 1730 target articles, Claude with RAG achieved the highest F1-score (58.4%) through high recall but lower precision, while fine-tuned Llama-70B and Med42-70B showed the opposite pattern. The ensemble strategies compensated for this precision–recall trade-off: majority voting (F1 = 67.8%) and reliability-weighted voting (F1 = 67.6%) achieved balanced performance, exceeding the best-performing Claude by more than nine points. Bayesian fusion achieved the highest recall (82.5%), and cascade achieved the highest precision (82.1%). These precision–recall profiles map onto specific stages of the MeSH indexing workflow: Bayesian fusion for candidate generation, cascade for filtering, and majority voting or reliability-weighted voting for end-to-end indexing. The study therefore gives indexing practitioners a basis for selecting a configuration by task rather than by aggregate accuracy alone.
