papers.title: Agentic AI-driven human digital twins for personalized healthcare: a comprehensive survey
papers.authors: Anuradha Singh, Bhavna Bajpai, Mohammad Arif
papers.abstract: Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

papers.title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design
papers.authors: Enes Üstüner, Mustafa Öz
papers.abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

papers.title: Barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales: findings from focus groups
papers.authors: Michal Pruski, Jasmine Rollings, Kathleen L. Withers
papers.abstract: Background Building on a previous Wales-wide survey, this study aimed to provide more in-depth exploration of the barriers and facilitators to healthcare artificial intelligence adoption in Wales. Objectives The study aimed to explore these barriers and facilitators among various social groups, to inform policy development in Wales. Methods Four focus groups were conducted with a group of members of the public and a group of healthcare professionals (both groups recruited from a previous survey), as well as a group Sixth Form students and a group of retired adults. Inductive thematic analysis was used to generate themes and to compare the issues raised by the various groups. Contiguity-based analysis was undertaken to underscore how themes related with each other. Results A total of 21 individuals participated in the focus groups (healthcare professionals=6, members of the public=6, sixth-form students=5, retirees=4). Seven thematic networks were identified. Across groups, seven themes were identified in the healthcare professional group, six in the general members of the public group, seven in the sixth form student group, and seven in the retiree group. All groups voiced concerns about data privacy and highlighted the importance of human oversight of AI and human contact during the clinical encounter as they expressed more trust in human practitioners. There were though differences between groups, such as greater trust in black-box systems by healthcare professionals, and between individual participants in regard to trust in private organisations developing AI for healthcare organisations. Conclusions All groups were concerned with information security and expressed a preference for human contact during the clinical encounter and a human-in-the-loop approach. There were differences between the groups, such as in attitudes towards black-box AI technologies and trust in clinicians. No additional barriers or facilitators were identified for proxy consent.

papers.title: Large-scale prospective evaluation of co-folding across hundreds of Mac1–ligand complexes and three virtual screens
papers.authors: Jongbin Kim, G.J. Correy, Brendan W. Hall, Moira M. Rachman, Olivier Mailhot, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of ligand-bound protein complexes and ranking them by affinity are central problems in drug discovery. While deep learning co-folding methods can help address these challenges, their evaluation has been hampered by the difficulties in assessing independence from training data and insufficiently large test sets. Here we test the ability of co-folding methods to predict the structures of 551 ligands, 489 of which are of sufficient quality for evaluation, bound to the SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain (Mac1) that were determined after the training cut-off dates. AlphaFold3 (AF3), Boltz-2, and Chai-1 each reproduced >50% of the Mac1 ligand poses to better than 2 Å RMSD of experiment. Despite the potential for co-folding to describe protein conformational changes that stabilize ligand binding, we did not find that common conformational rearrangements, including peptide flip and a large loop opening, were recapitulated by the co-folding prediction. For AF3 and Chai-1, ligand pose prediction confidence weakly, but significantly, tracked experimental potency, while DOCK3.7 energies were only weakly correlated. Boltz-2 affinity predictions showed the strongest correlation with measured potency and, after calibration, achieved lower mean absolute error than a baseline predictor. We next assessed whether co-folding scores could rescore docking hit-lists to distinguish true ligands from non-binders among hundreds of molecules prospectively experimentally tested against AmpC β-lactamase, the dopamine D4 and the σ 2 receptors. AF3 ligand pose confidence values did not separate true ligands from high-scoring false-positives as effectively as docking scores or Boltz-2 affinity predictions did. Taken together, the modest, but independent correlations of docking score and co-folding confidence or affinity suggests that integrating physics-based and deep-learning and approaches may help with hit prioritization and subsequent optimization in structure-based ligand discovery.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Digital Twin Ecosystems for Early Detection and Precision Management of Breast, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancers
papers.abstract: Background: The convergence of multi-omics profiling, radiomics, and advanced machine learning has opened new frontiers in precision oncology.Despite this progress, existing computational frameworks remain static, failing to incorporate evolving patient data or simulate treatment outcomes dynamically.A self-evolving digital twin ecosystem offers a solution by continuously synchronizing patient-specific virtual models with real-world clinical trajectories.Objective: To develop and validate a self-evolving digital twin ecosystem integrating clinical, genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, radiomic, and pathological data for early cancer detection, disease progression prediction, and personalized treatment optimization across breast, lung, colorectal, and ovarian cancers.Methods: A retrospective multi-center cohort of 400 patients (breast n=120, lung n=100, colorectal n=100, ovarian n=80; age range 25-75 years) was assembled.A six-layer digital twin framework was constructed, incorporating a cross-modal transformer foundation model alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Network comparators.Key performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the ROC curve (AUC).Virtual clinical trial simulations and feature importance analyses were performed.Results: The foundation model achieved superior performance across all metrics (accuracy 0.921, AUC 0.947) compared with Random Forest (0.812/0.847),XGBoost (0.841/0.879), and Deep Neural Network (0.873/0.906).Tumor stage, TP53 mutation, and EGFR mutation emerged as the most predictive features.Risk stratification identified 148 (37.0%) low-risk, 153 (38.3%) moderate-risk, and 99 (24.8%)high-risk patients.Virtual trial simulation demonstrated a 23.4% improvement in projected progression-free survival for the high-risk subgroup.Conclusion: The self-evolving digital twin ecosystem significantly outperforms conventional machine learning approaches and provides a clinically actionable, adaptive platform for real-time precision oncology decision support across multiple cancer types.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: Generative Health Data Science for Data-to-Dose Precision Pharmacology: A Critical Methodological Review and Translational Framework
papers.abstract: Precision pharmacology aims to select the most appropriate medicine, dose and monitoring strategy for an individual patient.Its translation is limited by fragmented records, incomplete biological characterization, timevarying physiology and the difficulty of converting high-dimensional evidence into a safe action.Generative health data science extends conventional prediction by learning structured representations of molecules, cells, patients and clinical trajectories and by producing reviewable candidates such as molecular structures, treatment options, synthetic records, counterfactual courses and dose scenarios.This critical review evaluates large language models, multimodal and biological foundation models, graph and diffusion architectures, syntheticpatient generators, digital twins and bounded agentic workflows across target discovery, repurposing, pharmacogenomics, treatment selection, individualised dosing and pharmacovigilance.Evidence is strongest for representation learning, structure-enabled discovery and selected pharmacogenomic pathways; autonomous patient-level treatment and dosing remain investigational.Recent advances include explainable drug-repurposing foundation models, multimodal clinical foundation models and a randomised phase 2a trial of a generative-AIdiscovered TNIK inhibitor.We propose a Data-to-Dose framework linking intended-use definition, data provenance, longitudinal patient-state modelling, constrained generation, mechanistic and causal checks, uncertainty-aware ranking, professional review and lifecycle monitoring.Generation must remain distinct from clinical authorisation, and synthetic-data fidelity must not be equated with privacy, fairness or external validity.Generative systems may become an enabling layer for precision pharmacology only when their creative capacity is bounded by pharmacology, evidence and accountable clinical judgment.
papers.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

papers.title: Hackathon on predictive modelling in systems pharmacology: design, implementation, and outcomes
papers.authors: Malvina Marku, The-Chuong Trinh, Racym Berrah, Guido Uguzzoni, Moreno Ursino, ...
papers.abstract: Background The growing availability of multi-omics data and machine learning methods creates both an opportunity and a challenge for the systems pharmacology community: the opportunity to model drug action at unprecedented mechanistic resolution, and the challenge of equipping a new generation of researchers with the computational literacy to do so. There is a particular need for training formats that bridge classical pharmacometrics with omics data science, and that foster interdisciplinary community building. Methods We organised a 4-day intensive hackathon on Predictive Modelling in Systems Pharmacology, bringing together 16 early-career researchers from the Horizon Europe CANVAS and French PEPR DIGPHAT consortia, spanning biology, bioinformatics, and computational science. The event pursued the dual aim of fostering a multidisciplinary consortium community and providing hands-on training that bridges classical pharmacometrics with omics data science. Three scientific tracks were delivered: (i) pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modelling, (ii) drug perturbation modelling through network diffusion in gene regulatory networks (GRN), and (iii) machine learning for pharmacogenomics. A theory-to-practice pedagogical framework structured each day, with morning workshops grounding participants in methodological foundations followed by afternoon coding sprints on real-world datasets. Results All three tracks produced working computational outputs within the hackathon timeframe. In the PK/PD track, all teams successfully identified a two-compartment structural model and key covariate effects. In the GRN track, participants implemented a network diffusion algorithm on gene regulatory networks, yielding patient-stratified therapy recommendations. In the pharmacogenomics track, four out of seven teams surpassed the logistic regression baseline in Matthews Correlation Coefficient on an external validation set. Conclusions The hackathon demonstrated that a structured multi-track format combining community-targeted outreach, theory-to-practice pedagogy, and real-world datasets constitutes a replicable model for interdisciplinary computational pharmacology training at the European level.

papers.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models
papers.authors: Nawaf Alampara, Santiago Miret, Kevin Maik Jablonka
papers.abstract: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.

papers.title: SENSE: SELF-SUPERVISED NEURAL EMBEDDINGS FOR SPATIAL ENSEMBLES
papers.authors: Hamid Gadirov, Lennard Manuel, Steffen Frey
papers.abstract: Analyzing and visualizing scientific ensemble datasets characterized by high dimensionality and structural complexity remains a significant challenge.While dimensionality reduction methods and autoencoders are widely used for feature extraction, their performance often degrades in high-dimensional settings.In this work, we propose an enhanced autoencoder framework that integrates clustering and contrastive loss functions into the latent space to improve the interpretability and visualization of scientific ensemble data.Clustering is guided by a soft silhouette score, encouraging compact and well-separated latent representations.To address the presence of unlabeled data, EfficientNetV2 is employed to generate pseudo-labels for partially unlabeled ensembles.The model is trained by jointly optimizing reconstruction, clustering, and contrastive objectives, resulting in improved grouping of similar samples and clearer separation of distinct structures in the latent space.UMAP is subsequently applied to the learned embeddings to produce two-dimensional visualizations, which are quantitatively evaluated using silhouette scores.We evaluate multiple autoencoder variants on two scientific ensemble datasets: subsurface channel structures generated via Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations and droplet-impact dynamics on a liquid film.The results show that incorporating clustering or contrastive objectives yields marginal but consistent improvements over baseline autoencoders.
papers.venue: JOURNAL OF BAKU ENGINEERING UNIVERSITY- MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTER SCIENCE

papers.title: The impact of GenAI on the future of requirements engineering
papers.authors: Travis D. Breaux, Anmol Singhal
papers.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

papers.title: Adapting Segment Anything Model 3 for concept-driven lesion segmentation in medical images: an experimental study
papers.authors: Guoping Xu, Jayaram K. Udupa, Yubing Tong, Xin Long, Ying Zhang, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate segmentation of lesions is fundamental for medical image analysis. However, most existing approaches are designed for specific anatomical sites and imaging modalities, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous clinical environments. Recent vision-language foundation models have enabled concept-driven segmentation of natural images, offering a promising path toward more flexible and generalizable medical image segmentation. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, concept-prompt-based lesion segmentation in medical images, particularly using the latest Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3), has not been thoroughly examined. In this paper, the authors present a systematic investigation of the SAM3 framework for lesion segmentation. An extensive evaluation of SAM3 was first conducted using geometric bounding boxes and concept-based text and image exemplars as prompts for lesion segmentation across multiple cancer types and imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, ultrasound, dermoscopy, and endoscopic imaging, with particular emphasis on volumetric medical imaging datasets. To improve robustness and segmentation accuracy, additional knowledge into the input representation was further integrated, including predictions from adjacent slices, multiparametric imaging information, and prior annotations. In addition, the study compared different SAM3 fine-tuning strategies on the BraTS2023-MET dataset, including partial module fine-tuning, adapter-based optimization, and full-model fine-tuning, under different training objectives. Extensive experiments conducted on 13 datasets covering 11 lesion types demonstrate that SAM3 achieves strong cross-modality generalization and accurate instance-specific lesion delineation. These results highlight the potential of concept-driven foundation models for scalable and practical medical-image segmentation in real-world clinical settings. The source code and dataset splits are publicly available at https://github.com/apple1986/lesion-sam3 .
papers.venue: Visual Computing for Industry Biomedicine and Art

papers.title: Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow
papers.authors: Chey M. Jones, Deeptak Verma
papers.abstract: Abstract Directed evolution consistently delivers engineered enzymes that facilitate diverse biocatalytic transformations. Despite advances in automation and high-throughput workflows, our ability to rapidly engineer novel enzymes is limited by our inability to thoroughly sample the vast protein design space. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods have alleviated this challenge to some degree, due to their ability to propose mutations based on learned patterns from complex protein data sets. However, the hidden logic of these AI-based methods can complicate our ability to reveal and exploit fundamental details of these enzymes. To complement these hidden-logic models, we present a structure- and physics-based workflow that mimics directed evolution in silico. This Virtual Protein EngineeR (referred to as ViPER) aims to simulate directed evolution by leveraging computational modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, in silico mutagenesis, and structure-based property evaluation to iteratively engineer an enzyme toward a desired target. In this work, we present a retrospective analysis to demonstrate ViPER’s ability to efficiently navigate the complex protein–protein interfaces associated with the oligomerization of a ketoreductase (KRED) enzyme. In addition to successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds), this dynamics-based methodology identifies a distal mutation that was incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution. This work provides a novel foundation for computationally driven directed evolution efforts, opening the opportunity to simultaneously pursue and evaluate multiple evolutionary routes through a physics-based lens.

papers.title: Cellular and spatial context of genetic convergence between insomnia liability and DTI ALPS perivascular diffusivity
papers.authors: Chenxu Xiao, Yuxuan Shen, Gang Yu, Lijun Pang, Chenxu Xiao
papers.abstract: Sleep has been linked to brain waste clearance and glymphatic/perivascular transport, yet whether insomnia shares genetic architecture with perivascular diffusivity remains unclear. Here we show that insomnia liability and diffusion tensor imaging measures along the perivascular space have little genome-wide genetic correlation but converge locally at chromosome 17q21.31. Polygenic enrichment, conjunctional false discovery rate, and Bayesian colocalization analyses support shared statistical signals in this region, which contains the MAPT inversion locus. Transcriptome-wide, gene-level fine-mapping, and summary-data Mendelian randomization analyses prioritize HEXIM1, ACBD4, EFTUD2, and MAPT. Tissue, cell-type, spatial transcriptomic, and sleep-perturbation analyses place these candidates in neuronal, glial, immune, vascular, and perivascular contexts, with effects varying by brain region and imaging phenotype. Together, these findings support localized genetic convergence rather than a genome-wide shared architecture and provide biological context for future studies of perivascular imaging phenotypes and neurodegeneration-related processes. Insomnia and MRI-derived perivascular diffusivity show little genome-wide genetic correlation but converge locally at 17q21.31, highlighting HEXIM1, ACBD4, EFTUD2 and MAPT.

papers.title: Assessment of AI development level in construction cost management using AHP- cloud model: a case study of China’s Yangtze River Delta Region
papers.authors: Rui Wang, Enmao Wang, Hafez Salleh, Yao Zhangfeng, Jianxun Xie
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration is crucial for solving traditional inefficiencies and data fragmentation in construction cost management, driven by the demands of Industry 4.0. However, a significant gap exists in holistically evaluating AI development levels, lacking a framework and empirical analysis that systematically bridges macro-environmental factors and micro-organizational readiness. This study aims to assess the AI development level in construction cost management across China’s Yangtze River Delta (YRD) region. A novel PEST-O (political, economic, social and technological-organizational) framework was established, and an integrated Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and cloud model approach was used to analyze expert data. Findings indicate the YRD’s overall AI development is “average” (Ex = 52.71), revealing a critical imbalance. Although the Political dimension shows strong support, the organizational, technological, and social dimensions remain “worse,” confirming organizational incapacity as the primary bottleneck. Regionally, Shanghai and Zhejiang significantly outperform Jiangsu and Anhui. This research theoretically validates the PEST-O model and provides quantitative diagnosis. Practically, the findings of this research provide policymakers and other stakeholders with a diagnostic tool tailored to specific regions. They also help facilitate the implementation of differentiated measures for leading and lagging regions.

papers.title: Selecting and generating web search based features using small language models for tabular data classification
papers.authors: Emrah İnan, Damla Oğuz
papers.abstract: In machine learning, the feature space is a key framework that converts data samples into vectors for analysis and modelling. Consequently, the results obtained from machine learning algorithms depend heavily on the ability to select and generate important features. Feature generation as a central technique converts raw data into a refined feature space that facilitates model training and further enhances its structure. Despite progress in automated feature selection and feature generation, major challenges remain, especially in terms of explainability and cross-domain generalization. One alternative is to adapt automatic feature engineering within deep learning, rather than relying on hand-crafted techniques in machine learning. Although deep learning models have proven highly effective in a variety of fields, they are often considered less effective when applied to tabular datasets. To tackle these problems, we present a methodology that uses small language models (SLMs) to select and generate features specifically for tabular datasets in machine learning classification tasks. Experimental results show that we reached highest F1 scores of 0.383 and 0.848 for two well-known tabular datasets for the machine learning multi-class classification task.

papers.title: Causality-driven hybrid intrusion detection with entropy-aware feature learning and federated intelligence
papers.authors: Subham Kumar Gupta, Yogesh Kumar Gupta, Atul Kumar Verma
papers.abstract: Modern IDSs should be capable of detecting and recognizing new forms of attack traffic (including both attacks from known adversaries) and to do so in ways that remain computational feasible when deployed across multiple, geographically distributed sites. Rule based, representation learning, and federated approaches have been used separately, or in combination in some cases. However, each approach operates independently in many cases. Therefore, they fail to support causal interpretability, efficient use of feature information, stable performance against adversarial attacks, and generalizability across multiple sites. This paper outlines a causality driven hybrid ids framework. The hybrid framework includes the Causal-Adaptive Signature Learning Engine; the Entropy-Guided Feature Compression Network; the attention-based Hybrid Cognitive Detection Synthesizer; the Adversarial Robustness Calibration Module; and the trust-weighted Federated Threat Intelligence Evolution Framework. The proposed framework has been tested on three separate publicly available network traffic datasets (cicids2017, unsw-nb15, and IoT-23). Testing included: use of dataset specific partitions that controlled for leakage in training; five fold validation to test the ability to learn patterns within the training data; ten different random seed controlled evaluations. A comparison of the hybrid ids framework was made to: block chain-based collaborative ids frameworks; traditional machine-learning based ids frameworks; optimized XGBoost-based ids frameworks. All comparisons were completed under similar preprocessing conditions and distributions of classes. The proposed ids framework produced detection accuracies of 97.4% and 96.1% on the cicids2017 and unsw-nb15 datasets respectively. An overall detection accuracy rate of 95.6% was achieved on the IoT-23 dataset. Additionally, the proposed framework reduced the number of features retained to 18 (a reduction of 70.9%) compared to the original number of features present in each of the datasets. Across ten iterations, the reported aggregate performance metrics were: overall accuracy = 96.37%; precision = 95.97%; recall = 95.43%; F1-score = 95.68%. In addition, the proposed framework had an average processing time per inference of 18.6 milliseconds. Finally, testing performed under bounded gradient-based perturbation conditions indicated that the proposed framework maintained high levels of detection accuracy (>91.5%).

papers.title: The Grounding Tax: How Domain Fine-Tuning Suppresses Context Utilisation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Usman Yunusa Labaran, Rufai Yauri Aliyu, Isah Charles Saidu, Rislan Abdulazeez Kanya, Ahmad Nurudeen Tambaya
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are routinely adapted to specialised domains through fine-tuning and grounded in external evidence through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The prevailing assumption is that these methods are complementary even though minimal empirical work examines whether domain-specific fine-tuning influences a model’s responsiveness to retrieved context. Thus, this study examines the interaction between fine-tuning and RAG through a controlled evaluation in a high-stakes public-finance domain. The evaluation is conducted through 12 model configurations built on two open-weight model families (LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B), using a frozen 100-query benchmark covering factual question-answering (factual-QA), risk assessment, and summarisation under both closed-book and context-matched conditions. The evidence confirms successful knowledge injection as domain fine-tuning raised closed-book numeric-fact accuracy (NFA) from 0.148 to 0.248. However, when retrieved context is introduced, the benefit collapses as the base model gained +0.183 from context while the fine-tuned model gained only +0.021. Across the backbone pairs, the change in context gain ranged from -0.161 to -0.348 and was statistically significant for the LLaMA Instruct and Qwen Base pairs. Further ablation analysis shows that prompt-template and instruction alignment can amplify this effect. We term this phenomenon the grounding tax: domain fine-tuning imposes a measurable cost on the model’s ability to use retrieved evidence because the adapted model relies on internally encoded knowledge rather than faithfully using the evidence supplied to it. Thus, these findings show that conventional closed-book evaluation can mask degradation in context utilisation and that fine-tuned RAG systems must be evaluated jointly under both closed-book and context-conditioned settings. Therefore, we argue for treating domain adaptation, instruction alignment, and retrieval grounding as distinct and potentially competing design dimensions.
papers.venue: Journal of Science Innovation and Technology Research

papers.title: Evaluation of Turkish artificial intelligence-generated responses about osteoporosis in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability
papers.authors: Meltem Güneş Akıncı, Alev Atıgan, Ceyda Suskun, Atakan Yenidünya
papers.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in patient education. This study evaluated the responses of AI chatbots to frequently asked questions about osteoporosis in Turkish in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate AI-generated responses to osteoporosis-related questions in Turkish.Materials and methods: Thirty-one of the most common frequently asked questions related to osteoporosis were subcategorized into general information, diagnosis, and treatment. The questions were submitted to the publicly accessible platforms ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity. Two physicians evaluated accuracy (six-point Likert scale) and completeness (three-point Likert scale) based on the 2025 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Osteoporosis and Metabolic Bone Diseases. Readability was assessed using the Ateşman Readability Formula.Results: No significant difference was found among the chatbots for accuracy. Accuracy rates ranged 80.5%-82.2% overall, 82.3%-85.2% general information, 58.3%-66.7% diagnosis, and 77.2%-81.7% treatment. Significant differences were found in completeness overall and in the general information (p=0.006, p=0.029; respectively). In pairwise comparisons, ChatGPT-5.3 showed significantly higher completeness than Perplexity (p=0.001, p=0.006; respectively). Completeness rates ranged 47%-64.3% overall, 46%-68.3% general information, 33.3%-50% diagnosis, and 48.3%-60.3% treatment. Readability differed significantly among the chatbots (p<0.001). Based on mean scores, the ranking was ChatGPT-5.3>Gemini=Copilot>Perplexity. ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, and Copilot were easy, whereas Perplexity was moderately difficult.Conclusion: All chatbots showed similar accuracy, but ChatGPT-5.3 performed better in completeness and readability. Chatbots may be useful in Turkish patient education. However, their standalone use in osteoporosis management without physician supervision is not appropriate.

papers.title: AI-Powered Healthcare Assistant with Drug Interaction Detection and Emergency Support
papers.authors: Savara Gnan Prakash, Diwakar Nallappagari, Gangana Jashwanth Reddy,  Veduruparthi Raja Krishna Deepak, Sulake Shanmuka Rao, ...
papers.abstract: Modern healthcare delivery continues to be con-strained by fragmented digital tools, delayed diagnosis, unmoni-tored drug-drug interactions (DDIs), and insufficient emergency response mechanisms, particularly for users without direct spe-cialist access. This paper presents an AI-Powered Healthcare Assistant—an integrated, secure, web-based platform that unifies conversational symptom analysis, hybrid disease-risk classifi-cation, knowledge-graph-based drug interaction detection, and geolocation-enabled emergency support within a single appli-cation. The system combines a GPT-based NLP pipeline for symptom interpretation, a hybrid rule-and-scoring risk engine classifying patient state into Low, Medium, High, and Emergency tiers, and a Neo4j biomedical knowledge graph modelling drugs, diseases, genes, and proteins to flag Mild, Moderate, or Severe medication interactions. Built on React.js, Node.js/Express.js, MongoDB, and Neo4j, and secured through JWT authentication, bcrypt password hashing, and role-based access control (RBAC), the platform achieved a validated disease-prediction accuracy of 87.3% and end-to-end response latency suitable for interactive clinical decision support. Grounded in an evaluation spanning healthcare microservices, explainable AI, clinical NLP, graph neural networks, and healthcare data security, the system demonstrates that a single, well-secured platform can meaningfully bridge the gap between AI-driven diagnostic guidance and actionable, real-time patient care
papers.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

papers.title: AN EXPLAINABLE DEEP LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR PREDICTIVE SOFTWARE QUALITY ENGINEERING AND AUTOMATED DEFECT DETECTION
papers.authors: Prathap Raghavan
papers.abstract: Software Quality Engineering (SQE) is evolving from reactive defect detection toward predictive and intelligent quality assurance. Traditional testing approaches identify defects after implementation and require extensive manual effort to analyze source code, test results, historical defects, and execution behavior. Machine learning and deep learning techniques enable prediction of defect-prone software components before failures occur; however, many deep learning models operate as black boxes, making their predictions difficult for developers, testers, and quality engineers to understand and validate. This paper proposes the Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Predictive Software Quality Engineering and Automated Defect Detection (XDL-SQE). The framework integrates static code metrics, change history, historical defect data, test execution results, runtime information, and source-code embeddings. A hybrid deep learning engine (CNN-LSTM-Transformer) generates defect-risk predictions, while an explainability layer based on SHAP and LIME provides feature attribution. A quality-prioritization layer converts predictions into actionable testing recommendations integrated with CI/CD pipelines. The framework addresses five key gaps: prediction without explanation, fragmented quality data, limited testing integration, human trust, and cross-project generalization. A comprehensive research protocol is proposed for evaluating predictive accuracy, explanation quality, testing efficiency, and operational usefulness. This work contributes a unified architecture for interpretable, actionable, and continuous predictive quality engineering.
papers.venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

papers.title: Monte Carlo and Neural Network-based Prediction of Base Shear Force in Airport Tunnels using the Pushover Method Considering Both Soil-Structure Interaction and Non-Interaction across Different Soil Types
papers.authors: Awatif EL BRIGUI, Mouna EL MKHALET, Nouzha Lamdouar
papers.abstract: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are powerful nonlinear function approximators that can learn complicated relationships from data. They offer increasing value in civil, seismic, and geotechnical engineering applications. Recent findings indicate that ANNs can also be applied to structural health monitoring, material behaviour prediction and the evaluation of deep buried structures, whereas their application to airport tunnels remains largely unexplored. This study expands the Monte Carlo framework developed for the seismic assessment of an airport tunnel. It integrates the principles of a neural network. 200 samples are generated for each scenario by incorporating uncertainties of peak ground acceleration and material strength into Monte Carlo simulations. The findings indicate a significant variation in the structure’s roof displacement and base shear and larger dispersion of these parameters is observed as the ground acceleration increases. In the case without SSI, the roof displacement varies between 1.40 and 3.44 cm while the base shear varies from 690.0 to 1,845.1 kN; these are the minimum and maximum values obtained over the 200 Monte Carlo samples and correspond exactly to the figures reported in Table 4. The performance of tunnels is sensitive to the interdependence between seismic input and material. As a whole, the results obtained by combining ANN concepts, nonlinear static procedures, and probabilistic Monte Carlo simulation yield a sound framework for evaluation of performance under uncertainties. A combination of data analysis and modelling would enhance accuracy and strengthen decision-making for airport tunnel design and safety management.

papers.title: A Disease-Memory Guided Framework for Radiology Report Generation from Multi-View Chest X-rays
papers.authors: Prajakta Dhamanskar, Chintan Bhupeshbhai Thacker, Saurabh A Shah
papers.abstract: Chest X-rays are widely used, low-cost diagnostic tools. Writing chest X-ray reports manually is a time-consuming and tedious task. The increasing number of X-rays burdens radiologists, creating a need for a clinically accurate, fast and automated report generation system. To solve this challenge, we propose a new disease-memory-guided vision-language framework for radiology report generation. Frontal and lateral chest X-rays (multi-view) are encoded using a Swin-Transformer. These encoded visual features are then passed through a multi-label classification head that predicts disease probabilities, from which the top three labels are converted into learnable disease-memory embeddings. These are concatenated with projected visual tokens and fixed task instruction embeddings to form a multimodal prompt which is fed into a frozen decoder. A LLaMA-2-7B model adapted to the radiology domain using LoRA fine-tuning on the train-only MIMIC-CXR subset is used as an autoregressive decoder. The disease-memory embeddings serve as disease guidance during report generation. An extensive experimental analysis of different experimental variants is conducted on the benchmark Indiana University Chest X-ray dataset using three aspects: 1) statistical n-gram overlap, 2) semantic similarity, and 3) clinical label-based metrics. Experimental results of the proposed system show improvements in semantic evaluation metrics, with BERTScore precision, recall, and F1 values of 0.898, 0.891 and 0.894, respectively, and ROUGE-L and METEOR scores of 0.327 and 0.281, indicating improved contextual consistency between generated and reference reports. However, performance on statistical metrics (e.g., BLEU4=0.068) and clinical evaluation metrics remains limited, with Micro-F1, Macro-F1, Precision and Recall values of 0.4211, 0.0640, 0.4272, and 0.4151, respectively, indicating only partial abnormality description. This framework improves abnormality grounding while maintaining computational efficiency and can be used as a supportive tool for preliminary report drafting in research or resource-constrained settings.
papers.venue: Journal of Electronics Electromedical Engineering and Medical Informatics

papers.title: Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
papers.authors: Amit Kumar Jaiswal, Sagar Uprety, Prayag Tiwari
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard source of query expansion terms but they hallucinate. They inject non existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise and can hurt strong retrievers. Existing remedies such as corpus grounding, mutual verification and preference alignment treat hallucinated terms as an undifferentiated nuisance to be filtered by agreement heuristics, without a mechanistic account of why a given term appears or a principled criterion for how many terms to keep. We propose Subsequence-Association Filtered, breadth-aware query expansion (SAFE-QE), a training-free, retriever agnostic method that draws on the subsequence-association account of hallucination. We score each candidate expansion term by its corpus conditioned cross-context reproducibility, terms that reappear under randomised query contexts yet lack support in the pseudo-relevant set are flagged as products of dominant hallucinatory associations and down-weighted. Drawing on the characterisation of language generation as a trade-off between consistency (no hallucination) and breadth (coverage), we cast term selection as constrained coverage maximisation over the pseudo-relevant set, keeping a set that is approximately broad but consistent and stable across resampling. We also introduce the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate, a query side faithfulness metric that counts injected expansion terms no relevant document supports. We evaluate our approach on benchmarked TREC and BEIR collections. Our SAFE-QE is statistically indistinguishable from generative and corpus-steered expansion on nDCG@10 while injecting fewer unsupported terms 4.3 per query against 27.8 for Query2doc and 57.5 for HyDE and on a strong learned sparse retriever, where every expansion method regresses. Faithfulness is therefore available at no measurable cost in ranking quality.

papers.title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
papers.authors: Jiwon Jeon, Myungsik Cho, Jeonghye Kim, Youngchul Sung
papers.abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.

papers.title: Training User Simulators with Latent Intrinsic Feedback
papers.authors: Tarek Naous, Craig Boutilier, Wei Xu, Ofer Meshi
papers.abstract: User simulators are gaining attention as environments to train LLM assistants that can better cope with the nuances of multi-turn conversations with real users. Prior work on user simulation has emphasized generating realistic user utterances, leaving unexplored their potential as a source of direct feedback on the assistant's responses. Such evaluation signals may not be explicitly communicated in language, but can instead reside in the latent reasoning of users. In this work, we introduce user simulators with intrinsic feedback, namely, models equipped with latent evaluation states: internal thoughts, reactions, and scalar ratings that evaluate the assistant from a first-person user perspective at each conversation turn. We train LLM-based simulators using interaction logs between real users and assistants and demonstrate that intrinsic feedback improves simulation realism and critiquing behaviors versus prompted simulator baselines, while also providing turn-level evaluations that existing fine-tuned simulators lack. Further, evaluations generated by our trained simulators correlate better with human judgments than those of prompted simulators of the same size. Lastly, our experiments reveal that simulators with intrinsic feedback provide effective reward signals for multi-turn RL training, matching setups that rely on external judge LLMs for rewards while cutting RL compute by more than half.

papers.title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection
papers.authors: Meysam Sabbaghan, Nikesh Gyawali, Arman Zareian Jahromi, Sebastian Loera-Lozano, Doina Caragea...
papers.abstract: Stance detection remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to implicit opinions, sarcasm, and context-dependent expressions of stance. Although automatic prompt optimization offers an alternative to fine-tuning without updating model parameters, existing structured approaches are not specifically designed around stance-label semantics and class-specific ambiguities. We introduce MoPrO-SD, a stance-specific prompt optimization framework that decomposes prompts into functional semantic modules and refines them sequentially using LLM-based feedback. We study three refinement strategies: instruction-only optimization (I), instruction with reasoning (I+R), and instruction with per-example reasoning (I+R+E), using class-conditioned errors for stance-label refinement. We also introduce VaccineStance, a new human-annotated benchmark for vaccine stance detection. Experiments across four datasets and five open-weight LLMs show that MoPrO-SD improves upon the human-written Base prompt in many settings. On SemEval-2016, class-conditioned feedback achieves higher mean Macro-F1 than pooled feedback for four of five backbones. Both reasoning-based strategies, I+R and I+R+E, achieve strong performance, with their relative effectiveness varying across models and datasets, while remaining competitive with recent prompt optimization methods. The MoPrO-SD code and VaccineStance dataset are available on GitHub.

papers.title: Retrieval-to-abstraction LLM-assisted literature synthesis: Case demonstrations in digital health technology-enabled randomized controlled trial outcome reporting
papers.authors: Taylor B. Harrison, Dian Hu, Heling Jia, Shyang Hong Tan, Fang Chen, ...
papers.abstract: Systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) support evidence-based clinical advancement. Clinical trial reporting guidelines, including CONSORT, establish common data elements that support systematic synthesis of published trial outcomes. However, the rapid rise of digital health technologies presents new challenges for reporting guidelines, and substantial real-world reporting heterogeneity has been observed. Therefore, machine-assisted evaluation of reporting adherence offers a pathway for more agile information management to accommodate the diverse and disruptive nature of digital health technology-enabled RCTs. Here, we propose an accelerated retrieval-to-abstraction literature synthesis framework to conduct article screening, text and table data preprocessing, and full-text review using an unmodified pretrained large language model. We apply this methodology in two digital health technology-enabled RCT case studies evaluating adherence to technology and digital health equity guideline reporting items. Large language model performance was on par with inter-annotator agreement F1 scores (≥0.9) in both screening and information-extraction tasks. These findings support the scalability and rigor of accelerated evidence synthesis and demonstrate the importance of common reporting elements across digital health technology-enabled RCTs.

papers.title: Advancing chemical reaction prediction in data-scarce drug discovery with active and geometric deep learning
papers.authors: Mason Minot, Yannick Stenzhorn, Jens Wolfard, Sebastian Strobel, Philippe Jablonski, ...
papers.abstract: The success of generative molecular design depends on the synthetic accessibility of the molecules it creates. While computational models can help predict chemical reactions, their current effectiveness is limited by a lack of reference data and the difficulty of accurately predicting reaction regioselectivity. Here, to address this, we present an integrated closed-loop workflow that combines efficient reaction data acquisition with high-accuracy deep learning. We developed an active learning strategy, driven by a tree-based ensemble, to guide the acquisition of the most informative laboratory experiments. This experimental campaign yielded a diverse benchmark for C-H borylation. The bespoke dataset allowed us to train and evaluate geometric graph neural networks. We demonstrate that augmenting these symmetry-aware models with self-supervised auxiliary tasks consistently improves performance for both reaction outcome prediction and regioselectivity prediction. Prospective tests on unseen substrates, featuring challenging N-heteroaryl motifs, pinpointed the correct borylation positions in all cases, illustrating the practical utility of our workflow for efficient drug optimization.

papers.title: A Controlled Single-Speaker Evaluation of Ambient Voice Technologies’ Speech-to-Text Function Using Narrated Surgical Case-Reports
papers.authors: Ruairí O’Kane, Daniel Stonehouse‐Smith, Melody Shirazi, Rachel Hutchinson, Morgan Gregg, ...
papers.abstract: Abstract Ambient voice technologies (AVT) utilise automatic speech recognition (ASR) and generative artificial intelligence for speech-to-text conversion, and are advocated as efficient, accurate tools for clinical documentation. We investigated ( n = 8) AVT systems using surgical case-reports as narratives in a controlled single-speaker evaluation prioritising safety outcomes: specifically 3 commercial transcription-systems (Dragon-Medical-One, Heidi-Health, Tortus); 4 ASR speech-to-text Application Programming Interfaces (Speechmatics-Enhanced, Amazon-Medical-Transcribe, Whisper, GPT4oTranscribe); and an experimental two-stage ASR–Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline incorporating GPT4oTranscribe with GPT-5-LLM generative error correction (GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5). Reference-transcripts ( n = 100; 32,897 words, range = 44–449, mean = 329/per-transcript) derived from surgical case-reports were recorded and input into AVT systems as audio-recordings for transcription-output generation. Primary outcome was proportion of transcription-outputs containing at least one clinically significant Class 3 error graded for potential harm. Secondary outcomes included transcription accuracy: Domain-Word-Error-Rate (DWER) against SNOMED-CT, lexical-accuracy (ROUGE score) and semantic similarity (BERT, BART scores). To investigate impact of the experimental pipeline on clinically significant errors, raw ASR and LLM-processed transcription-outputs were compared and errors classified as resolved, remaining or newly introduced. Across ( n = 800) transcript-outputs, 30–68% (GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5; Amazon-Medical-Transcribe and Dragon-Medical-One, respectively) contained at least one clinically significant Class 3 error. LLM-processing reduced the proportion of transcript-outputs affected (53% to 30%), amongst 89 clinically significant errors in ASR-output, 51 were resolved, 38 remained significant and 4 were newly introduced. Reference-transcript length significantly increased odds of Class 3 errors for 4 systems (GPT4oTranscribe, Tortus, Amazon-Medical-Transcribe, Dragon-Medical-One; odds ratio 2.65–3.34/additional 100 reference-words). Errors with potential to cause severe harm or death (NHS England Level 3–4) totalled ( n = 53) across systems, concentrated in the domains of medication-type/dose (39.6%), and investigations/laboratory results (30.2%). Performance varied across systems for transcription metrics ( P < 0.001). GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5 (DWER = 3.60%) and Heidi-Health (DWER = 5.67%) performed best for medical terminology; Amazon-Medical-Transcribe worst (DWER = 24.03%). For lexical and semantic similarity GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5 performed best, followed by Heidi-Health. The ASR–LLM pipeline reduced clinically significant errors but did introduce new ones in 3% of transcript-outputs. The safety and effectiveness of these systems in clinical practice requires further evaluation.

papers.title: Self-Replicating Neural Cellular Automata: Quantifying Emergent Phenotypic and Genotypic Diversity in an Open-Ended Substrate
papers.authors: Sanyam Jain, Felix Reimers, Stefano Nichele
papers.abstract: We study an in silico substrate in which every pixel of a two-channel cellular-automata grid carries a tiny neural network (an agent) that senses its Moore neighbourhood. A cell persists only by self-replication: a living neighbour is cloned, and its weights are mutated by a uniform perturbation, so that phenotype (cell state) is driven entirely by genotype (network weights). From a handful of seeded founders, the system grows into a spatially organized ecosystem of coexisting, competing and dominating species. Our main contribution is a battery of coarse-grained diversity metrics that make such growth measurable at two scales: four phenotypic tools based on cellular-type frequency, entropy and cell variance, and two genotypic tools that colour each agent by a hash of its full weight vector versus a sparse random-weight probe. Across a five-fold sweep of 1680 small runs and 24 long (1000-generation, 200 × 200) runs, the substrate is persistent and self-maintaining in 20 of the 24 long configurations and exposes a clear phenotype–genotype diversity trade-off: raising phenotypic diversity collapses genotypic diversity and vice versa. Full-genome hash colouring further reveals lineage structure that a random-weight probe systematically misses.

papers.title: TechBio 3.0 closes the drug discovery loop with multimodal AI and generative chemistry
papers.authors: Krish W. Ramadurai, Abhirup Banerjee
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed molecular prediction and design, yet these advances remain only partially integrated with experimental discovery. We define TechBio 3.0 as an emerging paradigm for closed-loop drug discovery that connects multimodal molecular representations, generative chemistry, and automated experimentation. We examine its early preclinical and clinical evidence, identify remaining technical and translational barriers, and argue that this convergence is beginning to define biotechnology’s next era.

papers.title: SSCHA-based evolutionary crystal structure prediction at finite temperatures with account for quantum nuclear motion
papers.authors: Daniil Poletaev, Artem Oganov
papers.abstract: Abstract Reliable crystal structure prediction (CSP) at finite temperatures, including quantum anharmonic effects, remains challenging but is particularly important for systems containing light atoms such as superconducting hydrides. Here, we integrate machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) to enable evolutionary CSP on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. Using LaH 10 as a test case, we compare three approaches: (i) active-learning MLIPs (AL-MLIPs) trained on the fly, (ii) universal MLIPs (uMLIPs), and (iii) temperature-dependent effective potentials (TDEPs) trained on SSCHA ensemble data. AL-MLIPs correctly predict the cubic Fm $$\bar{3}$$ 3 ¯ m phase but require thermodynamic perturbation theory corrections for consistent results. The foundation uMLIP Mattersim-5m enables SSCHA-based CSP without per-structure training, but fine-tuning is required for higher accuracy. Temperature-dependent effective potentials trained on SSCHA data enable accurate and very efficient CSP for large unit cells on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. We demonstrate that quantum anharmonicity simplifies the free-energy landscape and is essential for the correct energy ranking of LaH 10 structures.

papers.title: General-purpose LLMs as constrained crystal composition generators
papers.authors: Hedda Oschinski, Maximilian L. Ach, Konstantin S. Jakob, Christian Carbogno, Karsten Reuter
papers.abstract: Abstract The targeted discovery of inorganic materials remains challenging due to the vastness of compositional design spaces and the high cost of exhaustive screening. Task-specific generative artificial intelligence represents a particularly efficient alternative to screening, yet demands tedious collection of training data before providing real benefit. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently shown tremendous potential for the targeted generation of single, optimal materials compositions without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. However, it is unclear whether LLMs generally pose an advantage compared to specialized generative models, in particular in large design spaces. Here, we demonstrate that such models are capable of covering entire regions of the targeted property space effectively and systematically. Using Elpasolite materials as an established benchmark for generative tasks in large chemical spaces, we find that an iterative prompt-and-response framework is able to recover on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. This performance, driven mainly by iterative in-context learning, surpasses the generative abilities of previous, task-specific models. Our results establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows.

papers.title: A Lightweight Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Concrete Barrier Design
papers.authors: Wanting Wang, Xiye Ma, Yuyang He, Ran Cao
papers.abstract: The design of reinforced concrete (RC) highway barriers is a safety-critical engineering task that requires strict compliance with regulatory provisions, such as the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications. Current engineering practices rely largely on manual, iterative, and experience-driven procedures to satisfy complex material, geometric, and mechanical constraints. Although standalone general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in knowledge representation and text generation, their direct application to structural engineering design remains challenging due to hallucination risks, numerical reasoning errors, and insufficient integration with physics-based analysis. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel "generation-validation-modification" closed-loop framework for AI-assisted automated RC barrier design based on the multi-agent orchestration capability of AutoGen. Unlike standalone LLMs that directly generate design parameters from user prompts, the proposed framework integrates specialized agents for parameter generation, external mechanics-based calculation, target-interval evaluation, deviation diagnosis, and rule-based design modification. The performance of the proposed multi-agent framework (MAF) was evaluated using three barrier testing levels (TL-3, TL-4, and TL-5), including sixty RC barrier designs with different geometric configurations. Three DeepSeek models with different parameter scales, including DeepSeek (DS)-8B, DS-32B, and DS-671B, were investigated. All design results were evaluated according to Section 13 of the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, 10th Edition (2024). The results demonstrate that the proposed agentic framework (MAF-DS-8B) achieves a target-interval compliance rate of 98.3%, whereas the best-performing standalone LLM, DS-32B, achieves only 11.7%. These results highlight the potential of multi-agent architectures to improve the reliability, interpretability, and accessibility of AI-assisted engineering design systems for practical applications. The source code, agent prompts, and representative testing cases are publicly available at the project GitHub repository: https://github.com/MXY820/barrier-design.

papers.title: Reading and Steering Representations of Materials-Science Mechanisms in an Open-Weight Language Model
papers.authors: Markus J. Buehler
papers.abstract: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here, using three open-weight Gemma 4 models (google/gemma-4-E4B-it, google/gemma-4-12B-it, google/gemma-4-31B-it) we identify three experimentally separable signatures of materials-science mechanism information: selective concept readability, relational encoding of qualitative constitutive orientation, and causal, context-dependent control of constrained engineering answers. We combine matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark and causal interventions. In 50 held-out materials descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks, and target-free word sets from both readouts enabled blinded identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark produced mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that this apparent physical organization was equally explained by numerical comparison. We therefore compared otherwise identical prompts in which only the direction of the physical input was reversed, asking whether the resulting hidden-state movement followed the supplied constitutive law. These state transformations ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws, whereas lexical controls were near chance. Bidirectional interventions shifted answer probabilities toward or away from the physically appropriate outcome across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and answer formats. Physical relationships were therefore more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone.

papers.title: Metaphors' journeys across time and genre: tracking the evolution of literary metaphors with temporal embeddings
papers.authors: Veronica Mangiaterra, Chiara Barattieri di San Pietro, Paolo Canal, Valentina Bambini
papers.abstract: Metaphors are a distinctive feature of literary language, yet they remain less studied experimentally than everyday metaphors. Moreover, previous psycholinguistic and computational approaches overlooked the temporal dimension, although many literary metaphors were coined centuries apart from contemporary readers. This study innovatively applies tools from diachronic distributional semantics to assess whether the processing costs of literary metaphors varied over time and genre. Specifically, we used the Word2Vec algorithm and period-specific literary and nonliterary corpora, for a total of 124 million tokens, to generate word embeddings. Using these embeddings, we modeled changes in the semantic similarity between topics and vehicles of 515 19th-century literary metaphors, taking this measure as a proxy for metaphor processing demands. Overall, semantic similarity, and hence metaphor processing demands, remained stable over time. However, genre played a key role: metaphors appeared more difficult (i.e., lower topic-vehicle similarity) in modern literary contexts than in 19th-century literature, but easier (i.e., higher topic-vehicle similarity) in today's nonliterary language (e.g., the web) than in 19th-century nonliterary texts. This pattern was further shaped by semantic features of metaphors' individual terms, such as vector coherence and semantic neighborhood density. Collectively, these findings align with broader linguistic changes in Italian, such as the stylistic simplification of modern literature, which may have increased metaphor processing demands, and the high creativity of the web's language, which seems to render metaphor more accessible.

papers.title: SWT: Self-Supervised Video Object Segmentation via Sliding, Wavelet and Transportation
papers.authors: Zhengtong Zhu, Jiaqing Fan, Hanwen Qian, Fanzhang Li
papers.abstract: Video Object Segmentation (VOS) aims to accurately segment target objects from consecutive video frames and track the changes of the objects in each frame of the video. Conventional VOS methods typically demand substantial quantities of pixel-level labeled video sequences for fully supervised learning, which limits the performance of the model in sparse video scenes, while existing VOS methods have limited adaptability to global changes in objects. Based on this observation, in this paper, we propose self-supervised VOS with Sliding window, Wavelet transform and optimal Transport (SWT), a self-supervised VOS framework entirely trained on static dataset using contrastive learning. Firstly, a rolling sample buffer reuses overlapping groups of independently sampled images across successive updates. Secondly, to address the long-distance modeling difficulty caused by simple convolutional structures, we introduce wavelet transform to expand the receptive field of convolutional kernels, thus improving the model's representational capability. Finally, we incorporate optimal transport to assist the model in finding the globally optimal match between the target across two frames, improving the model's ability to handle non-rigid deformations of objects. SWT only requires training on the COCO dataset once and achieves excellent results on five VOS datasets as well as an additional body part propagation dataset. The code will be released soon at https://github.com/machine928/SWT.git .
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing Communications and Applications

papers.title: Why On-Policy Distillation Sometimes Fails: Vanishing Learning Signals
papers.authors: Lei Zhao, Qichao Zhao, Bowen Zuo, Qishi Zhan
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enables effective capability transfer between language models, yet the mechanisms underlying its failures are not fully understood. Across code generation and mathematical reasoning, OPD with larger-scale teachers exhibits early loss plateaus, with an average final loss reduction of 25.1% after 200 updates, compared with 96.2% for self-RL teachers, obtained by further reinforcement learning (RL) training of the initial student. To understand this difference, we analyze OPD as an idealized continuous-time dynamical system in the small-learning-rate limit. Our training-log diagnostics associate these plateaus with an early decline in a gradient-based learning-signal proxy while substantial loss remains; these measurements do not establish why the underlying gradient weakens. We further prove a local recovery guarantee for teachers sufficiently close to the initial student in a shared parameterization under regularity conditions, offering a conditional explanation for the success of self-RL teachers in our experiments. Across runs with and without loss plateaus, we observe small relative parameter changes (0.025-0.098%) and high similarity between the student's representations before and after OPD (linear CKA $>0.98$ across layers). These observations suggest that limited representation adaptation may contribute to learning-signal collapse, a hypothesis that remains to be tested. Code is available at https://github.com/leizhao7/opd-learning-signals.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Auditing the Quality of Electronic Nursing Records: A Critical Narrative Literature Review
papers.authors: João Gabriel Leal Sousa
papers.abstract: Electronic nursing records contain assessments, interventions, and evaluations that can be examined for documentation quality, but extracting information from a record is different from verifying its clinical accuracy. This critical narrative and thematic review asks which applications, results, and limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in auditing electronic nursing documentation are described in the scientific literature. Targeted scholarly web discovery, primary-source retrieval, and reference checking were completed on October 6, 2026, with a reproducible supplementary PubMed search on October 7, 2026. Twenty-six publications and official documents were retained and classified by their evidentiary role. The synthesis distinguishes direct documentation auditing from terminology mapping, AI-assisted documentation generation, contextual nursing research, and methodological or regulatory guidance. Only one of the 14 retained empirical publications directly evaluated AI-supported quality control of existing nursing documentation. That implementation reported fewer omissions and inconsistencies, although a nonrandomized design and inconsistent reporting limit causal interpretation. Terminology-mapping studies showed configuration-dependent performance and substantial residual errors; scenario-based instrument validation and documentation-generation studies support selected evaluation methods but do not establish comprehensive autonomous auditing. Across the corpus, documentation quality, classifier performance, workload, and patient outcomes require separate endpoints. An author-developed, unvalidated governance workflow is proposed to connect criterion definition, authorized data access, evidence-linked flags, nurse adjudication, and prospective monitoring. The literature supports supervised assistance for bounded audit tasks; it does not establish that AI can independently certify record truth, judge nursing performance, or improve patient safety across institutions. Multicenter validation, clinically weighted error analysis, transparent reference standards, and evaluation of total verification effort remain priorities.

papers.title: Transformer models in cardiovascular medicine: current applications, translational challenges, and future directions
papers.authors: Yang Yan, Gaoxiang Li, Taiwei Chen, Jinchuan Yan, Chen Wang, ...
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, highlighting the need for improved early detection, accurate diagnosis, and personalized therapeutic strategies. With advances in artificial intelligence (AI), Transformer-based models have attracted increasing interest because they can model long-range dependencies, support large-scale pre-training, and integrate heterogeneous data. Originally developed for natural language processing, Transformers have been extended to medical image analysis, physiological signal interpretation, and clinical text mining. In cardiovascular medicine, these models have been applied to electrocardiogram interpretation, cardiac imaging, electronic health record analysis, multimodal data integration, digital-twin development, and large language model-enabled workflows. Although many studies report promising performance, clinical value remains contingent on data quality, external validation, calibration, workflow integration, and trustworthy governance. This narrative review provides a focused overview of Transformer-based models in cardiovascular medicine, critically evaluates their translational limitations, and outlines priorities for clinically useful and responsible cardiovascular AI.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Medicine: Clinical Applications, Performance, and Challenges
papers.authors: Felipe Ferreira de Sousa
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established itself as a significant tool supporting veterinary medicine, with growing applications across various clinical specialties. This study aimed to review the scientific literature on the primary applications of AI in veterinary medicine, highlighting its diagnostic performance, benefits, and challenges for professional practice. A narrative literature review was conducted using articles published between 2019 and 2026, sourced from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar; a total of 43 scientific articles were selected. Evidence demonstrates that machine learning and deep learning algorithms exhibit significant performance in areas such as diagnostic imaging, cardiology, nephrology, clinical pathology, oncology, precision livestock farming, and electronic medical record mining, contributing to greater diagnostic accuracy, early disease detection, and the optimization of clinical processes. However, challenges persist regarding database standardization and validation, regulation, algorithm transparency, ethical considerations, and professional training. It is concluded that AI holds great potential to support veterinary medicine, provided its use is ethical, based on scientific evidence, and integrated with the veterinarian’s clinical judgment.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning With Chaos-Aware Gating Mechanism for Infant Cardiorespiratory Status Prediction via Heart Rate Variability and Bedside Data
papers.authors: Mingjie Li, Rui Liu, Rosemary S.C. Horne, Xiaojun Chang, Flora Y. Wong
papers.abstract: Predicting the cardiorespiratory status of extremely preterm infants using signals from bedside monitors is critical for timely intervention in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), potentially improving long-term outcomes. However, directly adapting existing time series data analysis methods to this task is challenged by the scarcity of neonatal data and the high noise levels inherent to physiological signals in this population. To address these challenges, we propose a novel hybrid neural network that integrates C urriculum L earning and a C haos-aware G ating mechanism, called CLCG. Given the long multivariate physiological sequences, we first apply a sliding-window strategy to segment the data into overlapping windows. For each window, a shared Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) fuses multi-modal signals and extracts localized representations. To increase data diversity and enhance generalization capability, we introduce a curriculum learning-based data augmentation scheme that progressively reduces the number of windows during training. This encourages the model to learn discriminative representations by exposing it to increasingly challenging scenarios with less temporal context. To further mitigate the impact of signal noise and improve temporal modeling, we extract handcrafted features, the Lyapunov exponent, from the heart rate variability (HRV) parameters. These features are incorporated into a novel chaos-aware gate mechanism within the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network.
